questions.q: The physical separation of racial or ethnic groups into different neighborhoods within the same metropolitan area is called:
o: Residential segregation
Correct: groups are physically separated into different neighborhoods.
Gentrification
Gentrification is wealthier newcomers moving in and pushing out longtime residents.
Suburbanization
Suburbanization is people moving from cities out to the suburbs.
Urban renewal
Urban renewal is rebuilding city areas, often by tearing down old housing.
questions.x: This is residential segregation: different racial or ethnic groups living in separate neighborhoods of the same city or metro area. It's a lasting pattern of where people live. In the US it was built up over time by unfair lending (like redlining, when banks refused loans in minority areas), zoning rules and housing choices. Gentrification is the tempting wrong answer because it also reshapes neighborhoods. But gentrification is a process of wealthier newcomers moving in and pushing out the people already there, not the separation pattern itself.

questions.q: A study finds that hazardous waste facilities are disproportionately located in low-income, majority-minority neighborhoods. This pattern is a central concern of which movement?
o: Anti-gentrification organizing
Anti-gentrification is about people being priced out by rising rents, not about pollution.
Environmental justice
Correct: environmental justice is about unfair exposure to pollution by race and income.
Meritocracy advocacy
Meritocracy is about handing out jobs and rewards by talent, not where waste sites go.
Deinstitutionalization
Deinstitutionalization means moving psychiatric patients out of hospitals into the community.
questions.note: Environmental justice = fair distribution of environmental burdens and benefits.
questions.x: This is environmental justice. That movement looks at who ends up living next to pollution, like waste sites, highways and factories, and points out that poor and minority neighborhoods get far more than their fair share. Its goal is to spread environmental harms and benefits fairly. Anti-gentrification is the tempting wrong answer, since it's also about poorer neighborhoods, but its focus is people being pushed out by rising rents, not pollution.

questions.q: Families randomly offered housing vouchers to move to low-poverty neighborhoods have children who later earn more as adults than children in control families. This most directly supports:
o: Social reproduction through cultural capital
The study changed where families lived, not what parents passed on to kids.
Intragenerational mobility of the parents
The outcome was the children's adult earnings, not the parents' careers.
Neighborhood effects on life chances
Correct: randomly changing the neighborhood changed outcomes, so place itself matters.
Reverse causation between income and residence
Random assignment is exactly what rules out reverse causation.
questions.x: This supports neighborhood effects: the idea that where you live shapes how your life turns out. The key is that families were randomly offered the vouchers. Random assignment means chance, not the families, decided who got to move, so the two groups were alike in every other way. That leaves the neighborhood as the main difference, so the higher adult earnings can be credited to place itself. Random assignment also rules out reverse causation, and the outcome measured was the children's earnings, not the parents' careers.

questions.q: A low-wage worker opposes a minimum wage increase because she believes business owners have earned their wealth and should not be burdened. A Marxist would most likely label her view:
o: Class consciousness
Class consciousness would mean seeing her shared interests with other workers. She doesn't.
False consciousness
Correct: she holds beliefs that serve the owning class and work against her own interests.
Relative deprivation
Relative deprivation is unhappiness from comparing yourself to others.
Status inconsistency
Status inconsistency is ranking high on one measure and low on another.
questions.x: A Marxist would call this false consciousness. Marx split society into owners of the means of production (the bourgeoisie, who own factories and businesses) and workers who sell their labor (the proletariat). False consciousness is when workers hold beliefs that help the owners and hurt themselves, usually picked up from the ideas that dominate society. A low-wage worker opposing her own raise to protect owners fits this exactly. Class consciousness is the opposite: workers seeing their shared interests and pushing back against owners.

questions.q: According to Marx, which development is most necessary for the proletariat to move from a 'class in itself' to a 'class for itself'?
o: Workers gaining ownership of capital through steadily higher wages
Higher wages don't give workers ownership of factories or businesses.
Upward intragenerational mobility of individual workers
One worker moving up doesn't create group awareness.
Recognition of shared interests in opposition to the bourgeoisie
Correct: a class for itself sees its shared interests and acts together.
Adoption of bourgeois cultural tastes and manners
Copying upper-class tastes is closer to false consciousness.
questions.note: Class in itself = objective position; class for itself = conscious, organized class.
questions.x: The workers need to recognize their shared interests against the bourgeoisie (the owning class). Marx made a distinction. A class in itself is a group that shares the same spot in the economy, like all wage workers, whether or not they realize it. A class for itself is that same group once it sees its shared interests and organizes to act on them. The bridge between the two is class consciousness. Individual wins, like a raise or a promotion, don't build that group awareness and can even weaken it.

questions.q: Research shows people more often learn about new jobs through casual acquaintances than through close friends. This finding emphasizes the value of:
o: Strong ties within a close, dense personal network
Close friends tend to know the same things the job seeker already knows.
Weak ties that bridge separate networks
Correct: acquaintances link you to other circles and fresh information.
Embodied cultural capital
Embodied cultural capital is skills and manners inside a person, not who you know.
Institutionalized cultural capital
Institutionalized cultural capital is credentials like degrees. That isn't the finding.
questions.note: Granovetter: 'the strength of weak ties.'
questions.x: This shows the value of weak ties that bridge separate networks. It's Granovetter's famous strength of weak ties idea. A strong tie is a close relationship, like family or a best friend. A weak tie is a looser one, like an old coworker or a friend of a friend. Your close friends mostly know the same people and hear the same news you do. Acquaintances move in other circles, so they carry new information, like a job opening you hadn't heard about. Strong ties are great for support; weak ties are better for spreading news.

questions.q: In Bourdieu's framework, a medical degree from a prestigious university is an example of:
o: Embodied cultural capital
Embodied capital lives inside the person: accent, manners, habits.
Objectified cultural capital
Objectified capital is physical cultural goods like art or books.
Institutionalized cultural capital
Correct: a degree is a formal credential that institutions recognize.
Bonding social capital
Bonding social capital is ties inside a close-knit group.
questions.x: A medical degree is institutionalized cultural capital. Cultural capital is the knowledge, skills and tastes that give someone a social edge. Bourdieu split it into three forms. Embodied is what's inside you, like your accent, manners and skills. Objectified is cultural things you own, like books or art. Institutionalized is official credentials that institutions recognize, like degrees and licenses. Embodied is tempting because medical training builds real skills, but the degree itself is the official stamp on those skills.

questions.q: Children of affluent parents tend to attend well-funded schools, earn advanced degrees, and enter high-status jobs, keeping the family's class position across generations. This is best described as:
o: Social reproduction
Correct: social structures pass class position from one generation to the next.
Structural mobility
Structural mobility is movement caused by changes in the economy.
Horizontal mobility
Horizontal mobility is a move to a different position at the same rank.
Exchange mobility
Exchange mobility is some people rising while others fall by the same amount.
questions.x: This is social reproduction: the way a society's structures pass class position down from parents to children. Well-funded schools, family wealth, connections and cultural know-how help affluent kids end up affluent too. The key clue is that nothing changes; the family keeps the same spot across generations. Structural mobility is the tempting wrong answer, but it describes people moving up or down because the economy changed, not staying put. When a question describes no change in rank, mobility terms are distractors.

questions.q: A sociologist argues that schools reward the speech patterns and behaviors of upper-middle-class children, so grades partly reflect home background rather than ability. This argument is most consistent with:
o: The functionalist view of schools as meritocratic sorting
Functionalists say schools sort fairly by merit. This argument denies that.
Bourdieu's theory of social reproduction
Correct: schools treat class-based habits as merit, which keeps inequality going.
Weber's theory of bureaucracy
Weber's bureaucracy is about formal rules and organization, not class bias.
Durkheim's concept of mechanical solidarity
Mechanical solidarity is unity from sameness in simple societies.
questions.x: This fits Bourdieu's theory of social reproduction. Bourdieu said that schools reward the cultural capital of the upper classes, meaning their way of talking, behaving and acting in class. Kids from those homes already match the school's style, and teachers read that as talent. So grades partly reflect home background, but they get presented as merit, and inequality gets passed down. The functionalist view is tempting because it also talks about schools sorting students, but it says the sorting is by real ability, which this argument rejects.

questions.q: Which finding would most strongly challenge the claim that a society is a meritocracy?
o: High-achieving students earn more as adults than low-achieving students
High achievers earning more is exactly what a meritocracy predicts.
Occupations requiring longer training tend to pay more
Longer training leading to higher pay fits rewards following effort and skill.
Parental income predicts children's adult earnings better than their test scores do
Correct: inherited position beating ability goes against meritocracy.
Most citizens believe that hard work leads to success
Believing in meritocracy isn't evidence of how rewards are really given.
questions.x: A meritocracy is a system where rewards like jobs and pay go to people based on talent and effort. If that's true, a child's own ability, like test scores, should predict their adult earnings better than anything they were born into. So if parents' income predicts kids' earnings better than the kids' own test scores do, inherited advantage is winning over ability. That challenges the meritocracy claim. Lots of people believing hard work pays off is tempting, but a belief doesn't show how rewards are actually handed out.

questions.q: A respected member of the clergy has high prestige but a low income. In Weber's multidimensional model, this is an example of:
o: Downward mobility
Nothing here describes a drop in position over time.
False consciousness
False consciousness is Marx's idea about beliefs that work against your own class.
Status inconsistency
Correct: high on one dimension, prestige, and low on another, income.
Horizontal mobility
Horizontal mobility means moving to a position of similar rank. No move is described.
questions.x: This is status inconsistency. Weber said social standing has three separate parts: class (wealth and income), status (prestige, or how respected you are) and power (being able to get your way). Because they're separate, a person can rank high on one and low on another. A respected clergy member with a low income is high on prestige and low on income, so the ranks don't match. Downward mobility is tempting because of the low income, but mobility means a change in position over time, and none is described.

questions.q: Researchers studying maternal health outcomes want to test an intersectional hypothesis about race and income. Which analysis is most appropriate?
o: Comparing outcomes by race alone
Race alone ignores how income changes race's effect.
Testing a race-by-income interaction
Correct: an interaction tests whether one factor's effect depends on the other.
Comparing outcomes by income while controlling for race
Controlling treats race and income as simply adding up, not combining.
Reporting only the overall national outcome rate
One overall rate hides every group difference.
questions.note: Intersectionality maps onto interaction effects, not simple main effects.
questions.x: Test for a statistical interaction between race and income. Intersectionality says identities like race and income overlap and combine to create effects you can't get by just adding them up. For example, being Black and low-income might affect maternal health more than you'd predict from race alone plus income alone. A statistical interaction tests exactly that: whether the effect of one factor depends on the level of the other. Controlling for race is tempting, but it assumes the effects simply add, which is the very idea intersectionality challenges.

questions.q: Between 1900 and 1960, many children of farmers moved into factory and office jobs because farm employment shrank while industrial jobs expanded. This is primarily:
o: Exchange mobility
Exchange mobility assumes a fixed set of positions with balancing moves.
Horizontal mobility
This shift changed income and job rank for many, so it isn't a same-rank move.
Structural mobility
Correct: changes in the economy itself drove large-scale movement.
Social reproduction
Social reproduction is class staying the same, not changing.
questions.x: This is structural mobility: people moving because the economy itself changed. Between 1900 and 1960, farm jobs shrank and factory and office jobs grew. That shift pushed huge numbers of farmers' kids into new kinds of work, whatever their individual effort. Exchange mobility is the tempting wrong answer, but it assumes the number of positions at each level stays fixed, with some people rising and others falling to match. Here the job structure itself changed.

questions.q: In a society with a fixed number of positions at each class level, some individuals rise while an equal number fall. This pattern is called:
o: Structural mobility
Structural mobility needs the number of positions to change.
Horizontal mobility
These moves change rank, so they're vertical, not horizontal.
Social reproduction
People are changing positions, so class isn't simply passed down.
Exchange mobility
Correct: balancing up and down moves within a structure that stays the same.
questions.x: This is exchange mobility. When the number of positions at each class level stays fixed, the only way someone can move up is if someone else moves down. People trade places. That's why exchange mobility tells you how open a society is, not whether it's growing. Structural mobility is the tempting alternative, but it needs the structure itself to change, like more professional jobs opening up. The phrase fixed number of positions is your signal for exchange.

questions.q: Cross-national data show that countries with greater income inequality tend to have stronger correlations between parents' and children's earnings. Higher inequality is therefore associated with:
o: Greater intergenerational mobility
A stronger parent-child earnings link means less mobility, not more.
Lower intergenerational mobility
Correct: earnings carry over more strongly from one generation to the next.
No relationship to intergenerational mobility
The data show a clear link between inequality and the correlation.
Greater horizontal mobility
Earnings correlations measure moving up or down, not sideways moves.
questions.note: A stronger parent-child correlation means less mobility.
questions.x: Higher inequality goes with lower intergenerational mobility. Intergenerational mobility is how much children's class position differs from their parents'. A strong correlation between parents' and children's earnings means you can predict a kid's income pretty well from their parents' income. That means not much movement between generations, so mobility is low. This pattern, where more unequal countries have less mobility, is called the Great Gatsby curve. Picking greater mobility comes from reading a strong link as more movement, when it means less.

questions.q: A researcher argues that persistent poverty results mainly from a lack of local jobs, underfunded schools, and discriminatory lending rather than from values held by the poor. This view rejects:
o: Structural explanations of poverty
Her view is a structural explanation, so she holds it rather than rejecting it.
Conflict theory
Conflict theory fits her focus on structural barriers.
The culture of poverty thesis
Correct: that thesis blames poverty on values of the poor, which she denies.
The concept of relative poverty
Her argument is about causes, not how poverty is defined.
questions.x: Her view rejects the culture of poverty thesis. That thesis says poverty lasts because poor people develop values and habits, like feeling there's no point in trying, that they then pass on to their kids. Structural explanations point instead to the system: few local jobs, underfunded schools and discrimination like unfair lending. The researcher blames those structural things, so her view is itself structural. Picking structural explanations is the trap: that's the view she holds, not the one she rejects.

questions.q: A study finds that low income predicts poor health. A critic argues instead that chronic illness causes people to lose jobs and fall into lower income brackets. The critic is proposing:
o: The social causation hypothesis
Social causation says low SES causes poor health, which is the original claim.
Intersectionality
The argument isn't about overlapping identities.
The health selection (social drift) hypothesis
Correct: poor health leads to falling income, the reverse of the original claim.
Fundamental cause theory
Fundamental cause theory says SES causes health, not the other way around.
questions.x: The critic is proposing health selection, also called social drift. The original study suggests social causation: low socioeconomic status (SES, a mix of income, education and job) causes poor health. The critic flips the arrow: chronic illness makes people lose jobs and slide down to lower incomes. That's health selection. Fundamental cause theory is tempting because it sounds deep, but it's a social causation idea. It explains why low SES keeps causing poor health, not the reverse.

questions.q: Researchers want to test whether low income causes poor health rather than the reverse. Which design provides the strongest causal evidence?
o: A cross-sectional survey of income and health
It measures both at one moment, so you can't tell which came first.
A case-control study of hospitalized patients
Starting from sick patients can't rule out illness causing income loss.
Correlating county income with county mortality
County-level links can't prove what's happening to individual people.
Randomly assigning families to receive an income supplement and tracking health
Correct: randomly assigning income isolates its effect on health.
questions.x: The strongest design is randomly giving some families an income supplement and tracking their health. To show that one thing causes another, you change the suspected cause yourself and see what follows. Random assignment makes the groups alike in every other way, and it fixes the order: the money comes first, then you watch health. So any later difference in health can be credited to income. Surveys and other observational studies only watch, so they can't rule out illness lowering income, or some other factor causing both.

questions.q: Despite lower average SES, Hispanic Americans have life expectancy similar to or higher than that of non-Hispanic white Americans. This finding is known as:
o: The gender health paradox
The gender health paradox is about women, not ethnicity.
The social gradient in health
The social gradient predicts worse health with lower SES, the opposite of this.
The Hispanic (Latino) paradox
Correct: better-than-expected health given lower average SES.
Reverse causation
No question of which causes which is being raised here.
questions.x: This is the Hispanic, or Latino, paradox. Socioeconomic status (SES) means a mix of income, education and job, and usually lower SES goes with worse health and shorter lives. The surprise is that Hispanic Americans, who on average have lower SES, live about as long as or longer than non-Hispanic white Americans. Suggested reasons include strong family and community ties and the fact that healthier people are more likely to migrate. The social gradient is tempting, but it predicts the opposite of this finding.

questions.q: Mid-20th-century federal maps rated minority neighborhoods as high-risk, denying residents mortgages. Today those neighborhoods still have lower home values and more heat-related illness. This illustrates:
o: Individual prejudice that ended with the policy
The effects lasted long after the maps stopped being used.
Institutional discrimination with long-term spatial effects
Correct: redlining was policy-based, and its harms stay in those places.
Voluntary self-segregation by residents
Residents were denied loans. They weren't choosing freely.
Horizontal mobility of homeowners
No sideways move between positions is described.
questions.note: Redlining shows how past policy shapes present health by place.
questions.x: This shows institutional discrimination with long-term effects tied to place. Institutional discrimination is unfair treatment built into the rules of organizations like governments and banks, even if no single person acts out of hate. Redlining was exactly that: official maps marked minority neighborhoods as risky, so residents couldn't get mortgages. Since a home is most families' main source of wealth, the harm lasted. Those neighborhoods still have lower home values, and with less investment and fewer trees, they run hotter. It's not individual prejudice, because the harm came from policy and outlasted the maps.

questions.q: William Julius Wilson argued that the loss of manufacturing jobs and the departure of middle-class families from inner-city neighborhoods produced:
o: Rapid gentrification of those neighborhoods
Wilson described jobs and families leaving, not wealthier people moving in.
Increased exchange mobility
Wilson described people stuck in place, not people trading places.
Concentrated poverty and social isolation
Correct: jobless, cut-off neighborhoods with few supports left.
The end of residential segregation
Segregation didn't end. Poverty got more concentrated within it.
questions.x: Wilson argued this produced concentrated poverty and social isolation. In his book The Truly Disadvantaged, he described deindustrialization, meaning factories closing and stable jobs disappearing, along with middle-class families moving out of inner cities. The people left behind were in neighborhoods where joblessness and poverty were packed together, with few stable institutions and few role models with steady work. They were cut off from jobs and networks outside. Gentrification is the opposite story: wealthier people moving in, not jobs and families leaving.

questions.q: Residents of high-poverty neighborhoods have higher asthma rates. A researcher wants to show that the neighborhood itself, not individual income, drives this. Which comparison is most useful?
o: High- and low-income residents within a single neighborhood
This changes income and holds the neighborhood steady, which tests the wrong factor.
Residents' beliefs about the causes of asthma
Beliefs about asthma don't separate the neighborhood's effect from income's.
Asthma rates measured only in high-poverty areas
With no comparison group, you can't isolate any effect.
People of similar income living in neighborhoods with different poverty levels
Correct: holding income steady isolates the neighborhood's effect.
questions.x: Compare people with similar incomes who live in neighborhoods with different poverty levels. To test whether one factor causes an outcome, you hold other possible causes steady and change only the one you care about. Here, individual income is held steady and neighborhood poverty varies. If similar-income people still have different asthma rates depending on where they live, the neighborhood itself matters, maybe through air quality or mold in housing. Comparing rich and poor people within one neighborhood is tempting, but it does the reverse: it holds the neighborhood steady and changes income.

questions.q: A neighborhood where immigrants of one ethnicity cluster together and maintain their own businesses and institutions is called:
o: A ghetto
A ghetto means forced segregation, often with concentrated poverty.
An ethnic enclave
Correct: an ethnic community clustered together with its own economy and institutions.
A food desert
A food desert is an area without easy access to healthy food.
A gated community
A gated community is a walled-off neighborhood, often wealthy.
questions.x: This is an ethnic enclave: a neighborhood where people of one ethnic group, often immigrants, choose to live close together and run their own shops, services and organizations. Think Chinatown or Little Italy. These neighborhoods can help newcomers find jobs, speak their own language and get support. A ghetto is the tempting alternative, but that word means people were forced to live there through segregation, often with concentrated poverty. The clue here is the group's own businesses and institutions.

questions.q: Which observation most directly undermines the Davis-Moore thesis?
o: Surgeons earn more than cashiers
This fits Davis-Moore, since surgery is important and demanding.
Many essential jobs pay little, while heirs gain wealth without filling any role
Correct: rewards here don't follow how important a job is or how rare the talent is.
Jobs requiring longer training tend to pay more
This supports the thesis: long training is supposed to be rewarded.
Wages for scarce skills rise when demand increases
This fits the thesis: scarce skills should earn more.
questions.x: The Davis-Moore thesis is a functionalist idea. It says inequality exists so the most important jobs, the ones that need rare talent and long training, get filled by the most qualified people. So pay should follow how important a job is and how scarce the talent is. Essential workers earning little, and heirs getting rich without doing any job at all, show rewards that don't follow importance or talent. That breaks the prediction. Surgeons out-earning cashiers feels like a challenge, but it actually fits the thesis.

questions.q: Despite rising average incomes, workers report greater dissatisfaction after learning that executive pay has grown much faster than their own. This is best explained by:
o: Absolute poverty
Their incomes are rising and basic needs are met, so this isn't absolute poverty.
Relative deprivation
Correct: unhappiness comes from comparing themselves to a group doing better.
False consciousness
They see the inequality clearly, so they aren't missing their own interests.
Downward mobility
Their incomes rose, so they didn't move down.
questions.x: This is relative deprivation: feeling worse off because you compare yourself to another group, not because you're actually going without. These workers' pay is going up, so their basic needs are met. But they're comparing themselves to executives, whose pay is growing much faster, and that comparison makes them unhappy. Absolute poverty is ruled out because it means lacking basic needs like food and shelter. And it isn't downward mobility, because their incomes rose.

questions.q: An immigrant community's tight mutual-aid networks help members survive hardship but rarely connect them to jobs outside the community. This describes:
o: Strong bonding social capital with limited bridging social capital
Correct: close inward ties give support but don't link members outward.
Strong bridging social capital
Bridging capital links people across groups, and that's what's missing here.
Institutionalized cultural capital
Institutionalized cultural capital is credentials like degrees, not networks.
Objectified cultural capital
Objectified cultural capital is cultural things you own, like books or art.
questions.x: This is strong bonding social capital with weak bridging social capital. Social capital is the value you get from your relationships. Bonding capital is close ties inside a similar group, like family and neighbors, and it gives support when times are hard. Bridging capital is looser ties that link you to different groups, and it's how people hear about jobs and chances outside their own circle. This community has plenty of support inside but few links outward. Bridging capital is tempting, but outside connections are exactly what's missing.

questions.q: A study finds that women earn less than men on average, but the gap shrinks substantially after controlling for occupation. This suggests that part of the gap reflects:
o: Occupational segregation by gender
Correct: men and women are concentrated in jobs that pay differently.
Differences in intelligence
The data say nothing about intelligence. Occupation explains the shrinking.
Purely random variation
A gap that changes when you add a control is a real pattern, not noise.
Women's higher educational attainment
More education would predict higher pay, not lower.
questions.x: Part of the gap reflects occupational segregation by gender: men and women working in different kinds of jobs that pay differently. Controlling for a variable means comparing people who are the same on it. Here, that means comparing men and women in the same occupation. If the pay gap shrinks a lot when you do that, then occupation explains part of the gap. Random variation is ruled out, because noise wouldn't shrink in a consistent way when you add a control. And since some gap remains, other factors are still at work too.

questions.q: Sociologists note that SES stays linked to mortality even as the leading causes of death change, because money, knowledge, and connections help people avoid whatever risks are current. This idea is:
o: The health selection hypothesis
Health selection says illness causes low SES, the reverse direction.
The culture of poverty thesis
The culture of poverty thesis blames poverty on the values of the poor.
Fundamental cause theory
Correct: SES works through flexible resources, so its link to health lasts.
The demographic transition model
That model describes birth and death rates changing as countries develop.
questions.x: This is fundamental cause theory, from the sociologists Link and Phelan. Socioeconomic status (SES), a mix of income, education and job, gives people flexible resources: money, knowledge, power and connections. Those can be used against whatever the main health risks are at the time. A century ago it might be infections; today it's heart disease. The diseases change, but people with more resources keep finding ways around them, so SES stays linked to death rates. Health selection is tempting, but it flips the arrow: it says illness causes low SES.

questions.q: A study finds that residents of racially segregated neighborhoods have higher rates of hypertension. Which unmeasured variable would most threaten the conclusion that segregation causes hypertension?
o: The total number of neighborhoods studied
The number of neighborhoods affects how precise the results are, not confounding.
Whether all blood pressures were measured in the morning
Measuring everyone the same way can't create a difference between groups.
Residents' individual household income
Correct: income could drive both where people live and their blood pressure.
The sex of the interviewers, held constant across sites
A factor held constant across all sites can't explain a difference between them.
questions.note: A confounder must relate to both the exposure and the outcome.
questions.x: Household income is the biggest threat. A confounder is a third variable that's linked to both the exposure (living in a segregated neighborhood) and the outcome (high blood pressure). It can make a link look causal when it isn't. Income affects where people can afford to live, and it also affects blood pressure through stress, diet and access to care. So income alone could create the link. Things held the same for everyone, like when blood pressure was measured or who did the interviews, can't confound, because they don't differ between groups.

questions.q: Adults who grew up poor but became affluent have better health than those who stayed poor, but worse health than those affluent throughout life. This pattern suggests that:
o: Health reflects cumulative SES exposure across the life course
Correct: both childhood and adult SES add to health.
Only childhood SES affects adult health
If only childhood mattered, upward movers would match those who stayed poor.
Only current SES affects adult health
If only current SES mattered, upward movers would match the always-affluent.
Upward mobility itself damages health
Upward movers were healthier than those who stayed poor, so moving up didn't hurt.
questions.x: This suggests health builds up from SES across your whole life. That's the life course perspective: advantage and disadvantage add up from childhood on. People who grew up poor and became affluent land in the middle, healthier than the always-poor but less healthy than the always-affluent. If only current SES mattered, they'd match the always-affluent. If only childhood SES mattered, they'd match the always-poor. Landing in between means both periods count.

questions.q: In the U.S., the median white household holds several times the wealth of the median Black household, a gap much larger than the income gap. What best explains why the wealth gap exceeds the income gap?
o: Differences in current hourly wages alone
Wage differences alone would make the wealth gap about the same as the income gap.
Differences in average household size
Household size doesn't explain how much a family builds up in assets.
Historical exclusion from homeownership, compounded by inheritance across generations
Correct: wealth builds up and gets passed down, so past exclusion keeps compounding.
Differences in educational attainment alone
Education mainly affects earnings, so it would show up in income more than wealth.
questions.x: Income is the money you earn over a period, like a year. Wealth is everything you own minus what you owe, like home equity and savings. The key difference: wealth builds up over time and can be passed down through inheritance and gifts. Black families were historically shut out of homeownership through things like redlining and denied home loans, and homes are the main way most families build wealth. That missing wealth was never passed down, so the gap keeps compounding across generations. Differences in current wages alone would make the wealth gap about as big as the income gap, not much bigger.

questions.q: Children of college graduates are more likely to finish college than other children, even when comparing children with equal test scores and equal family income. This persistence most likely reflects transmission of:
o: Economic capital
Family income was held equal, so money can't explain the gap.
Absolute poverty
Nothing here describes people lacking basic needs.
Horizontal mobility
Horizontal mobility is a sideways move, not an inherited advantage.
Cultural capital
Correct: parents' know-how about college passes to their kids, beyond money.
questions.x: This reflects cultural capital. When children have equal test scores and equal family income, money and measured ability can't explain why college graduates' kids still finish college more often. What's left is cultural capital, a term from Pierre Bourdieu: the know-how, habits and expectations that help people get ahead. Parents who went to college know how applications work, how to pick classes and how to talk to professors, and they expect their kids to finish. Economic capital is tempting, because educated parents often earn more, but income was held equal.

questions.q: Over 20 years, a country's GDP doubles and the share of people below a fixed subsistence income falls, while the gap between rich and poor widens. Which statement is correct?
o: Both absolute and relative poverty decreased
A widening gap means relative poverty didn't necessarily fall.
Absolute poverty rose while relative poverty fell
Fewer people are below the fixed line, so absolute poverty fell, not rose.
Absolute poverty fell while relative poverty may have risen
Correct: fewer people below the fixed line, but a bigger gap from typical living standards.
Neither form of poverty changed
Fewer people below the fixed line means absolute poverty did change.
questions.x: Absolute poverty fell, while relative poverty may have risen. Absolute poverty is measured against a fixed line, the income needed for basic needs like food and shelter. Fewer people are below that line now, so absolute poverty fell. Relative poverty is measured against what's typical in that society: having much less than most people around you. If the gap between rich and poor widened, the poor may be falling further behind the typical standard, so relative poverty may have gone up. Saying both fell is tempting because the economy grew, but growth alone doesn't close the gap.

questions.q: A metropolitan measure shows that 70% of Black residents would need to move to different neighborhoods for Black and white residents to be evenly distributed. This statistic is the:
o: Gini coefficient
The Gini coefficient measures income inequality, not where groups live.
Index of dissimilarity
Correct: the share of a group that would need to move for an even spread.
Poverty threshold
A poverty threshold is an income cutoff that defines who's poor.
Social distance scale
A social distance scale measures willingness to interact with other groups.
questions.x: This is the index of dissimilarity, a way to measure residential segregation. It tells you what percentage of one group would have to move to a different neighborhood so that every neighborhood has the same mix as the whole metro area. Scores near 0 mean groups are evenly mixed; scores near 100 mean they're completely separated. So 70% means a lot of segregation. The Gini coefficient is tempting because it also measures how unevenly something is spread, but it measures income, not where people live.

questions.q: The observation that the availability of good medical care tends to vary inversely with the needs of the population served is known as the:
o: Social gradient in health
The social gradient links health outcomes to SES, not care availability.
Hispanic paradox
The Hispanic paradox is about Hispanic Americans' better-than-expected health.
Inverse care law
Correct: the people who need care most often get the least.
Fundamental cause theory
Fundamental cause theory links SES to health through flexible resources.
questions.x: This is the inverse care law, described by the British doctor Julian Tudor Hart. Inverse means opposite: as a community's need for medical care goes up, the good care available to it tends to go down. Poorer, sicker communities often have the fewest doctors and clinics. The social gradient is tempting because it also links disadvantage and health, but it describes health outcomes (lower SES, worse health), not how much care is available.

questions.q: A sociologist argues that believing success depends only on hard work leads people to blame the poor for their poverty, which legitimizes inequality. This argument treats meritocratic belief as:
o: A functional source of social solidarity across classes
That's a functionalist take, not this critique.
Evidence of high actual mobility
Believing in mobility isn't a measure of how much mobility there really is.
An ideology that legitimizes existing inequality
Correct: a conflict view of meritocracy as a justification for inequality.
A form of institutionalized cultural capital
Institutionalized cultural capital is credentials, not beliefs.
questions.x: The argument treats meritocratic belief as an ideology that legitimizes inequality. In conflict theory, society is shaped by groups competing for power and resources, and an ideology is a set of beliefs that makes the current setup look fair and deserved. If people believe success depends only on hard work, they'll assume the poor just didn't try, and they'll accept inequality instead of challenging it. The functionalist answer is tempting, but a functionalist would say shared beliefs hold society together, not that they justify unfairness.

questions.q: What is the absolute threshold of a sensory system?
o: The smallest change in stimulus intensity that can be reliably noticed
That's the difference threshold (JND): the smallest change you can notice, not the weakest thing you can notice.
The intensity at which a stimulus becomes painful
That's the pain threshold, a separate idea.
The minimum stimulus intensity detected 50% of the time
Correct: the absolute threshold is the weakest intensity detected on half the trials.
The stimulus intensity detected on 100% of trials
Near threshold nothing is caught every time, so the line is drawn at 50%.
questions.note: Absolute threshold = 50% detection of a stimulus vs. no stimulus.
questions.x: The absolute threshold is the weakest stimulus you can detect half the time, so 50% of trials. Why half and not every time? Near that faint level, your nervous system has random background activity (noise) that goes up and down. So the same faint light or sound gets noticed on some tries and missed on others. Researchers pick the 50% point as the line. Don't mix this up with the difference threshold (the JND), which is the smallest change between two stimuli that you can notice.

questions.q: Weight discrimination has a Weber fraction of about 0.02, and brightness about 0.08. What does this imply?
o: Brightness is discriminated more precisely than weight
Backwards. Brightness needs an 8% change, weight only 2%, so brightness is the less precise one.
Smaller proportional changes are detected for weight
Correct: weight needs just a 2% change to notice; brightness needs 8%.
Weight has a lower absolute threshold than brightness
Weber fractions are about noticing changes, not about the weakest thing you can detect.
Brightness adapts more slowly than weight
Weber fractions say nothing about how fast a sense adapts.
questions.note: Smaller Weber fraction = more sensitive to relative change.
questions.x: A Weber fraction tells you how big a change has to be, compared with what you started with, before you notice it. Formula: Weber fraction = JND ÷ I, where JND is the smallest noticeable change and I is the starting intensity. Weight's fraction is 0.02, which is 0.02 × 100 = 2%. Brightness is 0.08, which is 0.08 × 100 = 8%. So you notice a 2% change in weight but need an 8% change in brightness. The smaller fraction means sharper judgment, so weight wins. A bigger number does not mean better.

questions.q: A radiologist is told that missing a tumor will lead to a lawsuit, so she flags more ambiguous scans. In signal detection terms, what changed?
o: Her sensitivity (d′) increased
Fear of a lawsuit doesn't make her better at seeing tumors, so sensitivity stays the same.
Her absolute threshold for light decreased
Nothing about her eyes or light detection changed.
Her criterion became more conservative
A conservative criterion means saying yes less often. She's flagging more, so it's the opposite.
Her response criterion became more liberal
Correct: the cost of missing makes her say yes more easily, a more liberal criterion.
questions.note: Payoffs move the criterion (β); stimulus clarity and skill move d′.
questions.x: Signal detection theory splits a yes/no judgment into two parts. Sensitivity (d′) is how well you can actually tell a real signal from background noise. The response criterion is how much evidence you need before you say yes. Rewards and penalties move the criterion. Here, missing a tumor is costly, so the radiologist says yes on weaker evidence. That's a more liberal criterion: more hits (real tumors flagged) and more false alarms (healthy scans flagged). Her eyes and skill haven't changed, so her d′ hasn't either.

questions.q: Two observers have identical hit rates of 80%, but observer X has a 10% false-alarm rate and observer Y has a 40% false-alarm rate. Which conclusion is best supported?
o: X has greater sensitivity (d′) than Y
Correct: same 80% hits, but X has far fewer false alarms (10% vs 40%).
Y has greater sensitivity than X
Backwards. Y says yes to 40% of noise trials at the same hit rate, so Y is worse.
X and Y have equal sensitivity because hit rates match
Sensitivity needs both hits and false alarms. Equal hits alone don't mean equal sensitivity.
X uses a more liberal criterion than Y
X says yes less often to noise, which points to a stricter criterion, not a looser one.
questions.note: Always compare hits against false alarms; hits alone are meaningless.
questions.x: Sensitivity (d′) is about how well someone tells real signals from noise, and you can only judge it by looking at hits and false alarms together. A hit is saying yes when a signal is there; a false alarm is saying yes when it isn't. A rough check is the gap: hit rate − false-alarm rate. X: 80 − 10 = 70. Y: 80 − 40 = 40. X has the bigger gap, so X discriminates better. Hit rate alone can't show sensitivity, because anyone can raise hits by saying yes to everything.

questions.q: On a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve, an observer performing at chance would produce:
o: A curve bowed sharply toward the upper-left corner of the plot
That bowed shape means lots of hits with few false alarms, which is high sensitivity.
A horizontal line at a 100% hit rate
A flat line at 100% hits would be perfect detection at every criterion.
A diagonal line where hit rate equals false-alarm rate
Correct: with no ability to discriminate, hits and false alarms rise together along the diagonal.
A single point at the origin
Chance covers every criterion, so it makes a whole line, not one point.
questions.note: The farther the ROC bows from the diagonal, the higher d′.
questions.x: An ROC (receiver operating characteristic) curve plots hit rate on the y-axis against false-alarm rate on the x-axis as a person's criterion shifts from strict to loose. If someone can't tell signal from noise at all, saying yes more often raises hits and false alarms by the same amount. That traces the straight diagonal where hit rate equals false-alarm rate, which is chance. The more a curve bows up toward the top-left corner, the better the person is at telling them apart. So a strongly bowed curve means good performance, not chance.

questions.q: In a psychophysics study, subjects detect a faint light on 20%, 50% and 85% of trials at intensities of 2, 4 and 6 units. When subjects are offered a bonus for every correct detection, detection at 4 units rises to 70%. The best interpretation is that:
o: The bonus increased retinal sensitivity to light
Money doesn't change how the eye's light receptors work.
The bonus shifted the response criterion, so the measured threshold is not purely sensory
Correct: the reward shifted the response criterion, so the measured threshold includes decision bias.
The true absolute threshold is now 2 units
The 2-unit level wasn't retested, and the change came from bias, not better senses.
Weber's law does not apply to vision
This study is about detecting a faint light, not about noticing changes, so Weber's law isn't tested.
questions.note: Classical thresholds mix sensitivity and bias; SDT separates them.
questions.x: The bonus made people more willing to say yes, not better at seeing. The older threshold method assumed detection depends only on your senses. But whether you say 'I saw it' also depends on how willing you are to say yes. Rewarding correct detections, with no cost for false alarms (saying yes when nothing is there), makes people more liberal. So detection at 4 units jumped from 50% to 70% while their eyes stayed the same. Signal detection theory was built to separate this decision bias from true sensitivity.

questions.q: Why does visual acuity from rods tend to be lower than from foveal cones?
o: Rods contain no photopigment
Rods do contain a photopigment: rhodopsin.
Rods are located behind the choroid, far from incoming light
Rods are in the retina itself, not behind the choroid.
Many rods converge onto each ganglion cell
Correct: pooling many rods boosts sensitivity but blurs spatial detail.
Rods respond only to long wavelengths
Rods are most sensitive around 500 nm (blue-green), not long wavelengths.
questions.note: Convergence: sensitivity up, acuity down.
questions.x: The reason is convergence: many rods send their signals into a single ganglion cell (the retinal neuron that carries signals toward the brain). Adding up many rods lets weak light signals pile up, so rods are great in dim light. But the brain can't tell which of those rods was hit, so fine detail gets blurred. Cones in the fovea (the center of the retina) each have an almost private line to a ganglion cell, which keeps detail sharp. Rods do have a pigment, rhodopsin, so that's not the reason.

questions.q: In darkness, a rod photoreceptor is depolarized. Which event directly causes it to hyperpolarize when light arrives?
o: Opening of voltage-gated Na⁺ channels
Light makes the rod hyperpolarize, so Na⁺ entry falls, not rises.
Closure of cGMP-gated Na⁺ channels
Correct: PDE breaks down cGMP, the cGMP-gated Na⁺ channels close, and the dark current stops.
Increased glutamate release onto bipolar cells
Glutamate release goes down when rods hyperpolarize, and it's a result, not the cause.
Conversion of all-trans-retinal to 11-cis-retinal
Light does the reverse: it turns 11-cis-retinal into all-trans-retinal.
questions.note: Light → less cGMP → channels close → hyperpolarize → less glutamate.
questions.x: Photoreceptors work backwards from most neurons. In the dark, a rod has lots of cGMP (a small signaling molecule) that holds Na⁺ channels open. Na⁺ flows in, keeping the rod depolarized (less negative inside). This is called the dark current. When light hits, rhodopsin turns on a protein called transducin, which turns on the enzyme phosphodiesterase (PDE). PDE breaks down cGMP, the channels close, Na⁺ stops coming in, and the rod hyperpolarizes (becomes more negative). So light shuts a current off.

questions.q: Photoreceptors release less glutamate in light. How does an ON-center bipolar cell respond to light in its receptive field center?
o: It hyperpolarizes because glutamate release decreases
That's what OFF bipolar cells do. ON cells respond the opposite way.
It fires action potentials directly to the thalamus
Bipolar cells use graded signals and pass them to ganglion cells, not the thalamus.
It depolarizes because glutamate had been inhibiting it
Correct: glutamate inhibits ON cells through mGluR6, so less glutamate in light lets them depolarize.
It is unaffected because only ganglion cells sense glutamate
Bipolar cells are the direct targets of photoreceptor glutamate.
questions.note: ON bipolars are inverted by glutamate (sign-inverting synapse).
questions.x: Photoreceptors release glutamate in the dark and less of it in light. Bipolar cells, the next cells in line, come in two types that react to that glutamate in opposite ways. ON bipolar cells have a receptor called mGluR6. When glutamate binds it, channels close and the cell hyperpolarizes, so glutamate holds the ON cell down. Light takes the glutamate away, the brake comes off, and the ON cell depolarizes. OFF bipolar cells are the reverse: glutamate excites them, so they hyperpolarize in light.

questions.q: A patient has a lesion of the optic chiasm that destroys fibers crossing the midline. What visual field loss is expected?
o: Complete blindness in one eye, with the other eye spared
One whole blind eye comes from an optic nerve lesion before the chiasm.
Loss of the temporal (outer) half of both visual fields
Correct: the crossing fibers come from the nasal retinas, which see the outer (temporal) fields.
Loss of the left visual field in both eyes
Losing the left field in both eyes comes from a lesion behind the chiasm, like the right optic tract.
Loss of the nasal half of both visual fields
Nasal fields are seen by temporal retinas, whose fibers don't cross.
questions.note: Nasal retina fibers cross; they see the temporal field.
questions.x: At the optic chiasm (where the two optic nerves meet), only the fibers from the nasal half of each retina cross over. Nasal means the half closest to the nose. The lens flips the image, so the nasal retina actually sees the temporal (outer) part of the visual field. Cut the crossing fibers and you lose the outer half of the view in both eyes. That's called bitemporal hemianopia, and a pituitary tumor pressing on the chiasm is the classic cause. Losing the nasal fields would need damage to the uncrossed fibers instead.

questions.q: Damage to the left optic tract would cause loss of vision in:
o: The entire left eye
Losing one whole eye points to an optic nerve lesion before the chiasm.
The left visual field of both eyes
The left field is handled by the right side of the brain, not the left tract.
The temporal fields of both eyes
Losing both outer fields comes from a lesion at the chiasm.
The right visual field of both eyes
Correct: the left tract carries both eyes' views of the right visual field.
questions.x: After the chiasm, each optic tract carries fibers from both eyes. The left tract holds the left eye's temporal (outer) retina fibers, which never crossed, plus the right eye's nasal (inner) retina fibers, which crossed at the chiasm. Both of those retina halves look at the right side of the world. So damage to the left optic tract wipes out the right visual field in both eyes. That's called right homonymous hemianopia. Losing one entire eye would need a lesion before the chiasm, in that eye's optic nerve.

questions.q: Hubel and Wiesel found that certain cells in primary visual cortex fire maximally to a bar of light at a specific orientation. These cells are best described as:
o: Photoreceptors
Photoreceptors are in the retina and respond to light, not to a bar's angle.
Ganglion cells with center–surround fields
Ganglion cells have round fields that respond to spots, not to angles.
Place cells
Place cells are in the hippocampus and fire for locations, not visual features.
Feature detectors
Correct: these neurons are tuned to specific features like edges, angles and movement.
questions.x: Hubel and Wiesel recorded from single neurons in the visual cortex of cats. They found cells in the primary visual cortex (V1) that fired hardest for a bar of light at one particular angle, like vertical or diagonal. Neurons tuned to a specific feature like this are called feature detectors. Earlier cells in the retina and thalamus work differently: they have round receptive fields that respond to spots of light and don't care about angle. The brain builds up full images by combining many simple features like these.

questions.q: A V1 neuron fires strongly to a vertical bar anywhere within a broad region and fires most when the bar moves rightward. This neuron is best classified as a:
o: Simple cell
Simple cells need the bar in one exact spot. This cell fires anywhere in a wide area.
Rod bipolar cell
Bipolar cells are in the retina and aren't tuned to line angle.
Complex cell
Correct: angle-tuned, fires anywhere in a broad area, and prefers one direction of motion.
Hair cell
Hair cells are sensory cells for hearing and balance, not vision.
questions.x: V1 (the primary visual cortex) has two main kinds of angle-tuned cells. Simple cells respond to a bar at one angle, but only when it falls in one exact spot, because their receptive field has fixed ON and OFF zones. Complex cells still care about the angle, but they respond wherever the bar lands in a bigger area, and many of them like movement in one direction. This neuron fires for a vertical bar anywhere in a broad region and prefers rightward motion. Position doesn't matter and direction does, so it's a complex cell.

questions.q: A patient after a stroke can identify objects by sight but cannot judge whether a car is moving toward or away from her; she sees the world as a series of still frames. Damage to which pathway is most likely?
o: The dorsal 'where/how' stream toward parietal cortex
Correct: motion is handled by the dorsal stream, including area MT.
The ventral 'what' stream projecting toward temporal cortex
She can still recognize objects, so the ventral 'what' stream is working.
The parvocellular layers of the LGN
Parvocellular layers carry color and fine detail; motion runs mainly through magnocellular layers.
The olfactory tract
The olfactory tract carries smell, not vision.
questions.note: Dorsal = where/how/motion; ventral = what/form/color.
questions.x: After the primary visual cortex (V1), vision splits into two streams. The ventral stream runs down to the temporal lobe and answers 'What is it?' The dorsal stream runs up to the parietal lobe and answers 'Where is it and how is it moving?' An area in the dorsal stream called MT (also V5) handles motion. Damage there causes akinetopsia: seeing the world as still frames. She can still name objects, so her ventral stream is fine. Her problem is motion, which points to the dorsal stream.

questions.q: After staring at a red square for 60 seconds and then looking at a white wall, a person sees a green square. Which theory best explains this?
o: Trichromatic theory
Three cone types explain color detection, but not opposite-colored afterimages.
Place theory
Place theory is about hearing pitch, not color.
Gate control theory
Gate control theory is about pain.
Opponent-process theory
Correct: tiring the red side lets the opposite green side take over for a moment.
questions.note: Afterimages = opponent process (red–green, blue–yellow, black–white).
questions.x: Opponent-process theory says that after the cones, color is coded in opposing pairs: red vs. green, blue vs. yellow, and black vs. white. Each pair works like a seesaw. Staring at red for a minute tires out the red side. When you then look at a white wall, the rested green side wins for a moment, so you see a green afterimage. Trichromatic theory (three cone types) explains how color is first detected, but it can't explain why the afterimage is the opposite color.

questions.q: A man cannot distinguish red from green, and genetic testing shows a defect in his M-cone opsin. Why is this condition far more common in males?
o: The S-cone opsin gene is on the Y chromosome
The S-opsin gene is on chromosome 7, not the Y, and this defect is in the M opsin.
The M and L opsin genes are on the X chromosome
Correct: males have only one X, so one faulty copy shows up.
Testosterone gradually damages the cone photoreceptors in the fovea
Red-green color blindness is inherited, not caused by hormones.
Males have fewer rods than females
Rods don't handle color vision at all.
questions.x: The genes for the M and L cone opsins (the light-catching proteins in medium- and long-wavelength cones) sit on the X chromosome. That makes red-green color blindness X-linked recessive. A male has only one X, so if that X carries a faulty copy, there's no backup and he shows the trait. A female has two Xs, so a normal copy on the other X usually covers for the faulty one. The S-cone opsin gene is on a non-sex chromosome (chromosome 7), and its defects cause rarer blue-yellow problems.

questions.q: Shining a light in a patient's left eye constricts the right pupil but not the left. Light in the right eye constricts the right pupil only. Where is the lesion most likely?
o: Left optic nerve (afferent limb)
If the left optic nerve were out, light in the left eye would shrink neither pupil. The right one did shrink.
Left oculomotor nerve (efferent limb)
Correct: both eyes sense light, but the left pupil can never shrink, so its outgoing nerve is damaged.
Right optic nerve
If the right optic nerve were out, light in the right eye would shrink neither pupil.
Right oculomotor nerve
The right pupil shrinks normally, so the right oculomotor nerve works.
questions.note: Afferent = CN II (sensing); efferent = CN III (constricting).
questions.x: The pupil reflex has two parts. The incoming (afferent) part is the optic nerve, cranial nerve II, which senses the light. The outgoing (efferent) part is the oculomotor nerve, cranial nerve III, which squeezes the pupil smaller. Light in either eye normally shrinks both pupils. Here, light in either eye shrinks the right pupil, so both optic nerves are sending their signal fine. The left pupil never shrinks, no matter which eye is lit. So the left pupil's own outgoing nerve, the left CN III, is the broken part.

questions.q: Researchers record from a retinal ganglion cell with an ON-center, OFF-surround receptive field. Which stimulus produces the highest firing rate?
o: A small spot of light filling only the center
Correct: light in the center excites the cell with nothing in the ring holding it back.
Uniform light covering both center and surround
Light on the ring quiets the cell, so full light cancels much of the center's effect.
A ring of light on the surround only
Light only on the ring quiets an ON-center cell, pushing firing below normal.
Complete darkness over the whole field
Darkness gives only the cell's normal background firing.
questions.note: Center–surround cells signal contrast, not overall brightness.
questions.x: A ganglion cell's receptive field is the patch of retina it pays attention to. An ON-center, OFF-surround cell has a middle zone where light excites it and a ring around that where light quiets it. So the best stimulus is a small spot that lights up only the middle: all excitement, no quieting. Light covering everything hits the ring too, and the ring cancels much of the middle's response. This setup means ganglion cells report contrast, like edges, rather than overall brightness.

questions.q: The middle ear amplifies pressure delivered to the oval window mainly because:
o: The cochlear fluid compresses easily
Fluid barely compresses at all, which is why the boost is needed, not how it happens.
The Eustachian tube adds air pressure
The Eustachian tube balances air pressure on both sides of the eardrum. It doesn't amplify.
Hair cells release extra glutamate
Hair cells are in the inner ear and act after the middle ear's mechanical work.
The tympanic membrane is much larger in area than the oval window
Correct: force gathered on the big eardrum lands on the small oval window, so pressure rises.
questions.note: Pressure = force/area: big drum, small window.
questions.x: Sound has to move from air into the fluid of the cochlea, and fluid is much harder to push than air. Without help, most of the sound would bounce off. The middle ear fixes this by focusing force. Pressure is force divided by area: P = F ÷ A. The eardrum (tympanic membrane) is big and collects the force. The ossicles pass that force to the oval window, which is much smaller. The same force on a smaller area gives a bigger pressure. The ossicles' lever action adds a smaller extra boost.

questions.q: Hair cells in the cochlea transduce sound when their stereocilia bend, opening channels that let in:
o: K⁺ from the endolymph, depolarizing the cell
Correct: endolymph is rich in K⁺, so K⁺ flows in and depolarizes the hair cell.
Na⁺ from the perilymph, hyperpolarizing the cell
The stereocilia sit in endolymph, not perilymph, and Na⁺ coming in would depolarize anyway.
Cl⁻ from the endolymph, depolarizing the cell
Cl⁻ isn't the ion that carries this signal. K⁺ is.
Ca²⁺ only, causing hair cell contraction
Ca²⁺ helps with transmitter release later, but the main current is K⁺, and the cell doesn't contract.
questions.note: Unusual: K⁺ flows IN because endolymph is K⁺-rich.
questions.x: Cochlear hair cells have tiny hairs on top called stereocilia, and those hairs sit in a fluid called endolymph. Endolymph is unusual: it's packed with K⁺ and has a positive voltage. When sound bends the stereocilia toward the tallest one, small links between their tips pull channels open. K⁺ rushes into the cell, pushed by that strong gradient, and the cell depolarizes. In most neurons K⁺ flows out, so this inward K⁺ current is the surprise to remember.

questions.q: A worker with years of exposure to loud machinery shows hearing loss mainly at high frequencies. Which explanation is best?
o: The ossicles have fused together
Fused ossicles cause a conductive loss across many pitches, not mainly high ones.
The apical hair cells have been destroyed
Apical hair cells handle low pitches, so losing them hurts low frequencies.
Hair cells near the cochlear base have been damaged
Correct: hair cells at the base handle high pitches and take the most noise damage.
The auditory nerve can no longer fire action potentials
A nerve that can't fire at all would cause deafness at every pitch.
questions.x: The cochlea is tonotopic, meaning each spot along it responds to a different pitch. The base, near the oval window, handles high frequencies. The apex, at the far tip, handles low frequencies. Loud noise hits the base hair cells hardest, so they wear out first. In mammals, lost hair cells don't grow back, so noise damage is permanent. It's a sensorineural loss (a problem with the hair cells or nerve), and it often shows up first around 4000 Hz. Damage at the apex would hurt low pitches instead.

questions.q: Cochlear implants bypass damaged hair cells by stimulating the auditory nerve directly. For an implant to convey different pitches, the electrodes should be arranged:
o: Along the length of the cochlea, with base electrodes for high frequencies
Correct: using the cochlea's pitch map, the place of stimulation tells the brain the pitch.
Together at the apex, varying only stimulus voltage
More voltage changes loudness. One spot can't make different pitches.
On the tympanic membrane
The eardrum is before the damage and doesn't make nerve signals.
In the semicircular canals
Semicircular canals sense head rotation, not sound.
questions.x: The cochlea is tonotopic: each spot along it responds to a different pitch. High frequencies are coded at the base and low frequencies at the apex (the far tip). A cochlear implant uses this. It lays a row of electrodes along the cochlea, and each electrode stimulates the auditory nerve at its own spot. The brain reads the spot as the pitch, so base electrodes give high sounds. Turning up the voltage at one spot just makes that sound louder. It can't change the pitch.

questions.q: A sound source is directly to a listener's right. Which cue lets the brain localize a low-frequency (200 Hz) tone in this position?
o: Interaural intensity difference
Low pitches bend around the head, so there's almost no loudness difference between the ears.
Interaural time difference
Correct: the long wave bends around the head, but it still reaches the near ear first.
Spectral filtering by the pinna
The outer ear's shape mostly helps with up-down and front-back, using high pitches.
The tone's place of vibration on the basilar membrane
Where the basilar membrane vibrates tells you pitch, not direction.
questions.note: Low frequencies: timing; high frequencies: level (head shadow).
questions.x: Your brain finds a sound's direction by comparing your two ears. There are two main cues. Interaural time difference is how much earlier the sound reaches one ear. Interaural intensity difference is how much louder it is at one ear. A 200 Hz sound wave is long, about 1.7 meters, which is much bigger than your head. So it bends around your head and arrives at both ears almost equally loud. What still differs is timing: it reaches the right ear first. So timing is the cue for low pitches.

questions.q: In an experiment, guinea pig outer hair cells are selectively destroyed while inner hair cells are spared. Auditory nerve recordings show reduced sensitivity and broader frequency tuning. What does this suggest?
o: Outer hair cells send most of the afferent signals on to the brain
Inner hair cells send most of the signals to the brain, not outer ones.
Inner hair cells are not needed for hearing
The inner cells were spared and the nerve still responded, so they're doing the sending.
Tuning depends entirely on the ossicles
The ossicles weren't touched, yet tuning changed, so the cochlea shapes tuning too.
Outer hair cells act as cochlear amplifiers that sharpen tuning
Correct: outer hair cells boost and sharpen the basilar membrane's vibration.
questions.x: The cochlea has two kinds of hair cells with different jobs. Inner hair cells are the real sensors: they send most of the signals (about 90 to 95%) up the auditory nerve. Outer hair cells act like tiny motors. They change length when their voltage changes, using a protein called prestin. This pushes on the basilar membrane, the strip that vibrates for each pitch, making quiet sounds bigger and each pitch's peak sharper. Remove the outer cells and signals still go out, but hearing gets less sensitive and less precise, exactly as seen.

questions.q: Two tones differ in frequency but have the same amplitude. A listener reports the 3000 Hz tone as louder than the 100 Hz tone. What best explains this?
o: Loudness depends only on frequency
Too extreme. Amplitude is still the main driver of loudness; frequency only adds to it.
The 100 Hz tone was below the human hearing range
People hear down to about 20 Hz, so 100 Hz is easy to hear.
Human hearing sensitivity varies with frequency, peaking around 2–5 kHz
Correct: the ear is most sensitive around 2000 to 5000 Hz, so 3000 Hz sounds louder.
Higher frequencies always have larger amplitudes
The question says the amplitudes are the same.
questions.x: Loudness depends mostly on amplitude, which is how big the sound wave is. But your ear isn't equally good at every pitch. Frequency is the pitch, measured in hertz (Hz), or cycles per second. Graphs called equal-loudness curves show the ear is most sensitive from about 2000 to 5000 Hz, partly because the ear canal resonates (naturally vibrates) around there. So a 3000 Hz tone sounds louder than a 100 Hz tone with the same amplitude. The 100 Hz tone is still audible, since people hear down to about 20 Hz.

questions.q: After spinning in a chair for 30 seconds and stopping suddenly, a person feels as if spinning in the opposite direction. Why?
o: Otoliths detach and float freely in the canals
Loose crystals cause dizziness when you change head position, not this after-spin feeling.
Endolymph keeps moving after the head stops, deflecting the cupula the opposite way
Correct: the fluid keeps moving after you stop and bends the cupula the opposite way.
The cochlea misinterprets the stop as a loud sound
The cochlea detects sound, not rotation.
The visual cortex adapts to the spinning image
The feeling stays with your eyes closed, so it comes from the inner ear, not vision.
questions.x: The semicircular canals are three fluid-filled loops in your inner ear that sense head rotation. The fluid is called endolymph. When you start spinning, the fluid lags behind and bends the cupula, a jelly flap holding hair cells, and you feel the turn. If you keep spinning steadily, the fluid catches up and the cupula straightens, so the feeling fades. When you stop suddenly, the fluid keeps moving (inertia) and bends the cupula the other way. Your brain reads that as spinning in the opposite direction.

questions.q: A patient with vestibular damage can stand steadily with eyes open but sways and nearly falls when she closes her eyes. What does this reveal?
o: Vision was compensating for lost vestibular input
Correct: vision was covering for the damaged inner ear, and closing her eyes removed that help.
Her visual cortex is the source of the damage
She stands steadily with her eyes open, so her vision works.
Her muscles are too weak to support standing
Weak muscles would make her unsteady with her eyes open too.
Proprioception from the legs is completely absent
Too extreme. She's steady with eyes open, and her known damage is in the inner ear.
questions.note: Balance integrates vestibular, visual and proprioceptive input.
questions.x: Your brain keeps you balanced using three inputs. Vestibular input comes from the inner ear. Visual input is what you see. Proprioception is your sense of where your body parts are, from sensors in muscles and joints. If one is damaged, the other two can cover for it. Her inner ear is damaged, but with her eyes open, vision fills the gap. Close her eyes and only one good input is left, so she sways. Doctors call this a positive Romberg sign. Weak muscles are ruled out, since she'd be unsteady with her eyes open too.

questions.q: A patient has a lesion on the right side of the spinal cord. Fine touch and vibration are lost on the right below the lesion, while pain and temperature are lost on the left. What explains this pattern?
o: Fine touch ascends ipsilaterally in the dorsal columns; pain fibers cross near entry
Correct: touch fibers stay on the same side until the medulla; pain fibers cross right after entering.
Both pathways cross in the medulla
If both crossed in the medulla, both losses would be on the right.
Pain fibers ascend ipsilaterally and touch fibers cross at entry
This flips which pathway crosses early and which crosses late.
The lesion affected only the motor cortex
A brain lesion wouldn't split the losses this way below one spinal level.
questions.note: Dorsal column (DCML): crosses in medulla; spinothalamic: crosses in cord.
questions.x: Two sensory pathways cross to the other side at different places. Fine touch, vibration and proprioception (body position sense) go up the dorsal columns on the same side they entered, and only cross in the medulla, at the base of the brain. So a right-side cord lesion knocks them out on the right. Pain and temperature fibers cross to the other side within a segment or two of entering the cord, then travel up the spinothalamic tract. So the same lesion knocks them out on the left. This split is called Brown-Séquard syndrome.

questions.q: Patients with congenital insensitivity to pain often have repeated injuries and shorter lifespans. This best supports which conclusion?
o: Pain protects by signaling tissue damage
Correct: without pain, people don't notice or avoid injuries.
Pain receptors also mediate fine touch
These patients usually feel touch normally, so touch uses separate receptors.
Pain is purely a learned emotional response
A condition present from birth points to biology, not just learning.
Pain sensitivity has no genetic component
An inherited condition shows pain does have a genetic part.
questions.x: Congenital insensitivity to pain is a rare condition people are born with, often caused by a broken sodium channel called Nav1.7. People with it can't feel burns, broken bones or joint damage, so they keep getting hurt without noticing, and many die young. That shows what pain is for: it's a warning signal that tells you tissue is being damaged so you can stop and protect yourself. Because it's present from birth and inherited, it also shows pain has a biological, genetic basis, not a purely learned one.

questions.q: After a leg amputation, a patient feels pain in the missing foot. Which explanation is best supported by research on phantom limb pain?
o: Nociceptors in the missing foot are still active
The foot and its pain receptors are gone, so they can't fire.
The patient is consciously imagining the pain
Phantom pain is real nerve activity, not something the patient is making up.
Cortical maps reorganize and remaining neurons still generate limb sensations
Correct: the brain's body map reorganizes, and leftover neurons still produce foot sensations.
Pain fibers regrow into the missing limb
There's no limb left for nerves to grow back into.
questions.x: Phantom limb pain is real pain felt in a body part that's gone. It comes from the nervous system, not the missing limb. The somatosensory cortex has a map of the body, with a patch for each part. After an amputation, the patch for that limb doesn't go quiet. Neighboring patches spread into it, and cut nerve endings and spinal circuits keep sending signals. The brain still reads that activity as coming from the missing foot. So it isn't imagined, and it can't come from receptors that no longer exist.

questions.q: Research shows that all taste qualities can be detected across all regions of the tongue. What does this indicate about the classic 'tongue map'?
o: It is inaccurate, because taste receptor cells for each quality are widely distributed
Correct: receptor cells for every taste are spread across the whole tongue.
It is accurate for sweet but not for bitter
Sweet isn't limited to one area either. No taste is.
Taste receptors exist only on the tip of the tongue
Taste buds are all over the tongue, plus the soft palate and throat.
Taste is determined entirely by smell
Smell adds to flavor, but taste receptors detect the basic tastes on their own.
questions.x: The old 'tongue map', with sweet on the tip and bitter at the back, came from a misread study. In reality, taste buds holding receptor cells for all five tastes (sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami, a savory taste) are spread across the whole tongue. They're also on the soft palate and in the throat. Some spots are a little more sensitive to certain tastes, but the differences are small. No taste is limited to one region, so the classic map is just wrong.

questions.q: Humans have about 400 types of odorant receptors yet can distinguish thousands of odors. What is the best explanation?
o: Each receptor type responds to only one odor
One receptor per odor would let you tell only about 400 odors apart.
The olfactory bulb creates new receptors for each new smell
Receptor types are set by your genes; the bulb doesn't build new ones.
Odor identity is coded by sniff strength
How hard you sniff changes how strong a smell seems, not which smell it is.
Each odor activates a unique combination of receptor types
Correct: each odor turns on its own mix of receptor types, giving far more codes than receptors.
questions.note: Combinatorial coding: patterns, not single labeled receptors.
