questions.x: Smell uses combinatorial coding: each odor is recognized by the pattern of receptor types it turns on. Most odor molecules bind to several receptor types, and each receptor type responds to several odors. So an odor isn't tied to one dedicated receptor. With about 400 receptor types, the number of possible combinations is enormous, far more than 400. That's how you can tell thousands of odors apart. It's the same reason 26 letters can spell a huge number of words.

questions.q: Mice with a knocked-out gene essential for vomeronasal organ signaling fail to distinguish males from females and court both sexes. This supports which conclusion?
o: The main olfactory epithelium is needed for all mouse social behavior
Only the vomeronasal system was changed, so this can't show anything about the main smell lining.
Vomeronasal pheromone detection helps mice identify sex
Correct: removing VNO signaling took away the mice's ability to tell the sexes apart.
Vision is the main cue mice use to identify sex
Only the chemical sense was changed; vision wasn't tested.
Pheromones have no role in mammals
The results show pheromones clearly do matter in these mammals.
questions.x: Pheromones are chemical signals one animal gives off that change the behavior of another animal of the same species. Many animals detect them with the vomeronasal organ (VNO), a small sensor in the nose that's separate from the main smell lining. Here, scientists knocked out (removed) a gene the VNO needs to work, and left the other senses alone. Those mice couldn't tell males from females and courted both. So VNO pheromone detection helps mice figure out another mouse's sex. Since vision wasn't changed, the study says nothing about vision being the main cue.

questions.q: In a study, subjects rate a constant odor's intensity every 30 seconds. Ratings drop steadily over 5 minutes, but a novel odor introduced at minute 5 is rated as strong. What best explains the results?
o: Adaptation was specific to the first odor
Correct: only the unchanging odor faded, while a new odor still came through strong.
General loss of olfactory function over time
A general loss of smell would make the new odor seem weak too.
The constant odor's concentration dropped
The question says the odor stayed constant.
Subjects habituated to all smells equally
If all smells faded equally, the new odor would also be rated weak.
questions.x: This is sensory adaptation: your response to a stimulus that doesn't change gets weaker over time. Smell adapts to one odor at a time. The constant odor's rating fell steadily, but a brand-new odor at minute 5 was rated strong. That new odor works like a control. It shows the nose and the person's attention still work fine, so this isn't a general loss of smell. Only the response to the unchanging first odor dropped. It's why you stop noticing your own home's smell but notice a new one right away.

questions.q: Researchers find that bitter-sensing taste cells respond to many structurally unrelated toxins, and that each bitter cell expresses many T2R receptor types. Which functional interpretation fits best?
o: Bitter taste is tuned to broadly detect and reject potential poisons rather than discriminate among them
Correct: many receptors in one cell feed a single 'reject this' bitter signal.
Bitter taste allows precise identification of each specific toxin
Pooling many receptors in one cell makes bitter things hard to tell apart.
Bitter taste is transduced by Na⁺ channels like salty taste
T2Rs are GPCRs. Salty taste is the one that uses Na⁺ channels.
Bitter cells evolved to attract animals to nutrient-rich foods
Bitterness warns of possible poison and makes animals avoid food, not seek it.
questions.x: Bitter taste works like a poison alarm. Bitter is detected by T2R receptors, which are G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs): proteins that start a chain of signals inside the cell when a molecule binds. Each bitter cell carries many T2R types, and they all feed into the same single 'bitter' signal. That lets one cell react to thousands of very different, possibly toxic chemicals, so animals spit them out. The cost is that bitter things all taste alike. Telling each toxin apart would need separate cells with separate signals, which isn't what was found.

questions.q: Which set lists the three components of emotion as usually described in psychology?
o: Sensory, perceptual, motor
These are steps in taking in and acting on a stimulus, not the parts of an emotion.
Conscious, preconscious, unconscious
These are Freud's levels of awareness, not the parts of an emotion.
Physiological, cognitive, behavioral
Correct: body arousal, the thought and feeling, and the outward expression.
Primary, secondary, tertiary
These words describe kinds of appraisal or reinforcers, not the parts of an emotion.
questions.x: Psychologists usually describe an emotion as having three parts. The physiological part is what your body does: heart pounding, sweating, breathing faster. The cognitive part is what's going on in your head: how you size up the situation and the feeling you have about it. The behavioral part is what you show or do: your facial expression, your voice, running away. Freud's conscious, preconscious and unconscious also come in a set of three, but they're levels of awareness, not the pieces of an emotion.

questions.q: Smiling, frowning, and clenching the fists during an emotional episode are examples of which emotion component?
o: Cognitive
The cognitive part is the inner judgment and feeling, which you can't see.
Physiological
Physiological means internal changes like heart rate and sweating, not visible expressions.
Perceptual
Perception is making sense of what your senses take in, not a part of emotion.
Behavioral
Correct: expressions and actions you can see make up the behavioral part.
questions.x: The behavioral part of an emotion is the part other people can see: facial expressions, posture, gestures and actions. Smiling, frowning and clenching your fists all fit. It's easy to confuse this with the physiological part, because both involve the body. But the physiological part means internal, automatic changes, like heart rate, blood pressure and sweating, that you can't see just by looking. Visible muscle movements, like a smile, count as behavior.

questions.q: Members of an isolated community with no media exposure correctly match photographs of Western faces to stories about fear and anger. This finding most directly supports which idea?
o: Emotions are learned through observational modeling
Learning by watching needs exposure. This group had never seen these faces.
Display rules are identical across cultures
Display rules differ between cultures, and this study is about recognizing faces anyway.
Physiological arousal precedes emotional labeling
The study is about recognizing expressions, not the order of arousal and labeling.
Some emotional expressions are biologically universal
Correct: recognizing faces with no cultural contact points to built-in, shared expressions.
questions.x: These people had never seen Western media, yet they still matched Western faces to stories about fear and anger. They couldn't have learned those expressions by watching Western people, so the expressions must be built in. That supports the idea that some emotional expressions are biologically universal, shared by all humans. Researchers like Paul Ekman did this kind of study. What does change from culture to culture are display rules: learned norms about when it's okay to show an emotion.

questions.q: In one culture, people suppress open displays of grief at funerals in public but weep freely in private. This pattern is best explained by:
o: cultural display rules
Correct: display rules are learned norms about when and where emotions can be shown.
the facial feedback hypothesis
Facial feedback is about expressions changing feelings, not social rules about showing them.
the absence of universal emotions
Weeping in private shows the grief is there; only showing it in public is held back.
the Cannon-Bard theory
Cannon-Bard is about the timing of arousal and feeling, not cultural rules.
questions.x: Display rules are learned cultural norms about when, where and how strongly you're allowed to show an emotion. In this culture, the rule says not to show grief openly in public. But people weep freely in private, so the grief itself is fully there. Only how it's shown in public is being controlled. The facial feedback hypothesis is a different idea: it says your facial expression can change how you feel. It isn't about social rules for showing feelings.

questions.q: Darwin argued that emotional expressions are similar across humans and other animals because they:
o: are learned in early childhood from caregivers
Darwin stressed inheritance and evolution, not learning from caregivers.
are produced solely by cognitive appraisal
Appraisal theories came much later and can't explain why animals share our expressions.
evolved as adaptive signals that aided survival
Correct: Darwin saw expressions as evolved signals that helped survival.
arise from conditioned associations with rewards
That's a behaviorist idea about learned rewards, not Darwin's evolutionary one.
questions.x: In his book The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals, Darwin argued that emotional expressions are inherited, like physical traits. They evolved because they helped animals survive, for example by warning others off or showing you're not a threat. If expressions came from evolution, you'd expect them to look similar across cultures and even across related species. If they were learned or conditioned, you'd expect them to vary with each individual's experience, which doesn't fit the similarity Darwin saw.

questions.q: Participants who hold a pen between their teeth (forcing a smile) rate cartoons as funnier than those who hold it with their lips (preventing a smile). Which idea does this support?
o: Schachter-Singer two-factor theory
Two-factor theory needs arousal plus a label. Only facial muscles changed here.
Cannon-Bard theory
Cannon-Bard says body changes don't cause emotion, which this result goes against.
Yerkes-Dodson law
Yerkes-Dodson links arousal to performance, not facial muscles to mood.
Facial feedback hypothesis
Correct: facial muscle activity feeds back and shapes the emotion felt.
questions.x: The facial feedback hypothesis says the position of your facial muscles sends signals back to your brain and shapes the emotion you feel. Holding a pen between your teeth pulls your face into a smile; holding it with your lips blocks one. The smile group found cartoons funnier. Only facial muscles were changed, not arousal or labels, so this tests facial feedback, not two-factor theory. One caution: large studies trying to repeat this exact pen task have had mixed results.

questions.q: A researcher finds that the facial feedback effect shrinks to near zero when participants are filmed during the task. What is the most reasonable interpretation?
o: Facial expressions are not universal across cultures
Universality is about recognizing faces across cultures, not about this lab setup.
Emotion is entirely determined by cognitive labels
Too sweeping. One thing weakening an effect doesn't prove thoughts are the only cause of emotion.
Self-awareness may disrupt the influence of facial muscles on feelings
Correct: being watched may disrupt the effect, without proving the effect is never real.
Physiological arousal and emotion occur simultaneously
Nobody measured the timing of arousal and emotion.
questions.x: A moderator is a variable that changes how strong an effect is. Here, the facial feedback effect almost disappears when people know they're being filmed. So being watched is a moderator. A sensible reading is that being filmed makes people more self-aware, and that self-focus gets in the way of the face-to-feeling link. Be careful not to over-conclude. One condition that weakens an effect doesn't prove the effect is fake, or that emotions come only from thoughts.

questions.q: Suppose patients with high spinal cord injuries, who receive less bodily feedback, reported that their emotions felt less intense. Which theory would this finding best support?
o: James-Lange
Correct: if feelings depend on body feedback, less feedback should weaken them.
Cannon-Bard
Cannon-Bard says feelings don't depend on body feedback, so it predicts no change.
Lazarus appraisal
Appraisal theory focuses on how you judge the situation, not on body feedback.
Opponent-process
Opponent-process theory is about emotional rebound over time, not body feedback.
questions.note: Reduced bodily feedback → weaker emotion would support James-Lange.
questions.x: James-Lange theory says an emotion is your awareness of your body's reaction: first the body reacts, then you feel. If that's true, less feedback from the body should mean weaker emotions. People with high spinal cord injuries get less feedback from their body, so finding that their emotions feel weaker would fit James-Lange. Cannon-Bard theory predicts no change, because it says the feeling and the body reaction happen separately. Real data are mixed: one early study found weaker emotions, later ones often didn't.

questions.q: Cannon also argued that visceral changes are too slow to be the source of emotion. Which finding would best support this objection?
o: Injecting epinephrine alone produces general arousal without any specific emotion
That supports Cannon's point that arousal looks the same for every emotion, not his timing point.
Facial expressions are recognized across cultures
That's about whether expressions are universal, not about timing.
People report feeling fear before autonomic changes such as sweating begin
Correct: if the feeling comes first, the body change can't be what caused it.
Emotions vary with cognitive appraisal of the stressor
That supports appraisal theories, not the timing objection.
questions.x: James-Lange says the body reacts first and the feeling is your awareness of that reaction. Cannon pushed back in a few ways. One was timing: visceral changes (changes in your internal organs, like sweating or a racing heart) take a few seconds to build up, but emotions can show up almost instantly. A cause can't come after its effect. So the finding that supports this objection is that people feel fear before the sweating starts. The epinephrine finding also argues against James-Lange, but it supports a different Cannon point: that arousal looks the same across emotions.

questions.q: In a study, aroused participants told 'the injection may cause a racing heart' showed little emotional reaction to an angry confederate, while uninformed participants became angry. Why did the informed group react less?
o: They experienced no physiological arousal at all
Both groups got the arousing injection. They differed in how they explained it.
They attributed the arousal to the injection
Correct: they had a non-emotional reason for the arousal, so they didn't label it as anger.
Their thalamus blocked the cortical experience of emotion
The thalamus isn't part of this explanation, and nothing showed it blocking anything.
They used problem-focused coping to remove the confederate
Nobody removed the confederate. The groups differed only in how they explained their arousal.
questions.note: Two-factor theory: explained arousal does not get an emotional label.
questions.x: Schachter-Singer two-factor theory says an emotion needs two things: body arousal and a mental label that explains it. Both groups got the same arousing injection, so both had racing hearts. The informed group already had a non-emotional explanation: 'It's the shot.' They didn't need to blame their racing heart on the angry person, so they didn't feel much anger. The uninformed group had no explanation, so they looked around, saw an angry confederate, and labeled their arousal as anger. The difference was the label, not the arousal.

questions.q: Men interviewed by an attractive researcher on a swaying suspension bridge more often called her later than men interviewed on a stable bridge. This result is usually explained by:
o: misattribution of arousal to attraction
Correct: fear arousal from the bridge was mistaken for attraction to the researcher.
the mere exposure effect
The men had about the same contact with her on both bridges, so familiarity can't explain it.
the facial feedback hypothesis
No one's facial expressions were changed in this study.
habituation to the fearful stimulus over time
Habituation would weaken the arousal, not turn it into attraction.
questions.x: In the classic bridge study, men crossing a swaying suspension bridge had racing hearts from fear. When an attractive researcher met them there, many mistook that fear arousal for attraction to her, so they were more likely to call her later. That's called misattribution of arousal: you feel aroused for one reason but credit it to something else nearby. It's a prediction of two-factor theory, which says unexplained arousal gets labeled using cues in the situation. Mere exposure can't explain it, since the men spent about the same time with her on both bridges.

questions.q: Two hikers see the same snake. One thinks 'harmless garter snake' and feels calm; the other thinks 'venomous!' and feels terror. Which theory best explains the different emotions?
o: James-Lange theory
James-Lange starts with the body's reaction, not with how each person judges the snake.
Cannon-Bard theory
Cannon-Bard doesn't explain why the same snake gives two different emotions.
Lazarus cognitive appraisal theory
Correct: the same snake caused different emotions because each hiker judged it differently.
Facial feedback hypothesis
Nothing about faces explains the difference here.
questions.x: Both hikers see the very same snake, yet one feels calm and the other feels terror. Since the stimulus is identical, the difference has to come from how each one judges it. That's Lazarus's cognitive appraisal theory. An appraisal is your quick mental judgment of whether something is a threat to you. 'Harmless garter snake' leads to calm; 'venomous!' leads to terror. James-Lange can't explain this well, because it starts with the body's reaction, and here the body's reaction itself depends on that first judgment.

questions.q: A researcher wants to distinguish Schachter-Singer from Lazarus. Which result would favor Lazarus?
o: Unexplained arousal is labeled according to a confederate's mood
That's the classic support for Schachter-Singer, not Lazarus.
Emotions feel weaker after spinal cord injury
Weaker emotions after spinal injury would support James-Lange.
Emotional reports change with appraisal even when arousal is held constant and explained
Correct: emotion follows the judgment even with arousal fixed and explained, which favors Lazarus.
Arousal and feeling begin at the same moment
Arousal and feeling starting together supports Cannon-Bard.
questions.x: To tell these two theories apart, you need a result where they predict different things. Schachter-Singer says emotion comes from labeling arousal you can't explain. Lazarus says emotion comes from how you judge the situation, and arousal follows from that. So hold arousal steady and give people a clear explanation for it. That takes labeling out of the picture. If emotions still change when people judge the situation differently, appraisal is doing the work, which favors Lazarus. The angry-confederate result is classic support for Schachter-Singer instead.

questions.q: In which theory of emotion does the thalamus play the central role in sending signals simultaneously to the cortex and the autonomic nervous system?
o: Schachter-Singer
Schachter-Singer is about arousal plus a label, not a thalamus relay.
Cannon-Bard
Correct: that's why Cannon-Bard is sometimes called the thalamic theory.
James-Lange
James-Lange focuses on feedback from body changes, not the thalamus.
Lazarus appraisal
Lazarus focuses on how you judge the situation, not a thalamus relay.
questions.x: In Cannon-Bard theory, a stimulus first reaches the thalamus, a relay station deep in the brain. The thalamus then sends two signals at the same time: one to the cortex, which produces the conscious feeling, and one to the autonomic nervous system, which produces the body's arousal (racing heart, sweating). That's why it's sometimes called the thalamic theory. The key idea is that the feeling and the body reaction happen together and separately. James-Lange instead says the body reacts first and the feeling comes from noticing it.

questions.q: A patient with hippocampal damage undergoes fear conditioning (tone paired with a loud noise). She shows a skin-conductance response to the tone but cannot say the tone was paired with the noise. A patient with amygdala damage shows the opposite. What does this double dissociation suggest?
o: The amygdala supports conditioned emotional responses and the hippocampus supports explicit memory of the pairing
Correct: each structure handles a different part of the fear memory.
Both structures are required for any form of fear learning
Each patient kept one kind of learning, so neither structure is needed for both.
The hippocampus generates autonomic fear responses
The hippocampus patient still had the body's fear response, so it doesn't need the hippocampus.
Fear conditioning depends only on the cerebellum
The damage was to the amygdala and hippocampus; the cerebellum isn't involved here.
questions.x: A double dissociation means damage to one structure knocks out function 1 but not function 2, while damage to another structure does the reverse. That shows the two functions rely on different parts of the brain. Here, the hippocampus patient still sweats to the tone (a skin-conductance response, a sign of fear arousal) but can't say what the tone was paired with. The amygdala patient knows the pairing but has no fear response. So the amygdala handles the learned emotional response, and the hippocampus handles the conscious memory of the pairing.

questions.q: Monkeys with bilateral temporal lobe lesions that include the amygdala become unusually tame, explore objects with their mouths, and show reduced fear. This pattern is called:
o: Klüver-Bucy syndrome
Correct: tameness, mouthing objects and less fear follow damage to both temporal lobes.
Korsakoff syndrome
Korsakoff syndrome is a memory disorder from low thiamine.
Wernicke aphasia
Wernicke aphasia is trouble understanding language.
Learned helplessness
Learned helplessness is giving up after stress you can't control, not a brain-lesion syndrome.
questions.x: This is Klüver-Bucy syndrome. It follows damage to both temporal lobes (bilateral), including the amygdala. The amygdala helps judge threats, so without it the monkeys lose their fear and become strangely tame. They also explore objects by putting them in their mouths, called hyperorality, and may show unusual sexual behavior and trouble recognizing objects by sight. Don't confuse it with Korsakoff syndrome, which also starts with K but is a memory disorder caused by a lack of thiamine (vitamin B1).

questions.q: In early experiments, cats whose cortex was removed but whose hypothalamus was intact showed sudden, poorly directed hissing and clawing. This 'sham rage' suggests that:
o: the cortex alone produces emotional behavior
Rage showed up with the cortex gone, so the cortex isn't needed to produce it.
the hippocampus produces aggression
The hippocampus wasn't the structure being tested; it's mainly about memory.
the hypothalamus can generate emotional behavior while the cortex helps direct and inhibit it
Correct: the rage happened without the cortex but had no aim or restraint.
emotion requires cognitive labeling
The cats had no cortex to do any labeling, yet they still showed rage.
questions.x: These cats had their cortex (the brain's outer thinking layer) removed but kept their hypothalamus, a small structure deep in the brain that helps control drives and body responses. They still showed sudden rage, hissing and clawing, so the hypothalamus can produce the rage pattern on its own. But the rage was poorly aimed and hard to stop. That suggests the cortex normally points the behavior at the right target and holds it back when it's not needed. It's called 'sham' rage because it lacks direction, not because it's fake.

questions.q: fMRI shows that when participants reappraise a disturbing image as staged, prefrontal activity increases and amygdala activity decreases. This best supports which statement?
o: The prefrontal cortex can down-regulate amygdala responses
Correct: prefrontal activity rose as amygdala activity fell during reappraisal.
The amygdala causes reappraisal to occur
Amygdala activity dropped, so it's unlikely to be the thing driving reappraisal.
Reappraisal has no effect on emotional processing
The amygdala changed, so emotional processing clearly was affected.
fMRI proves that the prefrontal cortex generates all emotions
Brain imaging shows correlation and can't prove one area causes all emotions.
questions.note: Imaging is correlational unless a variable is manipulated.
questions.x: Cognitive reappraisal means rethinking a situation to change how it makes you feel, like telling yourself a scary image is just staged. The prefrontal cortex, at the front of the brain, handles planning and self-control. The amygdala handles threat and fear. When people reappraised, prefrontal activity went up and amygdala activity went down. That fits the idea that the prefrontal cortex can calm the amygdala, a kind of top-down control. But fMRI only shows what happens together, so it's correlational. It can't prove the prefrontal cortex causes all emotions.

questions.q: Rats given a β-blocker right after a frightening training session later show weaker memory for it than controls given saline. What is the best conclusion?
o: β-blockers erase all previously stored memories
Only the newly trained memory was tested, not older ones.
Adrenergic signaling after an event helps strengthen emotional memories
Correct: blocking norepinephrine's β receptors right after training weakened the memory.
The hippocampus is not involved in memory
The study didn't test the hippocampus at all.
Cortisol has no effect on memory
Cortisol wasn't changed in this study, so we learn nothing about it.
questions.x: Consolidation is the process that turns a new memory into a lasting one. After a scary event, the body releases norepinephrine, which acts on β-adrenergic receptors, especially in the amygdala, and helps lock the memory in. A β-blocker is a drug that blocks those receptors. Giving it right after training weakened the memory compared with saline (salt water, the control). So adrenergic signaling after an emotional event helps strengthen the memory. Only the new memory was tested, so nothing here shows older memories were erased.

questions.q: LeDoux described a fast 'low road' for fear. Which pathway does it describe?
o: Sensory cortex to the hippocampus and then on to prefrontal cortex
That route goes through the cortex, so it's slower. It's not the low road.
Thalamus directly to amygdala, bypassing the sensory cortex
Correct: thalamus straight to amygdala, skipping the cortex, for a fast, rough reaction.
Amygdala to cerebellum to spinal cord
This isn't the fear pathway LeDoux described.
Retina directly to the hypothalamus only
The retina-to-hypothalamus path mainly sets your daily body clock, not fear.
questions.x: Joseph LeDoux described two routes for fear. The low road sends sensory signals from the thalamus, the brain's relay station, straight to the amygdala, skipping the sensory cortex. It's fast but rough, so you jump at a curved stick before you know what it is. The high road goes from the thalamus to the sensory cortex and then to the amygdala. It's slower but gives a detailed picture, and it can confirm the fear or cancel it ('It's just a stick'). The low road is the shortcut.

questions.q: Which division of the autonomic nervous system produces the 'fight-or-flight' response?
o: Parasympathetic
The parasympathetic division handles 'rest and digest', the opposite of fight-or-flight.
Somatic
The somatic system controls voluntary muscles and isn't part of the autonomic system.
Enteric
The enteric system runs the gut and doesn't drive fight-or-flight.
Sympathetic
Correct: the sympathetic division gets the body ready for action.
questions.x: The autonomic nervous system controls things you don't consciously steer, like heart rate and digestion. It has two main divisions that work in opposite directions. The sympathetic division produces the fight-or-flight response: faster heart rate, wider pupils, opened-up airways (bronchioles) and sugar released for energy. The parasympathetic division does the opposite, often called 'rest and digest'. The somatic nervous system isn't autonomic at all; it controls the skeletal muscles you move on purpose.

questions.q: Which neurotransmitter is released by preganglionic neurons in both divisions of the autonomic nervous system?
o: Norepinephrine
Norepinephrine is released by most sympathetic postganglionic neurons, not preganglionic ones.
Dopamine
Dopamine isn't the transmitter autonomic preganglionic neurons use.
Acetylcholine
Correct: every autonomic preganglionic neuron releases acetylcholine.
Epinephrine
Epinephrine is a hormone from the adrenal medulla, not a preganglionic transmitter.
questions.x: Autonomic pathways use two neurons in a row. The first, the preganglionic neuron, runs from the spinal cord or brainstem to a ganglion, a cluster of nerve cells. The second, the postganglionic neuron, runs from the ganglion to the target organ. Every preganglionic neuron, in both the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions, releases acetylcholine. The two divisions only differ at the second handoff: parasympathetic postganglionic neurons release acetylcholine, while most sympathetic ones release norepinephrine. That's why norepinephrine is the tempting wrong answer.

questions.q: A researcher plots exam scores against students' measured arousal and finds an inverted-U curve. If students take an easier exam instead, where would the peak most likely shift?
o: To a higher level of arousal
Correct: easy tasks are done best at higher arousal than hard ones.
To a lower level of arousal
Lower best arousal goes with harder tasks, not easier ones.
The curve would become a straight downward line
Easy tasks still give an upside-down U; only the peak moves.
The peak would stay at exactly the same arousal level
Task difficulty shifts the peak, so it won't stay put.
questions.x: The Yerkes-Dodson law says performance goes up with arousal to a point, then drops off. Plotted on a graph, that makes an upside-down U. The best level of arousal depends on the task. Simple or well-practiced tasks are done best at fairly high arousal. Hard or complex tasks get disrupted sooner, so they peak at lower arousal. An easier exam is a simpler task, so the peak should move toward higher arousal, to the right on the graph. The curve keeps its upside-down U shape; only the peak moves.

questions.q: A study finds that people with high Social Readjustment Rating Scale scores report more illness in the following year. Which conclusion is justified?
o: Life changes directly cause illness
Without random assignment, you can't conclude that one thing causes the other.
Illness causes people to experience more major life changes
This design can't prove that direction of cause either.
Positive life events protect against illness
The scale lumps good and bad events together, so it can't show good events protect.
High life-change scores are associated with later illness
Correct: the study is correlational, so it only shows an association.
questions.x: The Social Readjustment Rating Scale gives points for recent life changes, both good and bad, like a move, a wedding or a job loss, as a rough measure of stress. This study just measured people's scores and then their illness the next year. Nobody was assigned to have more or fewer life changes, so it's a correlational study. It can show that high scores go along with later illness. It can't show cause, because a third variable, like income, health habits or an existing illness, could drive both.

questions.q: A person wants a high-paying job but dreads the long commute it requires. As the start date approaches, her anxiety grows. This is an example of:
o: an approach-avoidance conflict
Correct: one goal with both an appealing side and an unappealing side.
an approach-approach conflict
Approach-approach is choosing between two good options. Here there's one option with a downside.
an avoidance-avoidance conflict
Avoidance-avoidance is being stuck between two bad options. She actually wants the job.
a catastrophic stressor
A catastrophic stressor is a huge disaster, not a personal job decision.
questions.note: Trap: one option with pros and cons = approach-avoidance.
questions.x: An approach-avoidance conflict is when one goal has both a good side and a bad side. Here it's one job: the high pay pulls her toward it, and the long commute pushes her away. As the goal gets closer, the urge to avoid usually grows faster than the urge to approach. That's why her anxiety climbs as the start date nears. The quick check is to count the goals. One goal with mixed feelings is approach-avoidance. Two options to choose between would be approach-approach or avoidance-avoidance.

questions.q: Volunteers who reported chronic stress were more likely to develop a cold after viral exposure. Why can this study NOT show that stress causes illness?
o: Stress was measured rather than randomly assigned, so other variables may explain the link
Correct: stress was measured, not assigned, so things like sleep or habits could explain the link.
All participants received the same virus
Equal virus exposure is a strength of the design, not the reason it can't show cause.
Illness was the dependent variable
Every study has an outcome measure; that doesn't block a causal claim.
Colds are not affected by the immune system
Fighting off colds clearly depends on the immune system.
questions.x: To show that one thing causes another, researchers have to manipulate the independent variable (the thing they change) and randomly assign people to groups. Here, stress was only measured, since people just reported how stressed they were. Highly stressed people may also sleep less, smoke more or eat worse, and any of those could weaken the immune system. Those outside factors are called confounds. Giving everyone the same virus is actually a strength, because it controls exposure. But it doesn't turn stress into something the researchers controlled.

questions.q: Chronically elevated cortisol is associated with damage to which brain structure, which may help explain memory problems in people under long-term stress?
o: Cerebellum
The cerebellum isn't the main area tied to stress-related memory problems.
Primary visual cortex
The visual cortex processes what you see, not memory storage.
Pons
The pons relays signals and helps control sleep and breathing.
Hippocampus
Correct: the hippocampus has many cortisol receptors and can shrink under long-term stress.
questions.x: Cortisol is a stress hormone made by the adrenal glands. The hippocampus, the brain area that forms new memories, has lots of receptors for it (called glucocorticoid receptors). When cortisol stays high for a long time, it can damage hippocampal neurons, slow the birth of new neurons there, and even shrink the hippocampus. That may help explain why people under long-term stress have memory problems. The cerebellum, pons and visual cortex aren't the main places where stress hormones affect memory.

questions.q: Selye's model has been criticized mainly because it:
o: fails to include any physiological measures
Selye's model is built on bodily changes, so it doesn't lack physical measures.
claims stress always improves health
Selye said long-term stress wears the body down and leads to illness.
applies only to positive events
Selye applied his model to stressors in general, not just positive ones.
describes a uniform bodily response and largely ignores cognitive appraisal
Correct: it treats the body's response as the same for everyone and ignores how people judge stressors.
questions.x: Hans Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS) describes the body's response to stress in three stages: alarm, resistance and exhaustion. He said the body reacts in basically the same way to any stressor. The main criticism is that this leaves out the mind. Later researchers, especially Richard Lazarus, showed that appraisal, meaning how a person judges a stressor, along with how predictable and controllable it is, strongly shapes the response. So the same event can hit two people very differently. Selye's model is all about the body, so it doesn't lack physical measures.

questions.q: Rats exposed to unpredictable shocks develop more stomach ulcers than rats given the same shocks preceded by a warning tone. What does this suggest?
o: Shock intensity is the only factor that matters
Shock strength was the same in both groups, yet the outcomes differed.
Warning tones increase stress hormone release
The warned rats did better, not worse.
Predictability reduces the harmful effects of a stressor
Correct: the shocks were equal; only predictability differed.
Ulcers are caused only by bacteria, never by psychological stress
The groups differed only in predictability, and that changed ulcer rates.
questions.x: Both groups of rats got exactly the same shocks. The only difference was whether a warning tone came first. The rats with no warning got more stomach ulcers, so the difference has to come from unpredictability. A warning tone does two things: it tells the rat a shock is coming, and it also tells the rat when it's safe. That lets it relax between shocks instead of staying on alert all the time. The lesson is that the psychological features of a stressor, not just its physical strength, decide how much harm it does.

questions.q: In a 'yoked' design, one rat can turn a wheel to stop shocks, while a second rat receives exactly the same shocks but has no control. The second rat develops more stress-related illness. The key variable shown to matter is:
o: the total amount of shock received
The two rats got exactly the same shocks.
perceived control over the stressor
Correct: the shocks were identical; only control differed.
physical exercise from turning the wheel
Exercise could be a confound, but the design was built to test control.
genetic differences between rats
Rats are randomly assigned to roles, so genetics is an unlikely explanation.
questions.x: In a yoked design, two animals are linked so they get exactly the same stressor. Here, one rat can turn a wheel to stop the shocks, and that stops them for both rats. So both get the same number and strength of shocks, but only one has any control. The rat with no control got sicker. Since the shocks were identical, the difference must come from control itself. Exercise from turning the wheel could be a confound, but the design was built to test control.

questions.q: Researchers randomly assign stressed employees to either an 8-week meditation course or a waitlist. Afterward, the meditation group has lower cortisol. Why can the researchers make a causal claim here?
o: Cortisol is an objective measure
An objective measure is good, but on its own it can't show cause.
The sample consisted only of stressed employees
A specific sample affects who results apply to, not whether cause is shown.
The study lasted eight weeks
How long a study lasts doesn't make it able to show cause.
Random assignment makes the groups equivalent except for the intervention
Correct: random assignment makes the groups alike except for the meditation.
questions.x: Random assignment means chance decides who goes into each group, like drawing names from a hat. That spreads out differences people bring with them, such as motivation, health and starting stress level, evenly across both groups. So the only consistent difference between the groups is the meditation course. If the meditation group later has lower cortisol, you can credit that to the meditation. An objective measure like cortisol, or a long study, makes a study better, but neither one by itself allows a cause-and-effect claim.

questions.q: Psychologists describe 'hardiness' as a set of traits that buffer stress. Which trio defines it?
o: Competition, urgency, and hostility
These are Type A traits, and hostility is linked to heart disease.
Commitment, control, and challenge
Correct: hardy people stay involved, feel in control, and see change as a challenge.
Denial, projection, and repression
These are defense mechanisms, not hardiness traits.
Alarm, resistance, and exhaustion
These are Selye's stages of the stress response.
questions.x: Psychologist Suzanne Kobasa described hardiness as three attitudes, the three Cs, that help people stay healthy under stress. Commitment means staying involved in your life and work. Control means believing you can influence what happens. Challenge means seeing change as a chance to grow instead of a threat. The distractors are other famous trios. Competition, urgency and hostility describe the Type A personality, and hostility is the part most linked to heart disease. Alarm, resistance and exhaustion are Selye's stress stages.

questions.q: A therapist teaches a client to replace the thought 'I'll fail this interview and ruin my life' with 'This interview is one opportunity among many.' This technique targets stress by changing:
o: the appraisal of the stressor
Correct: cognitive restructuring changes how threatening the stressor seems.
the stressor itself
The interview still happens; only the way the client thinks about it changes.
parasympathetic output directly
Any calming follows from the new thought; it isn't controlled directly.
the client's locus of control to external
Shifting control to outside forces would likely raise stress, and it isn't what's being taught.
questions.x: This technique is called cognitive restructuring: spotting extreme, catastrophic thoughts and swapping them for more realistic ones. The interview itself doesn't change at all. What changes is how threatening it seems, and that judgment is called appraisal. 'I'll ruin my life' makes it a disaster; 'one opportunity among many' makes it manageable. Once the interview feels less threatening, the client's body may calm down too. But that calming comes as a result of the new thought, not from the therapist directly controlling the parasympathetic nervous system.

questions.q: With repeated skydives, first-time terror lessens while post-jump elation grows. Opponent-process theory explains this by proposing that:
o: the initial emotion strengthens with each repetition
The theory says the felt first reaction gets weaker with repetition, not stronger.
cognitive labels of arousal become more accurate
Labeling arousal is the two-factor theory idea, not opponent-process.
the opposing process strengthens with repetition while the net initial reaction weakens
Correct: the growing opposite reaction cancels more of the first one.
the sympathetic system stops responding entirely
The body still gets aroused; what shifts is the balance of feelings.
questions.x: Opponent-process theory says every strong emotion sets off an opposite emotion that follows it. The first reaction (the a-process) is the main feeling, here terror. The opposing reaction (the b-process) is the after-feeling, here elation. With repetition, the first reaction stays about the same, but the opposing one grows stronger and starts sooner. It cancels more of the terror, so the net fear you feel shrinks, and the relief and elation afterward get bigger. The same idea is used to explain drug tolerance and withdrawal.

questions.q: Two groups give a stressful speech. Group A is told beforehand that arousal improves performance; Group B gets no instructions. Group A shows better cardiovascular efficiency and performance. Which concept best explains the result?
o: Group A experienced no arousal at all
Group A still had arousal; they just saw it differently.
The general adaptation syndrome skipped the alarm stage
Instructions can't make the body skip a stage of its stress response.
Reappraising arousal as helpful shifts a threat response toward a challenge response
Correct: seeing arousal as helpful moved them from a threat response toward a challenge response.
Group B used problem-focused coping
Group B wasn't taught any coping strategy at all.
questions.x: Both groups faced the same stressful speech and both got aroused. Group A was told that arousal helps performance, so they reappraised it: a pounding heart meant 'I'm ready', not 'I'm in danger'. That shifted them from a threat response to a challenge response. A threat response happens when you feel the demands are bigger than what you can handle. A challenge response happens when you feel you can handle them. Challenge goes with more efficient heart function and better performance. The arousal didn't vanish; its meaning changed.

questions.q: Which neurotransmitter is most closely linked to the brain's reward pathway and the reinforcing effects of addictive drugs?
o: Dopamine
Correct: dopamine released in the nucleus accumbens is the brain's reward and reinforcement signal.
Acetylcholine
Acetylcholine runs muscles and helps with attention and memory. It isn't the main reward signal.
Glycine
Glycine is a 'calm down' messenger, mostly in the spinal cord and brainstem.
GABA
GABA is the main 'calm down' messenger. Many drugs act on it, but it isn't the reward signal.
questions.note: Mesolimbic pathway: VTA → nucleus accumbens.
questions.x: The answer is dopamine. Your brain has a reward pathway (also called the mesolimbic pathway): dopamine neurons in a midbrain area called the ventral tegmental area (VTA) send signals to the nucleus accumbens, a small region deep in the brain. When something feels good, like food or sex, dopamine rises there, and that tags the behavior as worth repeating. Nearly every addictive drug pushes dopamine up in this same spot. GABA is the tempting wrong answer, since alcohol and sedatives act on it, but GABA is the brain's main 'calm down' signal, not the reward signal.

questions.q: A patient taking a drug that blocks dopamine D₂ receptors develops tremor and rigidity. Which brain pathway is most likely affected?
o: Nigrostriatal pathway
Correct: this pathway runs from substantia nigra to striatum and controls movement. Blocking it mimics Parkinson's.
Tuberoinfundibular pathway
This pathway controls prolactin. Blocking it raises prolactin, not tremor.
Mesocortical pathway
This pathway goes to the prefrontal cortex and affects thinking and motivation, not movement.
Mesolimbic pathway
Blocking this reward pathway is the intended antipsychotic effect, not the cause of movement problems.
questions.note: Antipsychotic motor side effects come from the nigrostriatal pathway.
questions.x: Antipsychotic drugs that block D₂ dopamine receptors don't pick just one pathway. They block dopamine everywhere, so the side effect tells you which pathway got hit. Tremor and rigidity are movement problems, and smooth movement depends on the nigrostriatal pathway, which carries dopamine from the substantia nigra to the striatum. That's the same circuit that breaks down in Parkinson disease, so blocking it looks like Parkinson's. The mesolimbic pathway is the tempting wrong answer: blocking it is the drug's intended effect on psychosis, not the cause of the shaking.

questions.q: A man becomes impulsive and socially inappropriate after a rod injures the front of his brain. Which region was most likely damaged?
o: Parietal lobe
The parietal lobe handles touch and sense of space. Damage causes problems like ignoring one side.
Medulla oblongata
The medulla runs breathing and heart rate. Damage there is often fatal.
Prefrontal cortex
Correct: the prefrontal cortex handles planning, impulse control and social judgment.
Temporal lobe
The temporal lobe handles hearing, understanding language and memory, not social conduct.
questions.x: This is the famous case of Phineas Gage, a railroad worker who survived an iron rod through the front of his skull in 1848. His memory and intelligence stayed mostly fine, but he became impulsive and rude. That points to the prefrontal cortex, the very front part of the brain. It acts like the brain's manager: it plans, weighs choices and holds back urges that don't fit the social setting. The temporal lobe is the tempting wrong answer, but damage there mainly hurts hearing, understanding language or memory, not social behavior.

questions.q: In split-brain patients, an image of a key is flashed only to the left visual field. What is the most likely result?
o: They see nothing because the corpus callosum is cut
The eyes and visual cortex still work. The image reaches the right hemisphere just fine.
They cannot name it but can pick out a key with the left hand
Correct: the right hemisphere saw it but can't speak, and it controls the left hand.
They can name it and pick it out with the right hand
The right hand is run by the left hemisphere, which never saw the key.
They can name it aloud but cannot pick it out with either hand
Naming needs the left hemisphere, which never got the image.
questions.note: Left visual field → right hemisphere → left hand.
questions.x: In a split-brain patient, the corpus callosum, the thick bundle of fibers that lets the two halves of the brain talk, has been cut. Each side of what you see goes to the opposite half of the brain, so an image in the left visual field reaches only the right hemisphere. In most people, speech lives in the left hemisphere. So the right side saw the key but can't say 'key.' The right hemisphere does control the left hand, though, so the left hand can reach out and pick the key by touch.

questions.q: Studies find that higher testosterone is associated with more dominance behavior, and winning a competition raises testosterone further. What do these findings best illustrate?
o: Behavior has no effect on hormone levels
Winning raised testosterone, so behavior clearly does affect hormones.
Testosterone is the sole cause of aggression
The data show a two-way link that goes together, not one single cause.
Hormones and behavior influence each other bidirectionally
Correct: testosterone shapes behavior, and how a contest turns out shapes testosterone.
Testosterone only matters in males
Testosterone affects behavior in all sexes. Nothing here limits it to males.
questions.x: These findings show a two-way street. Higher testosterone goes along with more dominant behavior, so hormones can shape behavior. But winning a competition then raises testosterone, so behavior also shapes hormones. When each one affects the other, we call it bidirectional. The tempting wrong answer says testosterone is the sole cause of aggression. That overreaches: the first finding is only a correlation (two things that go together), and the feedback from winning means you can't point to one thing as the only cause.

questions.q: A study reports a heritability of 0.6 for a personality trait in a population. Which interpretation is correct?
o: 60% of each person's trait level comes from genes
Heritability describes a group. It can't be applied to one person.
About 60% of the trait's variation in that population is attributable to genetic differences
Correct: heritability is the share of differences across a population linked to genetic differences.
Children have a 60% chance of inheriting the trait
Heritability isn't a chance of passing a trait to a child.
The trait cannot be changed by the environment
Highly heritable traits can still be shaped strongly by the environment.
questions.note: Trap: heritability is a population statistic, never individual.
questions.x: Heritability is a number from 0 to 1 that describes a group, not a person. A heritability of 0.6 means that about 60% of the differences between people in that population, at that time, are linked to differences in their genes. It does not mean 60% of your own trait comes from your genes, and it isn't the chance a child inherits the trait. It also doesn't mean the trait is fixed: heritability can shift if the environment changes, and highly heritable traits can still respond to environment.

questions.q: Why do twin studies comparing MZ and DZ twins raised together possibly overestimate heritability?
o: MZ twins come from two separate eggs
MZ twins come from one fertilized egg that splits. DZ twins come from two eggs.
MZ twins may be treated more alike
Correct: if MZ twins share more similar environments, that extra similarity gets wrongly credited to genes.
Twins never share an environment
Twins raised together do share a family environment. That's built into the design.
DZ twins share 100% of their genes
DZ twins share about 50% of their varying genes, like ordinary siblings, not 100%.
questions.note: Equal environments assumption.
questions.x: Twin studies compare identical twins, called MZ (monozygotic, from one egg, sharing about 100% of their genes), with fraternal twins, called DZ (dizygotic, from two eggs, sharing about 50%). If MZ twins are more alike, the extra similarity gets credited to genes. That only works if both kinds of twins share equally similar environments, which is called the equal environments assumption. But identical twins are often dressed alike and treated alike. That extra shared environment makes them more similar, the method wrongly credits it to genes, and heritability comes out too high.

questions.q: Children with a genetic tendency toward sociability seek out more social situations, which further builds their social skills. This is an example of what?
o: Evocative gene–environment correlation
Evocative is when a child's traits draw reactions from others. Here the child is choosing.
Epigenetic silencing
Epigenetics is chemical changes that switch genes on or off, not choosing settings.
Passive gene–environment correlation
Passive is when parents supply both the genes and the environment.
Active gene–environment correlation
Correct: the child seeks out settings that fit their inborn tendencies. That's niche-picking.
questions.x: Gene-environment correlation means your genes help shape the environments you end up in. There are three kinds. Passive: your parents give you both your genes and your home. Evocative: your traits draw certain reactions from other people. Active: you pick settings that fit your traits, also called niche-picking. Here the sociable child is the one choosing social situations, and those situations build more skill, so it's active. Evocative is the tempting wrong answer, but that's about other people reacting to you, not you doing the choosing.

questions.q: A patient has involuntary jerky movements, mood changes and cognitive decline, and genetic testing shows an expanded CAG repeat. Which disorder is most likely?
o: Parkinson disease
Parkinson's causes slow movement and a resting tremor from dopamine loss, not a CAG repeat.
Multiple sclerosis
MS is an immune attack on the coating of nerves, not a repeated stretch of DNA.
Alzheimer disease
Alzheimer's mainly causes memory loss, not jerky movements.
Huntington disease
Correct: a dominant CAG repeat kills striatum neurons, causing jerky movements, mood changes and decline.
questions.x: The giveaway is the expanded CAG repeat. Huntington disease is caused by a short DNA code, CAG, repeated too many times in one gene. It's autosomal dominant, meaning one bad copy from either parent is enough to cause it. The extra repeats slowly kill neurons in the striatum, part of the basal ganglia that helps control movement. The result is chorea (involuntary, jerky, dance-like movements), mood and personality changes, and declining thinking. Parkinson disease is the tempting wrong answer since it's also a basal ganglia movement disorder, but it causes slow movement and a resting tremor from loss of dopamine neurons, not jerky movements from a repeat.

questions.q: Researchers find that people with more education show the same amount of Alzheimer brain pathology at autopsy but fewer symptoms in life. Which concept best explains this?
o: Neurogenesis reversing plaques
Making new neurons doesn't clear plaques, and the damage at autopsy was the same.
Retrograde amnesia
Retrograde amnesia is losing memories from before an injury, not resisting damage.
Cognitive reserve
Correct: richer brain networks let the brain work around damage before symptoms show.
Diagnostic overshadowing
Diagnostic overshadowing is blaming new symptoms on an existing diagnosis.
questions.x: Cognitive reserve is the brain's ability to keep working well even when it's damaged. Years of education, mentally demanding work and learning build richer networks of connections between neurons. When disease damages part of the brain, a brain with more reserve can find other routes around the damage. That's why two people can have the same amount of Alzheimer damage at autopsy but very different symptoms in life. Neurogenesis (making new neurons) is the tempting wrong answer, but it doesn't remove plaques. The damage was the same here; the better-educated brains just worked around it.

questions.q: A critic argues that trait theories are limited because people's behavior varies widely across situations. This criticism was most associated with whom?
o: Walter Mischel
Correct: Mischel argued that behavior shifts across situations, starting the person-situation debate.
Raymond Cattell
Cattell built a trait model with 16 factors. He supported traits.
Hans Eysenck
Eysenck defended trait dimensions and tied them to biology.
Abraham Maslow
Maslow was a humanistic theorist known for the hierarchy of needs.
questions.x: Walter Mischel made this argument in the 1960s. Trait theories say people have stable traits, like being honest or outgoing, that show up everywhere. Mischel pointed out that people actually act quite differently from one situation to the next, so a trait score doesn't predict any single behavior very well. That started the person-situation debate. Today's answer is a middle ground called interactionism: traits predict behavior well when you average across many situations, and the situation matters too. Cattell and Eysenck were trait theorists who defended traits, not critics.

questions.q: Eysenck proposed that introverts avoid loud parties because of what biological difference?
o: A smaller amygdala
Eysenck focused on the brain's alertness system, not on the size of the amygdala.
Excess dopamine in the striatum
Eysenck didn't explain introversion with extra dopamine in the striatum.
Higher baseline cortical arousal
Correct: introverts are already highly aroused, so they avoid extra stimulation.
Lower baseline cortical arousal
Low baseline arousal is Eysenck's explanation for extraverts, who seek stimulation.
questions.x: Hans Eysenck linked introversion and extraversion to baseline cortical arousal, which is how alert and 'switched on' your brain is when nothing much is happening. He tied it to the reticular activating system, a brainstem network that controls alertness. Introverts start out with high arousal, so a loud party pushes them past their comfort level and they avoid it. Extraverts start out with low arousal, so they seek stimulation to feel just right. The 'lower baseline arousal' choice is the reversal trap: that's Eysenck's explanation for extraverts.

questions.q: A researcher gives participants a projective test in which they describe stories about ambiguous pictures. Which personality approach is she most likely using?
o: Social cognitive
Social cognitive researchers measure beliefs like self-efficacy, usually with questionnaires.
Psychoanalytic
Correct: projective tests like the TAT aim to bring out hidden, unconscious motives.
Trait
Trait researchers use fixed self-report questionnaires like the NEO-PI, not open-ended stories.
Behaviorist
Behaviorists watch behavior and its consequences, not hidden motives.
questions.x: A projective test shows a vague picture or inkblot and asks the person to say what they see or tell a story about it. Examples are the Thematic Apperception Test (TAT), which uses ambiguous pictures, and the Rorschach inkblot test. The idea is that people 'project' hidden, unconscious wishes and worries onto something unclear. That focus on the unconscious mind comes from the psychoanalytic approach started by Freud. Trait researchers measure personality very differently, with fixed questionnaires like the NEO-PI where everyone answers the same items.

questions.q: Which brain finding is most consistently reported in people with schizophrenia?
o: Increased gray matter in the temporal lobes
Gray matter tends to go down in schizophrenia, not up.
Enlarged ventricles
Correct: brain tissue shrinks, so the fluid-filled ventricles get bigger.
Absence of the corpus callosum
A missing corpus callosum is a rare birth condition, not a typical schizophrenia finding.
Enlarged frontal lobes
Schizophrenia is linked to lower frontal activity, not enlarged frontal lobes.
questions.x: The most consistent brain finding in schizophrenia is enlarged ventricles. Ventricles are fluid-filled spaces inside the brain. When the brain tissue around them shrinks, the ventricles look bigger, because fluid fills the space that tissue used to take up. People with schizophrenia also tend to have less gray matter (the tissue holding the bodies of nerve cells) and lower activity in the frontal lobes, called hypofrontality. So the choices about more gray matter or bigger frontal lobes get the direction backward: tissue goes down, ventricles go up.

questions.q: Schizophrenia concordance is about 45% in identical twins and 15% in fraternal twins. What can best be concluded?
o: Schizophrenia is entirely genetic
If it were all genes, identical twins would match close to 100% of the time, not 45%.
Genes play no role in schizophrenia
Identical twins match three times as often as fraternal twins. That gap shows genes matter.
Genes contribute substantially, but environment also matters
Correct: MZ above DZ shows genes matter, and MZ below 100% shows environment matters too.
Shared family environment is the main cause
Both twin types share a family home, yet they match at very different rates.
questions.x: Concordance is how often both twins have a condition when one does. Identical (MZ) twins share about 100% of their genes; fraternal (DZ) twins share about 50%. Compare MZ to DZ: 45% is three times 15% (15 × 3 = 45), so genes clearly matter. Now compare MZ to 100%: identical twins have nearly the same DNA, yet only 45% both get schizophrenia, so something besides genes matters too. This fits the diathesis-stress model: an inherited vulnerability (the diathesis) plus life stress sets the illness off.

questions.q: Seligman found that dogs exposed to inescapable shocks later failed to escape avoidable shocks. This model is most often used to explain which disorder?
o: Specific phobia
Phobias are explained mainly by learned fear through classical conditioning, not by giving up.
Schizophrenia
Schizophrenia involves hallucinations and delusions, which this model doesn't explain.
Obsessive-compulsive disorder
OCD involves rituals that ease anxiety. The dogs just stopped trying.
Major depressive disorder
Correct: learned helplessness models the passivity and hopelessness of depression.
questions.x: Martin Seligman gave dogs shocks they couldn't escape. Later, when the dogs could escape just by jumping over a low wall, many just lay there and took it. They had learned that nothing they did mattered, so they stopped trying. This is called learned helplessness. That giving up, plus the passivity and hopelessness that come with it, looks a lot like depression, so the model is used to explain major depressive disorder. Phobias are a tempting pick because shocks are scary, but phobias are about learned fear, not giving up.

questions.q: According to Beck's cognitive theory, depression is maintained by which pattern?
o: Overreinforcement of social behavior
Behavioral models say depression comes from too little reward, not too much.
Unconscious anger turned outward
Freud described anger turned inward, not outward, and that's not Beck's theory.
Excess dopamine activity in the mesolimbic reward pathway
Excess dopamine in this pathway is linked to psychosis, not Beck's view of depression.
Negative views of the self, the world and the future
Correct: Beck's cognitive triad is negative views of the self, the world and the future.
questions.x: Aaron Beck's cognitive theory says depression is kept going by how a person thinks. He described a cognitive triad: three sets of negative beliefs about the self ('I'm worthless'), the world ('everything is unfair') and the future ('it'll never get better'). Thinking errors called cognitive distortions keep those beliefs alive, like overgeneralization, where one failure becomes 'I fail at everything.' Cognitive therapy works by catching and challenging those thoughts. The anger choice is a distractor: Freud's psychoanalytic view said anger turned inward, not outward, and that isn't Beck's model anyway.

questions.q: A child is bitten by a dog and afterward panics whenever she sees any dog. Learning theory explains the onset of this phobia mainly through what?
o: Operant extinction
Extinction weakens a response that already exists. It can't create a new fear.
Classical conditioning
Correct: the dog was paired with the painful bite and became a conditioned trigger for fear.
Observational learning only
She was bitten herself, so she learned directly, not just by watching others.
Latent learning
Latent learning is hidden learning that shows up later when there's a reason to use it.
questions.note: Avoidance then maintains the phobia via negative reinforcement.
questions.x: Classical conditioning is learning by pairing. A neutral stimulus (something that didn't cause a reaction before) gets paired with an unconditioned stimulus (something that naturally causes a reaction). After that, the neutral stimulus causes the reaction by itself, and we call it a conditioned stimulus. Here the dog was neutral, the painful bite naturally caused fear, and now dogs alone trigger fear. Panicking at any dog, not just the one that bit her, is called generalization. Observational learning is tempting, but she was bitten herself, so direct conditioning explains it.

questions.q: Why does avoiding a feared object tend to maintain a phobia over time?
o: Avoidance causes spontaneous recovery
Spontaneous recovery is a faded response coming back after a break. Avoidance doesn't cause it.
Avoidance reduces anxiety, which negatively reinforces the avoidance
Correct: escaping anxiety feels like relief, which strengthens avoidance and keeps the fear from fading.
Avoidance positively punishes the fear response
Punishment makes a behavior less likely. Avoidance is getting stronger, so it's being reinforced.
Avoidance speeds extinction of the fear
Fear fades only with exposure. Avoidance blocks exposure, so it slows extinction.
questions.x: Avoiding a feared thing feels like relief, and that relief is the problem. In learning terms, negative reinforcement means a behavior gets stronger because it takes away something unpleasant. Avoidance takes away anxiety, so avoidance gets stronger. This is Mowrer's two-factor theory: the fear is learned by classical conditioning, then kept alive by operant conditioning through that relief. Avoidance also means the person never meets the feared thing and sees that nothing bad happens. Without that, the fear can't fade, which is called extinction.

questions.q: In the DSM-5, obsessive-compulsive disorder is grouped with which other condition rather than with the anxiety disorders?
o: Generalized anxiety disorder
Generalized anxiety disorder stays in the anxiety disorders class.
Posttraumatic stress disorder
PTSD left the anxiety class too, but into trauma- and stressor-related disorders.
Body dysmorphic disorder
Correct: OCD, body dysmorphic disorder, hoarding and hair pulling share their own class.
Panic disorder
Panic disorder is still an anxiety disorder in DSM-5.
questions.x: The DSM-5 is the manual clinicians use to diagnose mental disorders. In the 2013 edition, obsessive-compulsive disorder was moved out of the anxiety disorders into its own new class: obsessive-compulsive and related disorders. Body dysmorphic disorder (being stuck on a perceived flaw in your appearance) is in that class, along with hoarding, trichotillomania (hair pulling) and excoriation (skin picking). They all share repeated thoughts and behaviors. PTSD also left the anxiety disorders, but it went to a different class: trauma- and stressor-related disorders.

questions.q: After a severe argument, a woman suddenly cannot move her right arm, but neurological tests are normal. Which diagnosis is most likely?
o: Illness anxiety disorder
Illness anxiety is worrying about being sick with few or no symptoms. She has a real loss of function.
Factitious disorder
Factitious disorder means faking symptoms on purpose. Nothing suggests she's faking.
Somatic symptom disorder
Somatic symptom disorder centers on too much worry about symptoms, not a sudden unexplained paralysis.
Conversion disorder (functional neurological symptom disorder)
Correct: a real nerve-type symptom with normal tests, often after stress, and not faked.
questions.x: This is conversion disorder, also called functional neurological symptom disorder. The person has a real symptom that looks neurological, like a paralyzed arm, numbness or blindness, but tests show nothing wrong with the nerves or brain, and the symptom doesn't fit any known disease. It often shows up right after a stressful event, like this argument. Most important, she isn't faking. Somatic symptom disorder is the tempting wrong answer because it's also about the body, but that one centers on too much worry about symptoms, not a sudden loss of function.

questions.q: A patient has chronic pain and spends most of the day worrying about it, though she accepts the pain is real. Which DSM category does her primary diagnosis fall under?
o: Somatic symptom and related disorders
Correct: a real, distressing body symptom plus too much worry and attention spent on it.
Anxiety disorders
Her worry is about her body symptoms, and DSM-5 puts that in its own separate class.
Dissociative disorders
Dissociative disorders involve breaks in memory, identity or awareness.
Neurocognitive disorders
Neurocognitive disorders involve declining memory or thinking, like dementia.
questions.x: Somatic means 'of the body.' Somatic symptom disorder is when a person has one or more distressing physical symptoms and spends far too much time, worry and energy on them. The symptom can be completely real, like her chronic pain. It doesn't have to be medically unexplained. What makes it a disorder is how much the worry takes over her life. The anxiety disorders are the tempting wrong answer, because her worrying sounds anxious. But DSM-5, the diagnosis manual, puts worry focused on body symptoms in its own class: somatic symptom and related disorders.

questions.q: A woman has intense, unstable relationships, fears abandonment, self-harms and swings rapidly between idealizing and devaluing others. Which diagnosis fits best?
o: Dependent personality disorder
Dependent personality disorder is clinging and needing to be cared for, not idealizing then devaluing.
Borderline personality disorder
Correct: unstable relationships, self-image and emotions, fear of abandonment, self-harm and splitting.
Histrionic personality disorder
Histrionic personality disorder centers on seeking attention and dramatic emotion.
Bipolar II disorder
Bipolar mood episodes last days to weeks, not hours, and aren't tied to relationships.
questions.x: This is borderline personality disorder. It's marked by instability in three areas: relationships, sense of self and emotions. People with it often fear being abandoned and may make frantic efforts to avoid it, and self-harm is common. They also show splitting: seeing others as all good (idealizing) and then suddenly all bad (devaluing), with nothing in between. Bipolar II is the tempting wrong answer because of the mood swings. But bipolar mood episodes last days to weeks, while borderline mood shifts happen within hours and are usually set off by relationship events.

questions.q: A man avoids social contact because he desperately wants friends but fears rejection and criticism. Which diagnosis fits best?
o: Avoidant personality disorder
Correct: he wants connection but stays away out of fear of rejection and criticism.
Paranoid personality disorder
Paranoid people avoid others out of suspicion, not fear of rejection.
Antisocial personality disorder
Antisocial means disregard for others' rights, not avoiding people out of fear.
Schizoid personality disorder
Schizoid people don't want close relationships. This man desperately does.
questions.note: Avoidant wants friends; schizoid doesn't care.
questions.x: Two personality disorders leave people with few friends, but for opposite reasons. In avoidant personality disorder, the person wants close relationships but feels not good enough and is terrified of criticism or rejection, so he stays away. In schizoid personality disorder, the person simply isn't interested in close relationships and shows little emotion. The detail that he 'desperately wants friends' decides it: wanting friends but fearing rejection is avoidant. Paranoid personality disorder also keeps people apart, but the reason there is distrust and suspicion.

questions.q: How does obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (OCPD) typically differ from OCD?
o: OCPD involves intrusive unwanted thoughts the person resists
Intrusive, unwanted thoughts the person fights against describe OCD, not OCPD.
OCPD involves pervasive perfectionism seen as acceptable by the person, without true obsessions
Correct: OCPD is perfectionism the person sees as right, with no true unwanted obsessions.
OCPD is always more impairing than OCD
Neither one is always worse. How much each one disrupts life varies from person to person.
OCPD is a psychotic disorder
OCPD is a personality disorder. It involves no psychosis.
questions.x: These two have nearly the same name, but they're different. OCD (obsessive-compulsive disorder) has obsessions: intrusive, unwanted thoughts the person sees as wrong and tries to push away, often with rituals called compulsions. Psychologists call that ego-dystonic, meaning out of tune with who you are. OCPD (obsessive-compulsive personality disorder) is a lifelong personality style of perfectionism, order and control. The person thinks that's simply the right way to do things, which is called ego-syntonic, in tune with the self. There are no true obsessions. The two can occur together, but they're separate diagnoses.

questions.q: A clinician notes that a patient's distress about his symptoms is low because he sees his rigid traits as simply 'the right way to be.' This feature is most typical of which group of disorders?
o: Anxiety disorders
Anxiety symptoms are usually unwanted and upsetting to the person.
Dissociative identity disorder
Dissociative identity disorder usually comes with distress and memory gaps.
Personality disorders
Correct: personality disorder traits usually feel like part of the self, so distress is low.
Major depressive disorder
Depression comes with a lot of personal distress.
questions.x: When a trait feels like a natural part of who you are, psychologists call it ego-syntonic. This patient thinks his rigid traits are just 'the right way to be,' so they don't bother him much. That's typical of personality disorders. Because the traits feel normal to the person, they often feel little distress, may blame other people for conflicts, and often don't seek help. Most other disorders, like anxiety and depression, are ego-dystonic: the person experiences the symptoms as unwanted and upsetting, which often pushes them to get treatment.

questions.q: A hospitalized older patient suddenly becomes confused, with attention that fluctuates hour to hour, after starting a new medication. How does this differ from dementia?
o: Delirium is a personality disorder
Delirium is a neurocognitive disorder, not a personality disorder.
Delirium always progresses to death within months
Delirium often clears up once its cause is treated.
Delirium has acute onset and fluctuating attention and is often reversible
Correct: delirium is sudden, its attention swings, and it often reverses. Dementia is slow and keeps worsening.
Delirium involves only memory loss with intact attention
Trouble with attention is the core of delirium, and the question says her attention swings.
questions.x: This is delirium. Delirium is a sudden problem with attention and awareness. It starts over hours to days, gets better and worse through the day, and has a cause you can find, like a new medication, an infection or a chemical imbalance in the blood. Fix the cause and it often clears up. Dementia is different: it comes on slowly over months to years, keeps getting worse, and mainly hits memory first while attention stays fairly intact early on. Sudden onset, swinging attention and a new drug all point to delirium.

questions.q: Children who already enjoy drawing are paid for each picture. When payment stops, they draw less than before. What does this demonstrate?
o: Spontaneous recovery
Spontaneous recovery is a faded response coming back after a rest, not interest dropping.
The overjustification effect
Correct: an outside reward for something already enjoyed lowers the inner drive to do it.
Learned helplessness
Learned helplessness comes from bad events you can't control, not from being paid.
Drive reduction
Drive reduction is about meeting body needs like hunger. Drawing isn't a body need.
questions.x: This is the overjustification effect. Intrinsic motivation means doing something because you enjoy it. Extrinsic motivation means doing it for an outside reward, like money. These kids already loved drawing. Once they got paid for each picture, they started to see drawing as something they did for pay. When the pay stopped, their reason to draw seemed to disappear, so they drew less than they did before the payments started. Spontaneous recovery is a distractor: that's when a faded conditioned response comes back after a break, not motivation dropping below where it started.

questions.q: Opponent-process theory explains drug tolerance and withdrawal by proposing what?
o: Behavior aims at external incentives only
Behavior pulled by outside rewards is incentive theory, a different idea.
An initial emotional reaction triggers an opposing reaction that strengthens with repetition
Correct: the opposite reaction grows with each use, causing tolerance and the crash of withdrawal.
Drugs permanently destroy reward neurons after one use
One use doesn't permanently destroy reward neurons. That's not what this theory says.
Arousal stays constant regardless of drug use
The theory is all about feelings swinging one way, then the other.
questions.x: Richard Solomon's opponent-process theory says that when something causes a strong feeling, the brain kicks off an opposite feeling to bring you back to normal.
