With a drug, the first reaction is the high. The opposite reaction pulls you down. Each time the drug is used, that opposite reaction gets faster and stronger. So the same dose gives less of a high, which is tolerance. And when the drug wears off, the opposite reaction is still there with nothing to balance it, so you crash, which is withdrawal. Incentive theory is about outside rewards and doesn't explain this rebound.

questions.q: Students randomly assigned to argue one side of a debate later report attitudes closer to the side they argued. This best illustrates what?
o: Role-playing can change attitudes
Correct: arguing a position out loud led students to adopt matching attitudes.
Personality traits fully determine behavior
Sides were assigned at random, so prior traits can't explain the change.
Drive reduction
Drive reduction is about meeting body needs like hunger. Debating isn't one.
Attitudes always precede behavior
Here behavior came first and the attitude followed, so 'always' is wrong.
questions.x: We usually think attitudes come first and behavior follows. But it works the other way too: acting out a position can change what you believe. These students were assigned a side at random, then argued it out loud, and their attitudes moved toward that side. Two ideas explain it. Self-perception theory says we figure out our attitudes partly by watching our own behavior. Cognitive dissonance is the uncomfortable feeling when actions and beliefs clash, and we ease it by shifting the belief. Random assignment matters: it means prior traits or opinions can't explain the change.

questions.q: Per the theory of planned behavior, which factor besides attitude predicts a person's intention to exercise?
o: Subjective norms and perceived control
Correct: intention depends on attitude, what others expect, and how able you feel.
Id impulses and superego constraints
Id and superego are Freud's ideas, not part of this model.
Classical conditioning history only
This model is about conscious plans, not conditioning history.
Heritability of physical fitness
Heritability is a genetics idea and isn't a factor in this model.
questions.x: Icek Ajzen's theory of planned behavior says the best predictor of what you'll do is your intention, your plan to do it. Intention depends on three things. Attitude: how you feel about the behavior ('I like exercise'). Subjective norms: what the people who matter to you expect ('my friends think I should work out'). Perceived behavioral control: how confident you are that you can actually do it ('I have time and a gym nearby'). So the two factors besides attitude are subjective norms and perceived behavioral control. It's a model about conscious thinking, so Freudian ideas, conditioning and genetics aren't part of it.

questions.q: In the elaboration likelihood model, a person persuaded by a speaker's attractiveness rather than her arguments is using which route?
o: Central route
The central route means weighing the arguments carefully. This person ignored them.
Peripheral route
Correct: being swayed by surface cues like looks is the peripheral route.
Cognitive route
There's no 'cognitive route' in this model. It only has central and peripheral.
Affective route
There's no 'affective route' in this model. It only has central and peripheral.
questions.note: Central-route attitude change lasts longer.
questions.x: The elaboration likelihood model says there are two routes to being persuaded. 'Elaboration' just means thinking hard about a message. On the central route, you pay close attention and weigh how good the arguments are. That change tends to last. On the peripheral route, you're swayed by surface cues, like how attractive or famous the speaker is, or how long the message is. People take this route when they don't care much or can't think it through. Being won over by the speaker's looks instead of her arguments is the peripheral route.

questions.q: Researchers find that people who report positive attitudes toward a group respond more slowly when pairing the group with positive words on a timed task. What does this suggest?
o: Their explicit attitudes are definitely false
The result shows a gap, not that people are lying. 'Definitely false' is far too strong.
Their implicit attitudes may differ from their explicit attitudes
Correct: timed tasks like the IAT can reveal automatic links that differ from what people report.
Attitudes have no affective component
Attitudes do have a feeling part. This task doesn't remove it.
Implicit attitudes cannot be measured
Timed tasks like this one were built to measure implicit attitudes.
questions.x: There are two kinds of attitudes. Explicit attitudes are the ones you know about and can report, like on a survey. Implicit attitudes are automatic links in your mind that you may not even notice. Researchers measure implicit attitudes indirectly, often with the Implicit Association Test (IAT), which times how fast you pair a group with good or bad words. Faster pairing means a stronger automatic link. Here people said they felt positively, but they were slow to pair the group with positive words. That suggests their implicit attitudes may differ from their explicit ones. It doesn't prove anyone is lying.

questions.q: According to Zajonc's drive theory, the mere presence of others tends to:
o: Impair performance on every kind of task equally
An audience helps some tasks and hurts others. The word 'every' is the trap.
Strengthen dominant responses, aiding simple or well-learned tasks
Correct: others raise arousal, which boosts your go-to response, and that helps on easy, practiced tasks.
Lower arousal and make people calmer
Drive theory says other people raise arousal, not lower it.
Improve performance only on novel, complex tasks
This is backward. On new, complex tasks your go-to response is often wrong, so you do worse.
questions.note: Easy task + audience = better; hard task + audience = worse.
questions.x: Robert Zajonc noticed that having other people around raises arousal, meaning your body's alertness and energy. Arousal makes your dominant response stronger. The dominant response is whatever you're most likely to do, the thing that comes most easily. On a simple or well-practiced task, your dominant response is usually right, so an audience helps. On a hard or new task, your dominant response is often wrong, so an audience hurts. That's why an audience doesn't hurt every task equally, and why it doesn't mainly help on new, complex tasks.

questions.q: In a study, an audience improved performance on a simple task, but the effect vanished when the audience members were blindfolded. Which explanation does this most support?
o: Evaluation apprehension
Correct: blindfolded watchers can't judge, so worry about judgment drops and the boost disappears.
Mere presence theory
Mere presence predicts a boost even from watchers who can't see. The boost disappeared.
Diffusion of responsibility
Diffusion of responsibility explains people helping less in groups, not performance changes.
Social loafing
Social loafing happens when your effort is hidden in a group, not when you're watched.
questions.x: An audience made people better at a simple task. But when the audience wore blindfolds, the boost disappeared. Ask what the blindfold took away. The audience was still there, so it didn't remove presence. It removed the audience's ability to judge the performer. That supports evaluation apprehension: the idea that audiences raise arousal because we worry about being judged. Mere presence theory is the tempting wrong answer. It says just having people in the room is enough, so it predicts the boost should stay even with blindfolds. It didn't.

questions.q: A theory proposes that an audience raises arousal because the performer's attention is split between the task and the observers. This is known as:
o: Evaluation apprehension theory
This theory says arousal comes from fear of being judged, not from split attention.
Mere presence theory
Mere presence says others raise arousal just by being there, with no mention of attention.
Distraction-conflict theory
Correct: being pulled between the task and the audience creates the arousal.
Deindividuation theory
Deindividuation is losing self-awareness in a crowd, not split attention.
questions.x: This is distraction-conflict theory. It says an audience pulls some of your attention away from the task. Now you're torn between focusing on the task and noticing the people watching. That tug-of-war inside your head creates arousal (a keyed-up, alert state). Then the usual social facilitation pattern follows: easy tasks get better and hard tasks get worse. The key word in the question is attention. Evaluation apprehension is the tempting pick because there's an audience, but it says arousal comes from fear of being judged, not from split attention.

questions.q: The loss of self-awareness and sense of personal responsibility that can occur in large, anonymous groups is called:
o: Social loafing
Social loafing is putting in less effort on a pooled group task, not losing self-awareness.
Group polarization
Group polarization is discussion making a group's opinion more extreme.
Deindividuation
Correct: anonymity and arousal in a crowd lower self-awareness and self-restraint.
Conformity
Conformity is matching the group, which you can do while fully self-aware.
questions.x: This is deindividuation. In a big crowd where nobody knows who you are, people can lose their sense of self-awareness and personal responsibility. Three things set it off: anonymity (being unidentifiable), arousal (being keyed up) and getting absorbed in the group. Once that happens, people stop checking their behavior against their own values and just go with what's happening around them. That's how normally calm people can join in a riot. Don't confuse it with social loafing, which is slacking off on a group task, or conformity, which you can do while fully aware of yourself.

questions.q: Participants wearing loose hoods that hid their faces delivered longer noise blasts to a target than participants wearing large name tags. This finding is best explained by:
o: Deindividuation produced by anonymity
Correct: hidden faces lower accountability and self-checking, which raised aggression.
Social facilitation
Social facilitation is about how an audience changes performance, not about anonymity.
The bystander effect
The bystander effect is about people failing to help, not becoming more aggressive.
Informational social influence
Nobody was looking to others for the right answer in this study.
questions.x: The only thing that changed between the two groups was whether people could be identified. Hoods hid their faces; big name tags made them easy to identify. The hooded people gave longer noise blasts, meaning they were more aggressive. That's deindividuation: anonymity makes people feel less accountable and pay less attention to their own values, which can release aggression. Name tags make you identifiable, so people hold back. Social facilitation is tempting because it's about others being around, but the study changed anonymity, not whether an audience was watching.

questions.q: Anonymous participants dressed as hospital staff gave weaker punishments than identifiable controls, while anonymous participants dressed as executioners gave stronger ones. What does this suggest about deindividuation?
o: Anonymity always increases aggression
The hospital-staff group punished less, so anonymity didn't always raise aggression.
Costumes have no effect once anonymity is controlled
The costumes pushed behavior in opposite directions, so they clearly had an effect.
Deindividuation only occurs in groups larger than 10
Group size was never changed here, so no rule about 10 people can be drawn.
It heightens responsiveness to situational cues and norms
Correct: anonymous people follow the norms their situation suggests, caring or harmful.
questions.note: Deindividuation is not automatically antisocial; it amplifies salient norms.
questions.x: Everyone in these groups was anonymous, but the costume pointed them in different directions. Dressed as hospital staff, anonymous people punished less than identifiable controls. Dressed as executioners, they punished more. So deindividuation doesn't just unleash aggression. It makes people follow whatever norms (unwritten rules about how to act) the situation suggests. A nurse's uniform suggests caring; an executioner's costume suggests harm. Because the results went in opposite directions, 'anonymity always increases aggression' can't be right.

questions.q: A man collapses on a crowded train platform. Each onlooker assumes someone else will call for help, so no one does. Which process is most directly at work?
o: Deindividuation
Deindividuation is losing self-awareness, usually leading to wild behavior, not doing nothing.
Pluralistic ignorance
Pluralistic ignorance is misreading others' calm as 'no emergency,' not assuming someone else will act.
Diffusion of responsibility
Correct: with many onlookers, each person feels less responsible and assumes someone else will call.
Group polarization
Group polarization is about opinions getting more extreme after discussion.
questions.x: This is diffusion of responsibility. When many people see an emergency, the duty to act gets spread across all of them, so each person feels only a small slice of it. The clue in the question is that 'each onlooker assumes someone else will call.' That's part of the bystander effect: the more people around, the less likely any one of them helps. Pluralistic ignorance is the tempting wrong answer. It's also part of the bystander effect, but it means looking at everyone else's calm faces and deciding it isn't really an emergency.

questions.q: A bystander weighs the physical danger of intervening against the guilt and blame she would feel if she did nothing, and helps only when the balance favors it. This reflects the:
o: Arousal: cost-reward model
Correct: people help when the costs of not helping outweigh the costs of helping.
Diffusion of responsibility account
Diffusion of responsibility is about how many bystanders there are, not weighing costs.
Kin selection hypothesis
Kin selection explains helping your genetic relatives. No relatives are involved.
Just-world hypothesis
The just-world idea is that people get what they deserve. It tends to reduce helping.
questions.x: This is the arousal: cost-reward model of helping. Seeing an emergency creates arousal, an upset, tense feeling that you want to get rid of. You then pick the response with the best balance of costs. Helping has costs, like physical danger or effort. Not helping has costs too, like guilt and blame. You help when not helping would cost you more. That's exactly what this bystander is doing: weighing danger against guilt. Diffusion of responsibility is the tempting wrong answer since it's about bystanders, but it's about how many people are present, not weighing costs.

questions.q: Cyclists perform a simple pedaling task beside co-actors. In condition 1 each rider's output is displayed separately; in condition 2 only the combined output is shown. Which pattern is predicted?
o: Equal effort in both conditions, since co-actors are present in both
Others are present in both, but only condition 1 shows each person's output. That changes effort.
Lower effort in condition 1 and higher effort in condition 2
This flips it. Showing each rider's own output should raise effort, not lower it.
Lower effort in both conditions compared with riding alone
Being individually watched on a simple task usually raises effort, so condition 1 won't drop.
Higher effort in condition 1 and lower effort in condition 2
Correct: individually shown output boosts effort; pooled output lets people slack off.
questions.note: Others present + individually evaluated = facilitation; pooled = loafing.
questions.x: In both conditions, other riders are there. The difference is whether each person's own output can be seen. In condition 1, each rider's output is shown separately, so they can be judged. Being watched and evaluated raises arousal, and on a simple task like pedaling that boosts performance. That's social facilitation. In condition 2, only the group total is shown, so nobody can tell who's slacking. People tend to ease off, which is called social loafing. So effort should be higher in condition 1 and lower in condition 2. Presence alone doesn't decide it; being identifiable does.

questions.q: During discussion, group members hear new arguments that support the position most of them already favored, and their views become more extreme. This mechanism of polarization is best described as:
o: Normative social comparison
Social comparison is shifting to look as committed as others, not hearing new arguments.
Persuasive arguments (informational influence)
Correct: hearing new reasons that back the majority view pushes members further.
Diffusion of responsibility
Diffusion of responsibility explains less helping in groups, not opinion shifts.
Reduction of cognitive dissonance
Dissonance is discomfort when actions and beliefs clash. No clash appears here.
questions.note: Two polarization mechanisms: informational (new arguments) and normative (social comparison).
questions.x: Group polarization is when discussion pushes a group further in the direction it already leaned. There are two explanations. The informational one, called the persuasive arguments account, says discussion exposes people to new reasons supporting the majority view, and those new reasons push them further. The normative one, called social comparison, says people shift to look at least as committed as everyone else. The question says members 'hear new arguments' that support their side. New arguments are the signature of the informational, persuasive arguments mechanism.

questions.q: In a task matching tones to a reference pitch, participants conformed to a unanimous incorrect majority on 32% of trials. When one confederate gave the correct answer, conformity fell to 7%. What does this show?
o: Majority size is the only factor controlling conformity
The majority's size didn't change. Breaking the unanimous agreement did.
A single dissenter who breaks unanimity sharply reduces conformity
Correct: one ally who breaks the group's agreement makes resisting far easier.
Conformity in this task was purely informational
This design can't separate informational from normative influence, so 'purely' is too strong.
Conformity becomes permanent once it begins
Conformity dropped right away when one person disagreed, so it isn't permanent.
questions.x: Conformity means changing your answer or behavior to match a group. When the whole group agreed on a wrong answer, people went along with it on 32% of trials. When just one confederate (someone secretly working with the researchers) gave the right answer, conformity fell to 7%. The wrong majority was the same size both times. The only change was that the group was no longer unanimous. So one dissenter, one person who breaks from the group, makes it much easier to resist. This matches Solomon Asch's classic findings.

questions.q: A new resident starts composting because she admires her neighbors and wants to be like them, though she is not convinced it helps the environment. In Kelman's framework, this is:
o: Identification
Correct: she takes on the behavior to be like neighbors she admires.
Internalization
Internalization means truly believing in it. She isn't convinced.
Compliance
Compliance is driven by rewards or punishments. Admiration is driving her.
Obedience
Obedience is following an order from an authority. Nobody ordered her.
questions.note: Compliance (reward) < identification (relationship) < internalization (belief).
questions.x: Herbert Kelman described three reasons people go along with a behavior. Compliance: you do it to get a reward or avoid a punishment. Identification: you do it because you admire a person or group and want to be like them. Internalization: you do it because you truly believe it's right. This woman composts because she admires her neighbors and wants to be like them, but she isn't convinced it helps the environment. That's identification. Internalization is out because she doesn't believe in it, and compliance is out because nobody's rewarding or punishing her.

questions.q: After an obedience study, participants explained that they were simply carrying out instructions and that the experimenter bore responsibility. Milgram called this mindset the:
o: Agentic state
Correct: people see themselves as tools of the authority and shift responsibility onto it.
Foot-in-the-door effect
Foot-in-the-door is agreeing to a big request after a small one, not shifting blame.
Deindividuated state
Deindividuation comes from being anonymous in a crowd, not from deferring to an authority.
Cognitive dissonance
Dissonance is discomfort from inconsistency. Shifting blame to an authority is the agentic state.
questions.x: Stanley Milgram ran famous obedience studies in which participants were told to give what they thought were painful shocks to another person. He suggested that under an authority, people can slip into an agentic state. They stop seeing themselves as acting on their own and start seeing themselves as an agent, a tool carrying out someone else's wishes. Responsibility shifts to the authority in their minds: 'I was just following instructions.' That's what lets ordinary people do harmful things. Deindividuation is the tempting wrong answer, but it comes from anonymity in a crowd, not from deferring to an authority.

questions.q: In an obedience study, the shock level rose in small 15-volt steps, so each command was only slightly greater than the one already obeyed. This incremental structure exploits the:
o: Door-in-the-face technique
Door-in-the-face starts with a big request that's refused, then a smaller one.
Low-ball technique
Low-balling changes the deal for the worse after someone has agreed.
Reciprocity norm
Reciprocity is returning a favor. No favor was given here.
Foot-in-the-door effect
Correct: agreeing to small steps made each slightly bigger step hard to refuse.
questions.x: This is the foot-in-the-door effect: once people agree to a small request, they're more likely to agree to a bigger one. In Milgram's obedience study, the shocks went up in small 15-volt steps. Each new command was only a little more than what the person had already done, so refusing felt inconsistent: 'I already gave 150 volts, so why not 165?' Door-in-the-face is the tempting wrong answer since the names are similar, but it works the other way around: start with a huge request that gets turned down, then ask for something smaller.

questions.q: A city funds heritage festivals and offers public services in several languages so immigrant communities can keep their traditions while participating fully in civic life. This policy reflects:
o: Assimilation
Assimilation expects minority traditions to fade, not be kept.
Amalgamation
Amalgamation blends cultures into one new 'melting pot' culture.
Segregation
Segregation separates groups. This city is bringing them into civic life.
Multiculturalism
Correct: distinct cultures are valued and kept alive within one shared society.
questions.note: Multiculturalism = salad bowl; amalgamation = melting pot.
questions.x: This is multiculturalism, often called the 'salad bowl' model. Each culture keeps its own identity, like each ingredient in a salad, while everyone still shares one society and civic life. Funding heritage festivals and offering services in several languages helps immigrant communities keep their traditions while taking full part in the city. Compare the others. Assimilation expects minority cultures to fade into the majority. Amalgamation, the 'melting pot,' blends everything into one new combined culture. Segregation keeps groups apart. Keeping traditions alive points to multiculturalism.

questions.q: Researchers track an immigrant group across three generations. Host-language fluency rises steadily, and intermarriage with the majority group increases from 5% to 40%. These data most directly indicate:
o: Growing multiculturalism
Multiculturalism would show heritage practices kept. Rising host-language use and intermarriage show blending in.
Increasing residential segregation
More intermarriage means more contact between groups, not more separation.
Stronger transmission of the heritage culture
Rising host-language fluency and intermarriage point to the heritage culture weakening, not getting stronger.
Increasing assimilation
Correct: picking up the host language and marrying into the majority are classic signs of assimilation.
questions.x: Assimilation is the process of a minority group taking on the majority culture. Sociologists measure it with markers like speaking the host country's language, living in mixed neighborhoods and marrying into the majority group (intermarriage). Here, host-language fluency rises with each generation, and intermarriage climbs from 5% to 40%, which is 8 times higher (40 ÷ 5 = 8). Both markers show the group blending into the mainstream. Multiculturalism is the tempting wrong answer, but that would show heritage customs and language being kept, not fading.

questions.q: Some second-generation immigrants absorb the norms of a disadvantaged segment of society and experience downward mobility, while others keep strong ethnic ties and move up. This pattern is described by:
o: Straight-line assimilation
Straight-line assimilation predicts everyone moves steadily toward the mainstream. These paths split apart.
Segmented assimilation
Correct: outcomes depend on which part of society the family assimilates into.
Cultural pluralism
Cultural pluralism describes groups living side by side, not different paths up or down.
Amalgamation
Amalgamation is cultures blending into a new one, not different outcomes by group.
questions.x: Segmented assimilation theory says immigrant families don't all blend into one single 'mainstream.' Society has different segments, and which one a family's children assimilate into shapes how things turn out. Some move up into the middle class. Some take on the norms of a disadvantaged group and move down, which is called downward mobility. Others move up while keeping strong ties to their own ethnic community. The question describes exactly that split. Straight-line assimilation is the tempting wrong answer, but it predicts everyone moves steadily along one path toward the mainstream.

questions.q: Heavy television viewers estimate their chance of being a victim of violent crime as much higher than light viewers do, even after controlling for neighborhood crime rates. Which theory best explains this?
o: Agenda-setting theory
Agenda-setting is about which issues seem important, not distorted beliefs about real risk.
Two-step flow model
The two-step flow model says media ideas pass through opinion leaders first.
Uses and gratifications theory
Uses and gratifications explains why people choose media, not how media changes beliefs.
Cultivation theory
Correct: long-term heavy viewing shapes beliefs to match the violent TV world.
questions.note: Cultivation's 'mean world syndrome'.
questions.x: Cultivation theory says that watching a lot of TV over a long time slowly shapes how you see the real world, until it starts to look like the TV world. TV shows far more violence than real life has. So heavy viewers come to believe the world is more dangerous than it is, which is nicknamed 'mean world syndrome.' The researchers controlled for neighborhood crime rates, so real danger can't explain the gap. Agenda-setting is the tempting wrong answer, but it's about which issues seem important, not distorted beliefs about personal risk.

questions.q: A teen learns techniques for shoplifting and justifications for it, such as 'big stores can afford it', from his closest friends. Which theory best explains his behavior?
o: Labeling theory
Labeling theory is about how others' reactions shape later deviance, not how it's learned.
Strain theory
Strain theory is about the gap between goals and legal ways to reach them.
Differential association theory
Correct: rule-breaking is learned from close others, who teach the methods and the excuses.
Social control theory
Social control theory asks why people follow rules and points to social bonds.
questions.x: Edwin Sutherland's differential association theory says breaking rules is learned, just like any other behavior, through close relationships. The people closest to you teach two things: the techniques (how to do it) and the attitudes or excuses that make it seem okay (why it's fine). This teen learned both from his closest friends: how to shoplift, and the excuse that 'big stores can afford it.' That's a perfect match. Labeling theory is the tempting wrong answer since it's also about deviance, but it's about how others' reactions shape someone later, not how the behavior was learned.

questions.q: In Goffman's classification, stigma attached to a person's ethnicity, nationality or religion is called:
o: Abomination of the body
Abomination of the body means physical differences like deformities or disabilities.
Blemish of individual character
Blemish of character means perceived flaws like addiction or a prison record.
Courtesy stigma
Courtesy stigma falls on people connected to a stigmatized person, not on their own identity.
Tribal stigma
Correct: tribal stigma attaches to group identity passed down through family, like ethnicity or religion.
questions.x: Stigma is a mark that makes society see a person as less acceptable. Erving Goffman sorted stigma into three types. Abominations of the body are physical differences, like a deformity or disability. Blemishes of individual character are perceived flaws in someone's character, like addiction or a prison record. Tribal stigma is tied to group identity passed down through families, like race, ethnicity, nationality or religion. So stigma attached to ethnicity, nationality or religion is tribal stigma. Courtesy stigma is a separate idea: stigma that rubs off on people connected to a stigmatized person.

questions.q: A man with schizophrenia comes to believe the stereotype that people like him are incompetent, and he stops applying for jobs. This is an example of:
o: Courtesy stigma
Courtesy stigma falls on people connected to him, like family, not on him.
Public stigma
Public stigma is the general public believing the stereotype, not him believing it about himself.
Self-stigma
Correct: he's taken the stereotype in and applied it to himself, so he stops trying.
Structural stigma
Structural stigma lives in laws and institutional policies, not in personal beliefs.
questions.x: This is self-stigma. It happens when a person takes in the negative stereotypes society holds about their group and applies them to themselves. This man has heard that people with schizophrenia are incompetent, and now he believes it about himself. That lowers self-esteem and motivation, which can lead to the 'why try' effect: 'Why apply for jobs if I'll fail anyway?' Public stigma is the tempting wrong answer. It's the general public believing the stereotype. Self-stigma is when the person turns that belief on himself.

questions.q: Relatives of people with substance use disorders report being avoided by neighbors because of their family member's addiction. This is best described as:
o: Tribal stigma
Tribal stigma attaches to a person's own race, nationality or religion.
Courtesy stigma
Correct: stigma that spreads to people just because they're connected to a stigmatized person.
Self-stigma
Self-stigma is believing a stereotype about yourself. Here the neighbors are doing the judging.
Secondary deviance
Secondary deviance is a labeled person's own further rule-breaking. The relatives aren't breaking rules.
questions.x: This is courtesy stigma, also called associative stigma. It's disapproval aimed at people just because they're connected to someone who is stigmatized. These relatives haven't done anything wrong and don't have the stigmatized trait themselves. Neighbors avoid them only because a family member has an addiction. Tribal stigma is the tempting wrong answer because it involves family, but tribal stigma attaches to a person's own race, nationality or religion, passed down through their lineage. These relatives are judged for their connection, not their own identity.

questions.q: A nurse washes her hands far more often than her coworkers, who tease her for it, even though her practice reduces infections. Sociologically, her behavior is best described as:
o: Normative, because it is beneficial
Normative means matching what the group expects. Her coworkers tease her, so she doesn't match.
Not deviant, because it breaks no formal rule
Deviance includes breaking unwritten rules, not just formal ones.
Deviant, because it departs from the group's norms
Correct: deviance means departing from the group's norms, whether the act helps or harms.
Criminal, because it breaks workplace expectations
Crime means breaking a formal law. Washing hands breaks no law.
questions.note: Deviance can be positive; it is defined relative to group norms.
questions.x: In sociology, deviance simply means going against the norms of a group. A norm is a shared rule, often unwritten, about how people are expected to act. Deviance isn't about whether something is good or bad. The nurse washes her hands far more than her coworkers, and they tease her for it, which shows she's breaking their informal norm. So in that group, she's deviant. Because her behavior actually helps, it's sometimes called positive deviance. It isn't criminal, since crime means breaking a formal law, and there's no law against washing your hands.

questions.q: First-time juvenile offenders are randomly assigned to formal court processing or to an informal diversion program. Those formally processed later reoffend more often. Which theory do these results most directly support?
o: Strain theory
Strain theory is about blocked opportunities, which this study didn't change.
Functionalism
Functionalism doesn't predict that official processing makes reoffending more likely.
Social control theory
Social control theory focuses on social bonds, which weren't measured or changed here.
Labeling theory
Correct: being officially labeled an offender seems to push people toward more deviance.
questions.x: Labeling theory says that when society officially tags someone as deviant, the person may start to see themselves that way and break more rules. Being labeled an 'offender' can close doors, change how others treat you and reshape your identity. In this study, first-time offenders were randomly assigned to formal court or informal diversion. Random assignment means the two groups were alike at the start, so the only real difference was the formal label. The formally processed group reoffended more, which directly supports labeling theory. Strain and control theories don't fit, because the study didn't change opportunities or social bonds.

questions.q: A theory of crowd behavior holds that in ambiguous situations, crowd members collectively develop new norms that define what behavior is appropriate. This is:
o: Contagion theory
Contagion says emotions spread through a crowd and overwhelm judgment, not that new rules form.
Convergence theory
Convergence says crowds gather people who already think alike.
Value-added theory
Value-added theory lists the conditions needed for collective behavior to happen.
Emergent-norm theory
Correct: in unclear situations, crowd members build new rules together as they interact.
questions.x: This is emergent-norm theory. A norm is a shared rule about how to act. When a situation is unclear, like a sudden emergency or a protest with no plan, people in a crowd look at each other, talk and figure out together what to do. New rules 'emerge' right there, on the spot. So this theory sees crowd behavior as following rules, not as mindless. Contagion theory is the classic contrast: it says emotions sweep through a crowd and take over people's judgment, with no new rules being built.

questions.q: A researcher argues that violent protest crowds are not created by the crowd itself but form because people who already hold similar grievances and dispositions gather together. This view is:
o: Contagion theory
Contagion says the crowd itself changes people. This researcher says they were already alike.
Emergent-norm theory
Emergent-norm says new rules form inside the crowd, not that they existed beforehand.
Convergence theory
Correct: crowd behavior reflects like-minded people who chose to gather.
Diffusion of responsibility
Diffusion of responsibility explains people helping less, not why crowds form.
questions.x: This is convergence theory. It says a crowd doesn't change people. Instead, people who already share the same views, grievances and tendencies choose to come together. The crowd's behavior just shows what those individuals already felt. The researcher's words 'people who already hold similar grievances' are the giveaway. Contagion theory is the opposite: it says the crowd itself changes people, sweeping them up in emotion. Emergent-norm theory says new rules form inside the crowd, which also puts the cause in the crowd, not in the people beforehand.

questions.q: Investigators study an outbreak of headaches and fainting in a school. Which finding would most support a psychogenic rather than a toxic cause?
o: Elevated levels of a solvent in affected students' blood
A solvent measured in the blood is direct evidence of a real chemical exposure.
Symptom severity rising with proximity to an air vent
Symptoms getting worse closer to a vent point to a physical source like a toxin.
All affected students having been in a single room
Everyone being in one room fits a shared physical source.
Symptoms spreading along friendship networks, including to other buildings
Correct: spreading along friendships, even to other buildings, points to a social, not chemical, cause.
questions.x: Psychogenic illness means real symptoms, like headaches or fainting, that come from the mind and spread through social contact, not from a physical poison. A toxic cause follows physical patterns: you can measure the chemical in people's bodies, and symptoms are worse closer to the source. A psychogenic outbreak follows social patterns instead. It spreads from person to person as people see friends get sick. Symptoms moving along friendship lines, even into other buildings that share no air, fit a social cause, not a chemical one. The other three findings all point to a real toxin.

questions.q: A study finds parents in closely supervised jobs stress obedience in their children, while parents in self-directed jobs stress independence, even after controlling for income. Which conclusion is best supported?
o: Work conditions shape the values parents pass on to children
Correct: what parents experience at work shapes the values they teach their kids.
Children's personalities determine their parents' jobs
This flips cause and effect, and children's personalities weren't tested.
Income fully explains differences in parenting values
Income was controlled and the difference stayed, so income can't fully explain it.
Peer groups are the main source of children's values
Peers weren't measured, so the study can't say anything about them.
questions.x: Sociologist Melvin Kohn found that parents' jobs shape what they value and teach their kids. Parents whose work is closely supervised, where following orders matters most, tend to stress obedience. Parents with self-directed work, where they make their own decisions, tend to stress independence. The study controlled for income, meaning it compared parents with similar incomes, and the difference was still there. So income can't fully explain it. The best conclusion is that work conditions shape the values parents pass on. This connects the workplace to socialization, how children learn their society's values.

questions.q: An immigrant speaks the host language and follows host customs at work while keeping her heritage religion, language and cuisine at home. In Berry's acculturation model, this strategy is:
o: Assimilation
Assimilation means giving up the heritage culture. She keeps hers.
Integration
Correct: she keeps her heritage culture and also takes part in the host culture.
Separation
Separation keeps the heritage culture but avoids the host culture. She joins in at work.
Marginalization
Marginalization means losing touch with both cultures. She keeps both.
questions.x: Acculturation is the set of changes that happen when people from one culture live in another. John Berry's model asks two yes-or-no questions. Do you keep your heritage culture? Do you take part in the host culture? Yes to both is integration. Heritage only is separation. Host only is assimilation. Neither is marginalization. This woman follows host customs and speaks the host language at work, so she takes part in the host culture. She keeps her heritage religion, language and food at home, so she keeps her heritage too. Yes to both means integration.

questions.q: Students overestimate how much their peers drink. After a campaign shows that most students actually have fewer than four drinks when they go out, heavy drinking declines. The campaign most likely worked by:
o: Increasing obedience to campus authorities
Obedience means following commands from an authority. The campaign shared facts, not orders.
Reducing social loafing
Social loafing is putting in less effort on a group task. That's not what changed.
Increasing deindividuation
Nothing about anonymity or self-awareness changed. Beliefs about peers did.
Correcting a misperceived descriptive norm
Correct: students match what they think peers do, so fixing that belief changed behavior.
questions.x: A descriptive norm is what people believe others actually do. People tend to match it. These students thought their peers drank much more than they really did, so they drank more to keep up. The campaign showed the real number: most students have fewer than four drinks when they go out. Once students saw that, their idea of 'normal' dropped, and heavy drinking dropped with it. This is called the social norms approach. It isn't obedience, because no one in authority gave an order. The campaign only shared facts about peers.

questions.q: Most residents adopted a new health app not after seeing its ads but after hearing about it from respected acquaintances who closely followed tech news. This pattern supports the:
o: Cultivation theory
Cultivation is about long-term heavy viewing shaping how people see the world.
Hypodermic needle model
The hypodermic needle model predicts the ads would work directly. They didn't.
Two-step flow model
Correct: media reaches opinion leaders first, who then pass it on through personal contact.
Agenda-setting theory
Agenda-setting is about which issues seem important, not how a product spreads.
questions.x: The two-step flow model says media messages don't hit everyone directly. Step one: the message reaches opinion leaders, people who follow the news closely and whom others trust. Step two: those leaders pass it on to everyone else through everyday conversation, and that personal contact is what actually changes minds. Here, the ads alone didn't do much. People adopted the app after hearing about it from respected acquaintances who follow tech news. That's two-step flow. The hypodermic needle model is the opposite view: it says media 'injects' its message straight into a passive audience.

questions.q: An archival study finds that crowds watching a person threaten to jump from a building were more likely to jeer and urge the person on when the crowd was large and it was dark. This is best explained by:
o: Social facilitation
Social facilitation is about how an audience changes task performance, not hostile crowds.
Deindividuation
Correct: big crowds and darkness add anonymity, which lowers restraint.
The bystander effect
The bystander effect explains failing to help, not actively jeering.
Group polarization
Group polarization needs discussion that pushes views further. None is described.
questions.x: A big crowd and darkness both make people feel anonymous: nobody can tell who's who. Anonymity lowers self-awareness and the sense that you'll be held accountable. That state is called deindividuation, and it lets people do things they'd never do alone, like jeering at someone in danger. The bystander effect is the tempting wrong answer, since a crowd is watching someone in trouble. But the bystander effect explains people failing to help. This crowd isn't just standing there; it's actively urging the person on. That active, uninhibited behavior points to deindividuation.

questions.q: A student who moves next to a railway stops reacting to passing trains after a few weeks. Which process best describes this?
o: Extinction
Extinction needs a learned (conditioned) response first. Jumping at train noise was never learned.
Habituation
Correct: a smaller and smaller reaction to a repeated, harmless stimulus is habituation.
Sensitization
Sensitization is a bigger reaction, not a smaller one.
Stimulus discrimination
Discrimination means reacting differently to similar stimuli, not fading out on one.
questions.note: Habituation is a drop in an unlearned response to a repeated stimulus.
questions.x: This is habituation: you respond less and less to something harmless that keeps happening. At first the trains made the student jump. After weeks of the same noise with nothing bad attached, the reaction faded. Extinction is the tempting wrong answer, because responding also drops there. But extinction only applies to a response that was learned through conditioning (pairing two things). Jumping at a loud noise is built in, not learned, so there's nothing to extinguish.

questions.q: For hours after a nearby explosion, a soldier startles strongly at many unrelated quiet sounds. Which process does this illustrate?
o: Sensitization
Correct: an intense event made the soldier jumpier to many later sounds.
Habituation
Habituation would make startle smaller, not bigger.
Dishabituation
Dishabituation brings back a faded response to one stimulus, not a broad rise across many sounds.
Negative reinforcement
Nothing unpleasant is being removed to strengthen a behavior here.
questions.note: Sensitization: increased response after an intense or noxious stimulus.
questions.x: This is sensitization: after something intense or painful, you react more strongly, and the boost spreads to lots of other stimuli. The explosion was the intense event, and now even quiet, unrelated sounds make the soldier jump. Dishabituation is the tempting wrong answer. But dishabituation brings back a reaction to one specific stimulus that had faded. Here there's no faded reaction, just a broad jump in startle to many sounds after one scary event.

questions.q: Infants view one face until looking time drops, then see either that face again or a new face. Infants look much longer at the new face. What can researchers conclude?
o: Infants prefer the familiar face
They looked longer at the new face, not the familiar one.
Looking time had been operantly reinforced by the experimenter
Nothing followed looking, so there was no reward to reinforce it.
Infants can discriminate between the two faces
Correct: looking bounced back for the new face, so they saw it as different.
Infants were sensitized to all faces
Looking at the repeated face dropped, which is the opposite of sensitization.
questions.note: Habituation–dishabituation paradigms test perceptual discrimination in preverbal infants.
questions.x: Babies can't tell us what they see, so researchers use looking time. Show the same face over and over and the baby looks less (habituation). Then show a new face. If looking jumps back up (dishabituation), the baby must have noticed the face was different. So the infants can tell the two faces apart. Sensitization doesn't fit, because looking at the repeated face went down, not up.

questions.q: Which observation best distinguishes habituation from sensory adaptation?
o: A novel stimulus can quickly restore a habituated response
Correct: a new stimulus bringing the response back shows the senses still work, so the drop was learning.
Habituation occurs only in the retina
Habituation isn't limited to the eye. It's a learned change in the brain.
Sensory adaptation can be quickly reversed by a novel stimulus
That's true of habituation. Adaptation recovers only with time after the stimulus stops.
Habituation requires reinforcement
Habituation needs no reward. Just repeating a harmless stimulus is enough.
questions.note: Sensory adaptation happens at receptors; habituation is a learned change in responding.
questions.x: Both habituation and sensory adaptation make you notice something less, so you need a test that tells them apart. Sensory adaptation happens in the receptors (the sense cells): under constant stimulation they fire less. Habituation is a learned drop in response, happening in the brain. If a new, different stimulus can instantly bring the response back (dishabituation), the receptors must still be working fine. So the drop was learning, which is habituation.

questions.q: Many chemotherapy patients begin to feel nauseated as soon as they enter the clinic waiting room, before any drug is given. Which explanation fits best?
o: The drug causes nausea through negative reinforcement
Negative reinforcement strengthens a behavior by removing something unpleasant. That isn't happening here.
Patients have habituated to the clinic
Habituation would make patients react less to the clinic, not more.
Clinic cues have become conditioned stimuli for nausea
Correct: clinic sights and smells were paired again and again with drug nausea.
Nausea is an unconditioned response to the waiting room
Waiting rooms don't naturally cause nausea, so this reaction was learned.
questions.note: Anticipatory nausea is a classic real-world conditioned response.
questions.x: This is classical conditioning, where a neutral cue gets paired with something that naturally causes a reaction. The chemo drug is the unconditioned stimulus (UCS): it naturally causes nausea, the unconditioned response (UCR). The clinic's sights and smells were neutral at first, but they kept showing up right before the drug. Now the clinic alone is a conditioned stimulus (CS) that triggers nausea, a conditioned response (CR). The nausea isn't natural to waiting rooms; it was learned.

questions.q: A patient's fear of elevators is extinguished during sessions at a clinic, but the fear returns when he enters an elevator at his office, where the fear was learned. What does this renewal effect suggest?
o: Extinction learning is tied to the context where it occurred
Correct: the 'it's safe now' learning stayed tied to the clinic and didn't carry over.
Extinction permanently erased the original association
If the fear were erased, it couldn't come back in the office.
The office acts as a new unconditioned stimulus
The office doesn't naturally cause fear. It's a reminder of where fear was learned.
Fear returned because the person became sensitized to elevators
Sensitization is a general rise in reactivity, not fear returning in one specific place.
questions.note: Extinction is new learning layered on top of the old association.
questions.x: Extinction doesn't erase a fear. It adds new learning on top: 'in this place, elevators are safe.' That new learning is tied to the setting where it happened, here the clinic. The old fear memory is still there. So when the patient goes back to his office, where the fear was first learned, the old fear wins again. That's called renewal. If extinction had wiped out the fear, changing the setting couldn't bring it back.

questions.q: After a light reliably predicts food, a tone is repeatedly paired with the light, with no food given. The tone alone now elicits salivation. This is:
o: Stimulus generalization
Generalization needs a similar stimulus. A tone and a light aren't similar.
Higher-order conditioning
Correct: the already-learned light worked like food to teach the tone.
Sensory preconditioning
In sensory preconditioning, the two cues are paired before either is linked to food.
Blocking
Blocking stops a new cue from being learned. Here the tone was learned.
questions.x: This is higher-order (or second-order) conditioning. First the light was paired with food, so the light became a conditioned stimulus (a cue that now triggers drooling). Then the tone was paired with the light, with no food at all. The light acted like the food did, teaching the tone. Now the tone alone causes salivation. Sensory preconditioning uses the same pieces in the opposite order: the two neutral cues are paired first, and only later is one linked to food.

questions.q: Rats first learn that a tone predicts shock. Then a tone-plus-light compound is paired with shock. Tested alone, the light produces little fear. Which phenomenon is this?
o: Overshadowing
Overshadowing needs both cues to be new and trained together from the start.
Latent inhibition
Latent inhibition needs earlier exposure to the light alone, with nothing after it.
Extinction
The light was never conditioned, so there was nothing to extinguish.
Blocking
Correct: the tone already predicted shock, so the light added nothing new and wasn't learned.
questions.note: Blocking shows conditioning depends on predictive information, not mere pairing.
questions.x: This is blocking. Conditioning works best when a cue tells you something new. The rats already knew the tone meant shock. When the light was added, it predicted nothing the tone hadn't already told them, so they barely learned about it. Tested alone, the light causes little fear. Overshadowing is the tempting wrong answer, but overshadowing happens when two new cues are trained together from the start and the more noticeable one wins. Here the tone had a head start.

questions.q: A therapist teaches a client deep relaxation, then gradually presents images of spiders from least to most frightening while the client stays relaxed. This technique is:
o: Flooding
Flooding jumps straight to the scariest stimulus at full strength.
Aversive conditioning
Aversive conditioning pairs an unwanted behavior with something unpleasant.
Token economy
A token economy rewards target behaviors with tokens that can be traded in.
Systematic desensitization
Correct: relaxation plus a step-by-step fear list is systematic desensitization.
questions.x: This is systematic desensitization. First the client learns a calm response, deep relaxation. Then they work up a fear hierarchy, a ranked list of scary things from mildest to worst, staying relaxed at each step. You can't be fully calm and terrified at the same time, so the spiders slowly get linked with calm instead of fear. Swapping one response for an opposite one like this is called counterconditioning. Flooding also uses exposure, but it starts at the scariest level right away, with no gradual steps or relaxation.

questions.q: Long-term heroin users face higher overdose risk when they inject a usual dose in an unfamiliar setting. Which explanation is best supported by conditioning research?
o: The new setting acts as an unconditioned stimulus for the overdose
A setting can't naturally cause overdose. Its effect is learned.
Missing familiar cues fail to trigger compensation
Correct: familiar cues normally trigger the body's opposite, bracing reaction, which is missing in a new place.
Tolerance is purely pharmacological and unaffected by setting
If tolerance were purely chemical, the setting wouldn't change overdose risk.
Users generalize tolerance more strongly to novel settings
The problem is weaker tolerance in new places, not stronger.
questions.note: Conditioned compensatory responses explain context-specific tolerance.
questions.x: Shepard Siegel's research shows that drug tolerance is partly learned. Cues that always come before the drug, like the usual room, become conditioned stimuli. They trigger a compensatory response: the body starts pushing in the opposite direction of the drug, to brace for it. In an unfamiliar place, those cues are missing, so the body doesn't brace. The usual dose then hits much harder and can be deadly. If tolerance were purely chemical, the setting wouldn't matter at all.

questions.q: In a conditioning study, a control group gets the same number of tones and shocks, but at random, unpaired times. What is the main purpose of this group?
o: To measure spontaneous recovery
Spontaneous recovery needs an extinguished response and a rest period. Neither is here.
To increase the sample size of the paired group
A control group is a comparison, not extra people for the paired group.
To provide more conditioning trials
The aim is a comparison with no link between tone and shock, not more learning.
To rule out responses due to mere exposure rather than association
Correct: if only the paired group reacts to the tone, the reaction comes from the association.
questions.x: To prove conditioning happened, you have to show the pairing caused the response, not just hearing tones and getting shocks. The random control group gets exactly the same tones and shocks, but they're never linked, so the tone predicts nothing. If only the paired group fears the tone, the fear must come from the tone-shock link. That rules out effects like sensitization, where shocks alone make an animal jumpy to everything. The control is for comparison; it doesn't add trials or people.

questions.q: Dogs are first exposed to a tone many times with nothing following it. Later, they take longer than naive dogs to learn that the tone predicts food. This is:
o: Blocking
Blocking needs another cue that already predicts the food. There isn't one.
Latent learning
Latent learning is hidden learning that shows up once a reward appears.
Latent inhibition
Correct: hearing the tone alone many times beforehand slows later conditioning to it.
Spontaneous recovery
Nothing was conditioned and then extinguished, so nothing could recover.
questions.note: Trap: latent inhibition (classical) is not latent learning (Tolman).
questions.x: This is latent inhibition. The dogs heard the tone many times with nothing after it, so they learned it means nothing. Later, when the tone starts predicting food, that old lesson gets in the way and conditioning is slower than in dogs who'd never heard it. Latent learning sounds similar but is a different idea: Tolman's finding that rats can learn a maze without any reward and only show it once a reward appears. Blocking needs a second cue that already predicts the food.

questions.q: After a conditioned response is extinguished, re-pairing the CS and UCS restores the response in far fewer trials than the original learning took. What does this suggest?
o: The UCS has become more intense
The UCS didn't change. Faster relearning comes from leftover memory.
The original association was not fully erased
Correct: quick relearning (savings) means part of the original learning remained.
Extinction actually strengthened the original association
Extinction lowers responding. It doesn't strengthen the link.
The response is now an unconditioned reflex
The response still depends on the pairing, so it's still conditioned.
questions.x: This effect is called savings: relearning after extinction is much faster than learning the first time. It shows the original link between the cue (CS) and the thing it predicted (UCS) was never wiped out. Extinction just layered new 'it's safe now' learning on top, which suppresses the response. Once the pairing starts again, the old link comes back quickly. Spontaneous recovery and renewal point the same way: the original memory is still there.

questions.q: In general, which condition produces the fastest habituation?
o: A weak stimulus presented at short intervals
Correct: habituation is fastest when the stimulus is weak and repeated close together.
An intense stimulus presented at long intervals
Both strong stimuli and long gaps slow habituation.
An intense stimulus presented at short intervals
Strong stimuli resist habituation and can cause sensitization instead.
A weak stimulus presented at long intervals
Long gaps let the response recover between repeats, slowing habituation.
questions.x: Habituation is learning to tune out a repeated, harmless stimulus. Two things make it happen fastest. First, a weak stimulus: strong ones grab attention, resist being tuned out, and can even make you jumpier (sensitization). Second, short gaps between repeats: long gaps give the response time to recover before the next one. So a weak stimulus at short intervals wins. A strong, frequent stimulus is tempting, but the strength works against you.

questions.q: Rats pressing a lever for food stop pressing whenever a tone that previously preceded shock is played. Researchers use this drop in pressing mainly to measure:
o: Negative punishment of lever pressing
Shock never depended on pressing, so this isn't punishment.
Extinction of lever pressing
Pressing still earns food. It only drops while the tone plays.
Habituation to the food reward
Pressing picks back up when the tone ends, so the food still matters to the rat.
A classically conditioned fear response to the tone
Correct: the drop in pressing (conditioned suppression) measures fear of the tone.
questions.note: Conditioned suppression combines operant baseline with a classical CS.
questions.x: This setup is called conditioned suppression. Earlier, the tone was paired with shock, so through classical conditioning the tone now causes fear. While the rat presses a lever for food, the tone plays, and the frightened rat freezes and stops pressing. The bigger the drop, the more fear the tone causes, so researchers use it as a fear gauge. It isn't punishment, because shock never depended on pressing, and food keeps coming for each press the whole time.

questions.q: Group A rats get food for every lever press; group B gets food for about one in four presses. Food is then stopped for both groups. What is the most likely result?
o: Group A keeps pressing longer than group B
Rewarding every press leads to the fastest quitting once food stops.
Both groups stop at the same time
Reward history strongly affects how long pressing continues.
Group B keeps pressing longer than group A
Correct: rewarding only some presses makes behavior last longer after rewards stop.
Group B stops immediately
Group B is used to unrewarded presses, so it keeps going.
questions.x: Group B will keep pressing longer. This is the partial reinforcement extinction effect: behavior that was rewarded only some of the time lasts longer once rewards stop. Group B is used to lots of presses with no food, so when the food stops for good, it's hard to tell anything changed. Group A got food every single time, so the first empty press is an obvious change and they quit sooner. Rewarding every response makes learning fastest, but also makes quitting fastest.

questions.q: A therapist teaches a child to wash hands as a linked sequence: wet hands, apply soap, rinse, dry, with finishing each step serving as the cue for the next. This is best described as:
o: Shaping
Shaping polishes one behavior by rewarding closer and closer tries.
Latent learning
Latent learning happens without reward and shows up later.
Insight learning
Insight is a sudden 'aha' solution, not a trained sequence.
Chaining
Correct: separate behaviors are linked so finishing each one signals the next.
questions.note: Shaping builds one behavior; chaining links several.
questions.x: This is chaining: teaching a complex skill as a string of separate behaviors done in order. Finishing one step (wet hands) is the signal to start the next (apply soap), and it also feels like a small reward that keeps the chain moving. The last step earns the final reward. Shaping is the tempting mix-up. Shaping polishes one single behavior by rewarding closer and closer tries, while chaining links several different behaviors together.

questions.q: A woman with social anxiety declines every invitation and never feels anxious at parties. Why is such avoidance behavior especially resistant to extinction?
o: Avoidance is maintained by positive punishment
Avoidance is kept going by relief, which is negative reinforcement, not punishment.
She never learns that parties would not have been harmful
Correct: avoiding means she never learns parties are safe, so the fear never fades.
Avoidance responses are unconditioned reflexes
Turning down invitations is learned behavior, not an automatic reflex.
Each avoided party adds a pleasant stimulus
Nothing pleasant is added. Relief comes from removing expected anxiety.
questions.x: Every time she turns down an invitation, she feels relief from the anxiety she expected. That relief is negative reinforcement: taking away something unpleasant makes a behavior more likely. So avoiding keeps getting stronger. Worse, because she never goes, she never finds out that the party would have been fine. Fear only fades when you face the feared thing and nothing bad happens. Avoidance blocks that, which is why exposure therapy is used to break the cycle.

questions.q: Dogs given inescapable shocks later fail to jump a low barrier to escape shock, even though escape is now possible. This is best explained by:
o: Stimulus discrimination
The dogs failed to act, not to tell stimuli apart.
Extinction of the escape response
The dogs never learned to escape, so there was nothing to extinguish.
Learned helplessness
Correct: shocks they couldn't control taught them that trying is pointless.
Habituation to shock
The shocks still upset the dogs, so they hadn't gotten used to them.
questions.note: Learned helplessness is a cognitive model of depression.
questions.x: This is learned helplessness, first shown by Martin Seligman. The dogs first got shocks they couldn't escape no matter what they did. They learned that their actions don't matter. Later, when escape was easy, they didn't even try. It isn't habituation: the shocks still upset them, they just gave up. Learned helplessness is used as a model for some kinds of depression, where people stop trying because they believe nothing will help.

questions.q: Behaviorists often advise pairing punishment of an unwanted behavior with reinforcement of an alternative behavior. Why?
o: Punishment always strengthens the unwanted behavior it follows
By definition, punishment lowers the behavior it follows.
Reinforcement and punishment cannot be used separately
Each can be used alone. Combining them just works better.
Punishment is a form of classical conditioning
Punishment is part of operant conditioning, not classical.
Punishment shows what not to do but not what to do instead
Correct: punishment says what to stop, and reinforcing an alternative shows what to do instead.
questions.x: Punishment can make a behavior happen less, but it only tells the learner what not to do. It doesn't teach what to do instead, so the need behind the behavior is still there. Punishment can also cause side effects like fear, aggression or avoiding the person who punishes. Rewarding a better alternative fills that gap: the learner now has a way to get what they want that actually pays off. Punishment, by definition, never strengthens the behavior it follows.

questions.q: A pigeon receives food every 15 seconds no matter what it does. It soon begins turning in circles before each delivery. This behavior is best explained by:
o: Instinctive drift toward species-typical feeding behaviors
Turning in circles isn't a natural feeding behavior creeping back.
Shaping by the experimenter
No one deliberately rewarded closer and closer tries.
Classical conditioning of turning to a tone
No tone or cue was used. Food following the turning strengthened it.
Accidental reinforcement of whatever preceded food
Correct: food happened to follow turning, which strengthened it into a superstition.
questions.x: In this famous Skinner study, food came on a timer, not because of anything the pigeon did. But whatever the bird happened to be doing right before the food arrived got strengthened by chance. If it was turning, turning became more likely, so it was more likely to be turning when the next food came, and so on. Skinner called this superstitious behavior. It's accidental operant reinforcement, not shaping, because no one picked which behavior to reward.

questions.q: Prisoners can shorten their sentences by following rules, and rule-following increases. Which operant process best describes this?
o: Negative reinforcement
Correct: removing something unpleasant (prison time) made rule-following go up.
Positive reinforcement
Nothing pleasant is added. Prison time is taken away.
Negative punishment
The behavior went up, so this is reinforcement, not punishment.
Positive punishment
Nothing unpleasant is added, and the behavior went up.
questions.x: Start with two questions. Did the behavior go up or down? Rule-following went up, so it's reinforcement. Was something added or taken away? Time in prison was taken away, so it's negative. Negative reinforcement means a behavior gets stronger because it removes something unpleasant. Positive reinforcement is tempting because getting out early feels like a reward, but nothing pleasant is being added. Part of something unpleasant, the sentence, is being removed.

questions.q: A student gets detention each time he is late, yet his lateness does not decrease. In behavioral terms, detention is:
o: Positive punishment
Lateness didn't drop, so detention doesn't meet the definition of punishment.
Negative punishment
Nothing is taken away, and the behavior didn't go down.
Not functioning as a punisher for lateness
Correct: a punisher has to lower the behavior, and lateness didn't drop.
Negative reinforcement
Lateness didn't go up, and nothing unpleasant was removed.
questions.note: Consequences are defined by their effect on behavior, not intent.
questions.x: In behavioral terms, a consequence is named by what it does to behavior, not by what the adult meant it to do. A punisher, by definition, makes the behavior it follows happen less. The student's lateness didn't go down, so for him detention isn't working as a punisher. It might even be rewarding him somehow, for example with attention or a break from class. Calling it positive punishment assumes it works, but the facts show it doesn't.

questions.q: Researchers record a child's on-task behavior at baseline, while tokens are given for on-task work, and after tokens are withdrawn. Which pattern best shows the tokens are reinforcers?
o: Behavior rises steadily across all three phases
A steady rise could come from practice or growing up, not the tokens.
Behavior is unchanged across all three phases
No change means the tokens didn't reinforce anything.
Behavior rises with tokens and falls when they are withdrawn
Correct: behavior that rises and falls with the tokens shows they caused the change.
Behavior falls with tokens and rises when withdrawn
That pattern would mean tokens act as punishers.
questions.x: This is an ABA reversal design. A is the baseline (normal behavior), B is the intervention (tokens), and then A again (tokens removed). If on-task behavior rises when tokens start and drops when they stop, the behavior is tracking the tokens. That's strong evidence the tokens caused it, and since behavior went up, they're working as reinforcers. A steady rise across all three phases could just be practice or the child growing up, so it can't point to the tokens.

questions.q: A lab switches a rat from FR-20 to VR-20, keeping the average number of presses per pellet the same. Which change in responding is most expected?
o: Overall response rate drops sharply
Variable-ratio schedules keep pressing fast, not slow.
Post-reinforcement pauses become shorter or disappear
Correct: any press could pay off, so the rat has little reason to pause.
A scalloped pattern appears
Scallops belong to fixed-interval schedules, not ratio schedules.
Behavior becomes much less resistant to extinction afterward
Variable-ratio behavior is harder to extinguish, not easier.
questions.x: In a fixed-ratio schedule (FR-20), the rat gets food after exactly 20 presses. Right after each pellet, it knows a full block of 20 unrewarded presses is coming, so it takes a break, called a post-reinforcement pause. In a variable-ratio schedule (VR-20), food comes after an unpredictable number of presses that averages 20. Any press might pay off, so stopping to rest means possibly missing food. Pauses shrink or vanish, and pressing becomes fast and steady.

questions.q: A raccoon trained to drop coins into a box for food begins rubbing the coins together and dipping them instead, even though this delays food. This is:
o: Instinctive drift
Correct: the raccoon's natural food-washing habits crept into the trained behavior.
Extinction burst
Food was still given for dropping coins, so rewards hadn't stopped.
Stimulus generalization
No new, similar stimuli are involved.
Shaping
The behavior moved away from the goal, not toward it.
questions.note: Biological constraints limit what operant conditioning can produce.
questions.x: This is instinctive drift, described by Keller and Marian Breland, who trained animals for shows. Trained behaviors tend to slide back toward an animal's natural, built-in habits. Raccoons naturally rub and dip their food in water. Once coins became linked with food, the raccoon started treating them like food, even though that delayed its reward. This shows biology limits what operant conditioning (learning from consequences) can teach. It isn't an extinction burst, because food was still being given for dropping coins.

questions.q: Rats quickly learn to run away to avoid shock but learn very slowly to press a lever to avoid the same shock. This difference best reflects:
o: A failure of negative reinforcement
Both responses can be strengthened by avoiding shock. They just differ in how easily.
Stimulus discrimination between lever and runway
The difference is in the response required, not telling stimuli apart.
The rats' lack of motor ability to press levers
Rats press levers easily for food, so they can physically do it.
Biological constraints favoring species-typical defense responses
Correct: responses that match natural defenses, like fleeing, are much easier to learn for avoidance.
questions.x: Robert Bolles proposed that animals have species-specific defense reactions: built-in ways of handling danger, like fleeing, freezing or fighting. Avoidance is learned fastest when the response asked for matches one of these. Running away is a rat's natural defense, so it's learned quickly. Pressing a lever isn't, so it's learned slowly, even though rats press levers easily for food. This is a biological constraint on learning, not a problem with the rats' ability to move.

questions.q: Children who saw a model punished for hitting a toy imitated less than children who saw the model rewarded. When all children were then offered a treat to show what the model did, both groups imitated equally well. What does this show?
o: Learning occurred even when performance was suppressed
Correct: seeing punishment lowered doing the behavior, not learning it.
Vicarious punishment prevented any learning of the behavior
The punished-model group did the behavior fine once offered a treat.
Observational learning requires direct reinforcement
The children learned without being rewarded themselves.
Treats caused the children to learn the behavior
The treat came after watching and only revealed what they'd already learned.
questions.note: Learning and performance are separable in social cognitive theory.
questions.x: This comes from Albert Bandura's Bobo doll studies, and it separates learning from performing. Children who saw the model punished copied less at first. But once every child was offered a treat to show what the model did, both groups did it equally well. So all of them had learned the behavior just by watching. Seeing the model punished (vicarious punishment) only changed whether they chose to do it, not whether they learned it.

questions.q: fMRI studies show overlapping human brain activation when people perform an action and when they watch it. Why is this weaker evidence for mirror neurons than monkey single-cell recordings?
o: fMRI cannot detect activity in the frontal lobe
fMRI measures activity across the whole brain, frontal lobe included.
fMRI cannot show that the same neuron responds in both conditions
Correct: each voxel holds thousands of neurons, so overlap could come from separate cells.
fMRI measures electrical spikes too slowly to detect any activity
fMRI tracks blood oxygen, not electrical spikes, so speed isn't the main problem.
Humans do not imitate others' actions
Humans imitate others all the time.
questions.x: A mirror neuron is a single brain cell that fires both when you do an action and when you watch someone else do it. In monkeys, researchers recorded from one cell at a time and saw the same cell do both. fMRI can't do that. It measures blood-oxygen changes in small blocks of brain called voxels, and each one holds many thousands of neurons. So overlap in a voxel could just be one group of cells for doing and a different, nearby group for watching.

questions.q: Students hear strong or weak arguments for a new exam policy said to begin either at their own school next year or at a distant school in 10 years. Which result does the ELM predict?
o: Argument strength matters more for the distant policy
A far-off policy gets less careful thought, so argument quality matters less.
Argument strength matters more when the policy affects them next year
Correct: personal relevance makes people think harder, so argument quality decides.
Argument strength matters equally in both conditions
The ELM predicts relevance changes how much argument quality matters.
Weak arguments persuade best when relevance is high
When people think hard, weak arguments get rejected.
questions.x: The Elaboration Likelihood Model (ELM) says there are two routes to persuasion. On the central route, people think hard about the arguments. On the peripheral route, they lean on shortcuts like how attractive or famous the speaker is. People take the central route when a topic matters to them. A policy hitting their own school next year matters, so they'll scrutinize: strong arguments persuade and weak ones fall flat. A far-off policy gets less thought, so argument strength matters less.

questions.q: Participants paid 2 dollars to tell others a dull task was fun later rated it more enjoyable than participants paid 50 dollars. This best supports:
o: Cognitive dissonance theory
Correct: low pay gave too little reason for the lie, so attitudes shifted to match it.
Positive reinforcement of enjoyment
Then bigger pay should mean more liking, which is the opposite of what happened.
The sleeper effect
The sleeper effect is about forgetting a message's source over time.
The overjustification effect
Overjustification lowers interest in something already enjoyable. This task was dull.
questions.x: This supports cognitive dissonance theory. Dissonance is the uncomfortable feeling when your actions and beliefs don't match. People told others a dull task was fun.
