Those paid 50 dollars had a good reason for the lie: the money. Those paid only 2 dollars didn't, so the clash between 'I said it was fun' and 'it was boring' felt worse. They eased it by deciding the task really was fun. Reinforcement theory predicts the opposite, more liking with more pay.

questions.q: A man who seldom thinks about recycling notices he has been recycling every day and concludes that he must care about the environment. Which theory best explains his conclusion?
o: Cognitive dissonance theory
Dissonance needs uncomfortable clashing thoughts, and none are described.
Self-perception theory
Correct: with a weak attitude, he works it out by watching his own behavior.
Elaboration likelihood model
The ELM is about how people process persuasive messages. No message here.
Reciprocal determinism
Reciprocal determinism is about person, behavior and environment shaping each other.
questions.x: This is self-perception theory, from Daryl Bem. When our attitudes are weak or unclear, we figure them out the same way we'd judge someone else: by watching what we do. He sees himself recycling every day and concludes he must care about the environment. Cognitive dissonance is the tempting wrong answer. Dissonance needs an existing attitude that clashes with a behavior and causes discomfort. This man had no strong attitude to begin with, and no discomfort is described.

questions.q: Mild distraction during a speech with weak arguments can increase persuasion. What is the most likely reason?
o: It increases the listener's motivation to elaborate
Distraction lowers the ability to think it through, not the motivation.
It makes the source seem more expert
Distraction doesn't change how expert the speaker seems.
It disrupts the listener's ability to generate counterarguments
Correct: distracted listeners can't easily think up objections to the weak points.
It strengthens the arguments themselves
The arguments stay the same. Only how they're processed changes.
questions.x: In the Elaboration Likelihood Model (ELM), people need both motivation and ability to think carefully about a message. Mild distraction lowers ability. When arguments are weak, a focused listener would spot the flaws and mentally argue back, called counterarguing, and then reject the message. Distraction takes up the mental space needed for that, so the flaws slip by and persuasion can go up. With strong arguments, distraction does the reverse: listeners can't appreciate the good points, so persuasion drops.

questions.q: Lab-raised monkeys watching edited videos learn to fear snakes after seeing a model monkey react fearfully to them, but do not learn to fear flowers from the same fearful reactions. What does this suggest?
o: Monkeys cannot learn by observation
They did learn to fear snakes by watching.
Observational fear learning is shaped by biological preparedness
Correct: some fears, like of snakes, are learned from models far more easily than others.
Flowers are unconditioned stimuli for fear
Flowers don't naturally cause fear, and no flower fear was learned.
Fear of snakes is fully innate in lab-raised monkeys
The monkeys feared snakes only after watching the model, so it was learned.
questions.x: These studies come from Susan Mineka. Lab-raised monkeys had never seen a snake. After watching videos of another monkey acting scared, they quickly learned to fear snakes. But when the videos were edited so the same scared reactions appeared next to flowers, they learned no fear of flowers. So fear can be learned by watching, but some fears are much easier to pick up. This is biological preparedness: evolution has primed animals to link certain things, like snakes, with danger.

questions.q: A student expects that studying will lead to good grades but doubts she can make herself study effectively. In social cognitive terms, she has:
o: Low outcome expectancy but high self-efficacy
She does believe studying leads to good grades.
High outcome expectancy but low self-efficacy
Correct: she trusts that studying works but doubts she can do it.
An external locus of control
She links grades to her own studying, which is internal.
Learned helplessness about grades
She believes grades can be controlled by studying.
questions.x: Albert Bandura split this into two separate beliefs. Outcome expectancy is believing a behavior will lead to a result: 'If I study, I'll get good grades.' Self-efficacy is believing you can actually carry out that behavior: 'I can make myself study.' This student is sure studying works (high outcome expectancy) but doubts she can do it (low self-efficacy). Locus of control doesn't fit, because she credits grades to her own studying, which is an internal cause.

questions.q: According to the ELM, when can a model's attractiveness act as a central-route argument rather than a peripheral cue?
o: Whenever the audience is distracted
Distraction cuts careful thinking, which keeps attractiveness a peripheral cue.
When the audience has low need for cognition
People who dislike effortful thinking lean on shortcuts, so attractiveness stays peripheral.
Never; attractiveness is always peripheral
The ELM says one feature can play different roles in different situations.
When attractiveness is directly relevant to the product's claims
Correct: for a beauty product, the model's looks can count as real evidence.
questions.note: A variable's role in the ELM depends on context.
questions.x: In the Elaboration Likelihood Model (ELM), the same feature can play different roles depending on the situation. Usually a model's attractiveness is a peripheral cue, a shortcut that persuades without much thought. But if the product's claim is about looks, like a skin cream, the model's clear skin is actual evidence that the product works. A careful thinker on the central route would treat it as an argument. So attractiveness becomes central when it's directly relevant to what the product promises.

questions.q: To test source credibility, researchers give participants the same essay attributed either to a Nobel-winning scientist or to a high school student, then measure agreement. What is the independent variable?
o: The attributed author of the essay
Correct: the researchers change only who supposedly wrote the essay.
Participants' level of agreement
Agreement is what's measured, so it's the dependent variable.
The content of the essay
The essay stays the same in both groups.
Participants' prior education
Prior education is a trait of participants, not something the researchers changed.
questions.x: The independent variable is what the researchers deliberately change between groups. Here they change only who supposedly wrote the essay: a Nobel-winning scientist or a high school student. That changes the source's credibility, meaning how believable it seems. The dependent variable is the outcome they measure, which is how much participants agree. The essay itself stays exactly the same, so any difference in agreement can be traced to who people thought wrote it.

questions.q: Which term refers to the full set of beliefs and knowledge a person holds about who they are?
o: Self-concept
Correct: self-concept is your whole picture of who you are.
Self-esteem
Self-esteem is how much you value yourself, not the full set of beliefs.
Self-efficacy
Self-efficacy is believing you can succeed at specific tasks.
Identity foreclosure
Foreclosure is one of Marcia's identity statuses: committing without exploring.
questions.note: Concept = what I think I am; esteem = how I feel about it.
questions.x: Self-concept is the whole picture you hold of who you are: your traits, roles, values and beliefs about yourself. It's a description. Self-esteem is the tempting wrong answer, but it's narrower. It's how you feel about that picture, your sense of how good or worthy you are. A handy way to keep them apart: self-concept is the description of you, and self-esteem is the grade you give it.

questions.q: A person's overall evaluation of their own worth is best described as:
o: Self-schema
A self-schema is a belief about yourself in one area, not a judgment of worth.
Self-esteem
Correct: self-esteem is your overall sense of your own worth.
Self-efficacy
Self-efficacy is confidence in doing tasks, not overall worth.
Locus of control
Locus of control is about where you think outcomes come from.
questions.x: Self-esteem is the feeling side of the self: how much you like and value yourself overall. That's exactly what 'overall evaluation of their own worth' means. The other choices are narrower or about something else. A self-schema is a belief about yourself in one area, like 'I'm a good cook.' Self-efficacy is confidence that you can succeed at a particular task. Only self-esteem is a global judgment of your worth as a person.

questions.q: After failing her driving test, Maya says the examiner was unfair and the route was unusually difficult. Her explanation best reflects:
o: An internal locus of control
An internal locus credits your own effort or skill. Maya blames outside factors.
High self-efficacy
She says nothing about whether she can pass next time.
An external locus of control
Correct: she puts the cause of her failure outside herself.
Identity achievement
Identity achievement is one of Marcia's statuses, not a way of explaining outcomes.
questions.x: Locus of control, a concept from Julian Rotter, is where you believe the causes of your outcomes lie. An internal locus puts them inside you: your effort or skill. An external locus puts them outside: luck, other people, or circumstances. Maya blames an unfair examiner and a hard route, both outside herself, so this is an external locus. Self-efficacy is tempting, but it's a belief about whether you can succeed in the future, and Maya says nothing about that.

questions.q: According to Bandura, which source most strongly builds self-efficacy?
o: Mastery experiences
Correct: your own past successes are the strongest source of self-efficacy.
Vicarious experiences
Watching others succeed helps, but less than succeeding yourself.
Verbal persuasion
Encouragement helps, but it's weaker and easier to doubt.
Physiological states
How you read your body's arousal matters, but it's the least reliable source.
questions.x: Albert Bandura named four sources of self-efficacy, which is your belief that you can succeed at a specific task. They are: mastery experiences (your own past successes), vicarious experiences (watching people like you succeed), verbal persuasion (others telling you that you can), and physiological states (how you read your body's signals, like a racing heart). Mastery is the strongest because your own successes are direct, hard-to-argue-with proof that you can do it.

questions.q: Dogs exposed to inescapable shocks later fail to escape shocks that they could easily avoid. This phenomenon is best termed:
o: Operant extinction
Extinction is a response fading when its reward stops. Nothing was removed here.
Habituation
Habituation is a smaller reaction to something repeated and harmless.
Learned helplessness
Correct: believing they had no control made the dogs stop trying, even when escape was possible.
Social facilitation
Social facilitation is about performing differently when others are watching.
questions.note: Learned helplessness links to an external locus of control and depression.
questions.x: This is learned helplessness, described by Martin Seligman. The dogs first got shocks they couldn't escape, whatever they did. They learned that their actions made no difference. Later, when escape was easy, they didn't even try. It isn't extinction: extinction is a learned response fading when its reward stops, and nothing was taken away here. Instead, the dogs learned an expectation that they have no control. Learned helplessness is used as a model for depression.

questions.q: An adult who is excessively orderly, rigid and stingy would, according to Freud, most likely be fixated at which stage?
o: Anal
Correct: being orderly, rigid and stingy are anal-retentive traits tied to toilet training.
Oral
Oral fixation shows up as dependency or mouth habits like smoking.
Phallic
Phallic fixation involves Oedipal issues and vanity.
Genital
The genital stage is the healthy endpoint, not a place to get stuck.
questions.x: Freud said children pass through psychosexual stages, each focused on a different body area and conflict. If a conflict isn't resolved, the person gets 'fixated' (stuck) and shows related traits as an adult. The anal stage, around ages 1 to 3, centers on toilet training, which is all about control. Freud said harsh, rigid training produced an anal-retentive adult: orderly, stubborn and stingy. Oral fixation looks different, showing up as dependency and mouth habits.

questions.q: In Freud's theory, a period from about age 6 to puberty in which sexual impulses are dormant is called the:
o: Genital stage
The genital stage starts at puberty, when mature sexual interest returns.
Phallic stage
The phallic stage, about ages 3 to 6, involves the Oedipal conflict.
Latency stage
Correct: sexual impulses are quiet, and energy goes into school and friends.
Anal stage
The anal stage is about toilet training in toddlers.
questions.x: This is Freud's latency stage, from about age 6 to puberty. During latency, sexual impulses are repressed, meaning pushed out of awareness, and stay quiet. The child's energy goes into schoolwork, hobbies and friendships, usually with kids of the same sex. Latency comes after the phallic stage, where the Oedipal conflict plays out, and it ends when puberty reawakens sexual drives in the genital stage. The word 'latent' means hidden or inactive, which fits.

questions.q: A college student has explored several majors and religious views but has not yet committed to any. Which of Marcia's identity statuses fits best?
o: Foreclosure
Foreclosure is committing without exploring.
Diffusion
Diffusion means neither exploring nor committing.
Moratorium
Correct: actively exploring without committing yet is moratorium.
Achievement
Achievement needs a commitment after exploring.
questions.x: James Marcia sorted identity into four statuses using two questions. Has the person explored options? Have they committed to one? This student has explored lots of majors and religious views but hasn't committed to any. Exploring without committing is moratorium, and it's a very normal phase in college. Achievement is tempting because the student is clearly thinking things through, but achievement needs a commitment after exploring, and that hasn't happened yet.

questions.q: Marcia's four identity statuses are defined by crossing which two dimensions?
o: Autonomy and intimacy
These are themes from Erikson's stages, not Marcia's two dimensions.
Exploration and commitment
Correct: having or lacking each one gives the four statuses.
Assimilation and accommodation
These are Piaget's ways of handling new information.
Conformity and obedience
These are social influence topics, not identity dimensions.
questions.note: Diffusion (−/−), foreclosure (−explore/+commit), moratorium (+/−), achievement (+/+).
questions.x: James Marcia built his four identity statuses from two questions. Has the person explored options (sometimes called crisis)? Have they committed to one? Crossing those gives a 2 by 2 grid: diffusion (neither), foreclosure (commitment only), moratorium (exploration only) and achievement (both). Autonomy and intimacy are tempting because they sound developmental, but they're themes from Erik Erikson's stages, not Marcia's two dimensions.

questions.q: A physician breaks a hospital rule to save a patient, arguing that preserving human life outweighs any rule. Which Kohlberg stage is this?
o: Law and order
A stage 4 thinker would follow the rule to keep order.
Universal ethical principles
Correct: stage 6 follows deep personal principles, even against rules.
Good interpersonal relationships
Stage 3 reasons from wanting others' approval.
Obedience and punishment
Stage 1 reasons from avoiding punishment.
questions.x: Lawrence Kohlberg described stages of moral reasoning. At the highest, stage 6 (universal ethical principles), people follow their own deeply held principles, like the value of human life, even when those clash with rules or laws. The physician breaks a hospital rule because saving a life matters more, so this is stage 6. Law and order (stage 4) is tempting since a rule is involved, but a stage 4 thinker would say the rule must be followed to keep order.

questions.q: Carol Gilligan criticized Kohlberg's theory mainly because it:
o: Ignored cognitive development entirely
Kohlberg's theory is all about how moral thinking develops.
Overemphasized unconscious drives
Unconscious drives are Freud's focus, not Kohlberg's.
Was based on male samples and stressed justice over care
Correct: she argued it undervalued a care-based ethic and relied on male samples.
Proposed too few stages
Her complaint was about bias, not the number of stages.
questions.x: Lawrence Kohlberg built his moral stages mostly from interviews with boys and men, and he scored justice-based reasoning (fairness, rights, rules) as the most advanced. Carol Gilligan argued that this left out an ethic of care, which focuses on relationships and responsibility to others. She found care-based reasoning more often in women and argued it was just as mature, not a lower stage. Her complaint was about bias in the sample and scoring, not the number of stages.

questions.q: Researchers score moral development by the justification participants give for their answer to a dilemma, not by whether they answer yes or no. This reflects Kohlberg's view that:
o: Moral behavior directly predicts moral reasoning
Kohlberg measured reasoning, not behavior.
Children are amoral until adolescence
Kohlberg said young children reason at the preconventional level, so they aren't amoral.
Culture determines the order in which the stages appear
Kohlberg claimed the stage order is the same in every culture.
The reasoning, not the decision, indicates the stage
Correct: the same choice can be justified at different stages, so reasoning is what counts.
questions.x: Kohlberg placed people in stages based on why they made a moral choice, not what they chose. In his famous Heinz dilemma, a man has to decide whether to steal a drug to save his dying wife. 'Steal it' can be justified by 'he won't get caught,' by 'a good husband would,' or by 'life matters more than property,' and those are three different stages. So a yes or no answer alone can't tell you someone's stage. Only the reasoning can.

questions.q: A tutor gives a student detailed hints on early problems, then gradually removes them as the student gains skill. This is called:
o: Assimilation
Assimilation is fitting new information into what you already know.
Scaffolding
Correct: temporary help that fades as the learner improves is scaffolding.
Shaping
Shaping rewards closer and closer versions of a behavior.
Accommodation
Accommodation is changing what you know to fit new information.
questions.x: This is scaffolding, an idea built on Lev Vygotsky's work. A more skilled helper gives support that's just enough for the learner to succeed, then gradually takes it away as the learner gets better. It works inside the zone of proximal development (ZPD): the range of tasks a learner can't do alone but can do with help. Shaping is tempting because it also goes step by step, but shaping rewards closer and closer versions of a behavior. It doesn't give and then remove hints.

questions.q: A child playing soccer anticipates what teammates and opponents will do and follows the rules of the game. This best reflects Mead's concept of the:
o: Significant other in the play stage
The play stage involves one specific role at a time.
Imitation in the preparatory stage
This child understands roles and rules, not just copying.
Generalized other in the game stage
Correct: grasping the whole team's expectations at once marks the game stage.
Looking-glass self
The looking-glass self is Cooley's idea about how we imagine others see us.
questions.x: George Herbert Mead said children develop a sense of self by learning to take other people's roles. In his game stage, children can keep track of many roles and rules at once, like knowing what every player on a soccer field will do. That internalized sense of what the group as a whole expects is called the generalized other. In the earlier play stage, a child takes on just one specific role at a time, like pretending to be a parent.

questions.q: A toddler copies his father's shaving motions without understanding what shaving is for. Which of Mead's stages does this represent?
o: Game stage
The game stage involves understanding many roles and rules.
Play stage
The play stage involves acting out roles with some understanding.
Generalized-other stage
'Generalized-other stage' isn't a stage. The generalized other forms in the game stage.
Preparatory stage
Correct: copying without understanding marks the preparatory stage.
questions.x: George Herbert Mead described three stages of learning social roles. The preparatory stage comes first, in infancy and toddlerhood: children simply imitate what they see, without understanding what it means. A toddler copying shaving motions with no idea what shaving is for fits exactly. In the play stage, children act out roles with some understanding, like playing house. In the game stage, they handle many roles and rules at once.

questions.q: Participants rated their own intelligence after viewing profiles of either highly accomplished peers or average peers. Those who viewed the accomplished peers rated themselves lower. This best illustrates:
o: Downward social comparison
Comparing to people worse off tends to raise self-ratings.
Upward social comparison
Correct: comparing with better-off peers lowered self-ratings.
Self-verification
Self-verification is seeking feedback that matches how you already see yourself.
Cognitive dissonance
No clashing beliefs or actions are involved.
questions.x: Social comparison theory, from Leon Festinger, says we judge ourselves by comparing ourselves to others. Comparing with people who are doing better is upward comparison, and it tends to make us rate ourselves lower. Comparing with people doing worse is downward comparison, and it tends to make us feel better. People who saw highly accomplished peers rated their own intelligence lower, so this is upward social comparison.

questions.q: According to self-discrepancy theory, a gap between one's actual self and ought self is most associated with:
o: Depression and dejection
Sadness and dejection come from a gap with the ideal self.
Pride
These gaps cause bad feelings, not pride.
Apathy
The theory links each gap to specific kinds of distress, not apathy.
Anxiety and guilt
Correct: falling short of your duties leads to anxiety and guilt.
questions.note: Ideal gap → sadness; ought gap → anxiety.
questions.x: E. Tory Higgins's self-discrepancy theory describes three selves. Your actual self is who you are now. Your ideal self is who you hope to be. Your ought self is who you feel you should be, based on duties and obligations. A gap between actual and ideal leads to sad, dejected feelings. A gap between actual and ought leads to agitated feelings like anxiety and guilt. This question asks about the ought self, so the answer is anxiety and guilt.

questions.q: When asked to complete 'I am ___' 20 times, participants from Japan listed more social roles and group memberships than U.S. participants. This best supports the idea that:
o: Individualist cultures foster interdependent selves
Individualist cultures foster independent, trait-based selves.
Collectivist cultures foster interdependent self-construals
Correct: the self is defined more by relationships and roles.
Self-esteem is higher in collectivist cultures
The study measured how people describe themselves, not self-esteem.
Self-concept is unaffected by culture
The cultural difference shows culture does shape self-concept.
questions.x: Hazel Markus and Shinobu Kitayama described two ways people define themselves, called self-construals. An independent self-construal defines you by your personal traits and goals ('I am smart, I am outgoing'). It's common in individualist cultures like the U.S. An interdependent self-construal defines you by your relationships and roles ('I am a daughter, I am a member of my company'). It's common in collectivist cultures like Japan. The Japanese participants' answers fit an interdependent self.

questions.q: Children who saw a model punished for aggression imitated less, but when later offered rewards to imitate, they reproduced the aggression as well as children who saw the model rewarded. This shows that:
o: Learning can occur without being performed
Correct: they had learned the behavior, and consequences only affected whether they did it.
Punishing a model erases what observers learned
The reward test showed the learning was still there.
Imitation requires direct reinforcement of the observer
They learned without being rewarded themselves.
Modeling works only when the model is a peer
The model was an adult, and modeling works with many kinds of models.
questions.note: Bandura: acquisition vs. performance.
questions.x: Albert Bandura separated learning a behavior from actually doing it. Children who saw the model punished copied less at first. But when they were offered rewards to imitate, they reproduced the aggression just as well as the children who saw the model rewarded. So they had learned it all along. Seeing a model's consequences (vicarious punishment or reward) changes how motivated you are to do the behavior, not whether you learned it.

questions.q: Researchers measure locus of control, then give participants an unsolvable puzzle described as either skill-based or chance-based. Theory predicts which group will persist longest?
o: Internals in the skill condition
Correct: they believe effort decides success, and the skill label agrees.
Externals in the skill condition
Externals expect outcomes to depend little on their effort.
Internals in the chance condition
Effort can't help on a chance task, even for internals.
Externals in the chance condition
Both their outlook and the chance label discourage effort.
questions.x: People keep trying when they expect their effort to pay off. Locus of control is whether you believe outcomes come from your own actions (internal) or from luck and outside forces (external). Internals already believe effort matters. Telling them the puzzle is skill-based backs that up. So internals in the skill condition have the most reason to keep going, even on a puzzle that can't be solved. Labeling it as chance makes effort seem pointless, even to internals.

questions.q: Before an exam, a student stays out late so that if he does poorly he can blame fatigue rather than lack of ability. This strategy is best described as:
o: Self-verification
Self-verification is seeking feedback that matches your self-view, not making excuses.
Learned helplessness
He's acting on purpose, not passively giving up after failures he couldn't control.
Downward social comparison
He isn't comparing himself with people who are worse off.
Self-handicapping
Correct: he creates an obstacle ahead of time so failure can be blamed on it.
questions.note: Self-handicapping protects self-esteem at the cost of performance.
questions.x: This is self-handicapping: setting up an obstacle before a performance so that if you fail, you can blame the obstacle instead of your ability. Staying out late gives the student a ready excuse: 'I was tired.' If he does well anyway, he looks even more talented. It protects self-esteem, but it costs him real performance. Self-verification is different: it's seeking feedback that matches how you already see yourself, not building excuses.

questions.q: Identity theory proposes that a person's many identities are arranged in a hierarchy of salience. The most salient identity is the one that:
o: Is most likely to be enacted across situations
Correct: the most salient identity is the one most likely to come into play.
Was assigned at birth
Salience depends on commitment, not on being assigned at birth.
Is suppressed under stress
Salient identities guide behavior. They don't disappear under stress.
Is determined only by how others perceive the person
Salience reflects your own commitment, not only how others see you.
questions.x: Identity theory, from Sheldon Stryker, says each person holds many identities, like student, sibling or athlete, ranked in a salience hierarchy. Salience means how likely an identity is to come into play across different situations. The most salient identity is the one you act on most often. It grows with your commitment, meaning how many important relationships depend on that identity. It isn't about whether you were born into it or how others see you.

questions.q: Participants assigned to groups by a coin flip still give more rewards to members of their own group. This finding best supports the claim that:
o: Competition over scarce resources is needed for bias
There was no real conflict between the groups, yet bias still appeared.
Prior friendships drive in-group favoritism
Participants were strangers assigned by coin flip.
People default to equal allocation
They favored their own group, so they didn't split rewards equally.
Mere categorization is enough to produce in-group favoritism
Correct: the minimal group paradigm shows bias from trivial grouping alone.
questions.x: This is Henri Tajfel's minimal group paradigm. People were split into groups for random or trivial reasons, with no history, no contact and no competition. Even so, they gave more rewards to their own group. That shows simply being put into a category is enough to create in-group favoritism, which means treating your own group better. Competition over resources is tempting, but that's realistic conflict theory from the Robbers Cave study. Here there was nothing to compete over.

questions.q: People with negative self-views sometimes prefer friends who see them negatively over friends who see them positively. This is best explained by:
o: Self-verification
Correct: people seek feedback that confirms how they already see themselves.
Self-enhancement
Self-enhancement would favor the friends with positive views.
Self-handicapping
Self-handicapping is creating excuses before a performance.
Downward social comparison
Downward comparison is comparing with people who are worse off.
questions.x: This is self-verification, from William Swann. People want others to see them the way they see themselves, even if that view is negative, because consistency feels predictable and under control. So someone who thinks poorly of themselves may feel more comfortable with friends who agree. Self-enhancement is the tempting wrong answer. It says people want positive feedback no matter what, so it would predict they'd prefer the friends who see them positively.

questions.q: A 5-year-old talks aloud to herself while working through a puzzle. Vygotsky viewed this private speech as:
o: Egocentric speech with no function
That was Piaget's view, not Vygotsky's.
A sign of language delay
Talking to yourself is normal at this age.
A self-regulation tool that later becomes inner speech
Correct: she's using speech to guide herself, and it will later go silent as inner speech.
Mere imitation of parents with no cognitive role
Vygotsky saw private speech as important for thinking, not empty copying.
questions.x: Lev Vygotsky saw private speech, a child talking out loud to herself while working, as a tool for guiding her own thinking and actions. He believed speech starts as talk with other people, turns into out-loud self-talk, and gradually goes silent as inner speech, the voice in your head. So the 5-year-old is using words to steer herself through the puzzle. Jean Piaget saw it differently: as egocentric speech that didn't serve much purpose.

questions.q: A key difference between Erikson's and Freud's developmental theories is that Erikson:
o: Emphasized social conflicts spanning the entire lifespan
Correct: Erikson stressed social relationships and carried development through old age.
Rejected stage models of development
Erikson proposed eight stages, so he kept a stage model.
Focused only on childhood sexuality
Focusing on childhood sexuality describes Freud, not Erikson.
Denied that development involves conflicts
Every Erikson stage is defined by a conflict.
questions.x: Both Sigmund Freud and Erik Erikson described development in stages, each built around a conflict. The big difference is focus and timespan. Freud's five psychosexual stages centered on sexual drives in childhood, and he thought personality was mostly set by about age 5 or 6. Erikson's eight psychosocial stages centered on social relationships and continued through the whole lifespan, all the way into old age. So Erikson emphasized social conflicts across the entire life.

questions.q: Successful resolution of Erikson's identity vs. role confusion stage yields which virtue?
o: Hope
Hope comes from trust vs. mistrust in infancy.
Fidelity
Correct: fidelity, staying loyal to your commitments, comes from resolving identity.
Wisdom
Wisdom comes from integrity vs. despair in old age.
Competence
Competence comes from industry vs. inferiority in the school years.
questions.x: In Erik Erikson's theory, each of the eight stages has a conflict, and resolving it well gives a virtue, a lasting strength. The teen stage, identity vs. role confusion, is about figuring out who you are. Resolving it gives fidelity: the ability to stay loyal to the values and commitments you choose. Here's the full list in order: hope, will, purpose, competence, fidelity, love, care and wisdom.

questions.q: A citizen argues that an unjust law should be changed through democratic means because laws are agreements meant to serve the common good. Which Kohlberg stage fits best?
o: Law and order
Stage 4 treats laws as fixed duties to uphold.
Good interpersonal relationships
Stage 3 reasons from wanting others' approval.
Social contract
Correct: stage 5 sees laws as changeable agreements for the common good.
Obedience and punishment
Stage 1 reasons from avoiding punishment.
questions.x: This is Kohlberg's stage 5, social contract. At this stage, people see laws as agreements a society makes to serve the common good. If a law fails to do that, it should be changed, but through fair democratic means. Stage 4 (law and order) is tempting because it's also about laws, but stage 4 treats laws as fixed duties to uphold, not something to change. Stage 6 would go further, appealing to universal principles that might justify breaking the law.

questions.q: Researchers find that people in some collectivist societies rarely score at Kohlberg's postconventional stages, yet show sophisticated community-centered moral reasoning. This most directly challenges:
o: The universality of Kohlberg's scoring criteria
Correct: it suggests the scoring reflects Western, individualist values.
The order of Erikson's stages
Erikson's theory is about social development, not moral reasoning.
Vygotsky's zone of proximal development
The zone of proximal development is about learning with help.
Freud's latency stage
Latency is a Freudian stage, unrelated to moral reasoning.
questions.x: Kohlberg claimed his stages of moral reasoning are universal, the same everywhere. But his top stages reward Western, individualist ideas like personal rights and abstract justice. If people in collectivist cultures, which put the group first, reason about morality in sophisticated, community-centered ways and still score low, the scoring may be biased. That challenges the claim that Kohlberg's criteria apply equally to every culture. The other choices are about different theories that don't deal with moral reasoning.

questions.q: In a study, adults watching the same crying infant described it as 'angry' when told it was a boy and 'scared' when told it was a girl. This best illustrates:
o: Biological sex differences in emotion
The infant was identical in both conditions, so biology can't explain it.
Gender constancy in infants
Gender constancy develops in early childhood, and this study is about adults.
The infant's temperament
The infant's temperament stayed the same in both conditions.
Adults' gender expectations shaping how a child is perceived
Correct: adults' gender expectations shaped how they read the same crying.
questions.x: This is a classic 'Baby X' style study. Adults watched the exact same crying infant. The only thing that changed was the label: boy or girl. Told 'boy,' they saw anger. Told 'girl,' they saw fear. Since the baby's behavior was identical, the difference has to come from the adults' gender expectations. This shows gender socialization, the way others teach and expect gender roles, starts in infancy with how people interpret a child.

questions.q: Among cardiac patients with similar disease severity, those with higher exercise self-efficacy attended more rehab sessions. What most limits causal conclusions?
o: Patients were randomly assigned
Random assignment would strengthen causal claims, not limit them.
The study was double-blind
Blinding reduces bias. It doesn't weaken causal conclusions.
Self-efficacy was measured, not manipulated
Correct: measuring without manipulating can't rule out other causes or a reversed direction.
The sample was too homogeneous in disease severity
Matching on severity removes one confound. It's a strength, not a limit.
questions.x: This study only measured self-efficacy (patients' belief that they can exercise) and attendance as they naturally were. That makes it correlational: it shows the two go together, but not that one causes the other. Something else, like motivation or family support, could drive both. Or the arrow could point the other way: attending rehab could build self-efficacy. Only an experiment that changes self-efficacy on purpose, ideally with random assignment, could show cause. Matching on disease severity helps, but controls just one possible confound.

questions.q: Researchers find that global self-esteem correlates only weakly with exam scores, whereas academic self-efficacy correlates more strongly. Which explanation fits best?
o: Self-esteem is unrelated to the self-concept
Self-esteem is the judging part of the self-concept, so they're related.
Self-efficacy is the same construct as self-esteem
The different correlations suggest they're separate ideas.
Task-specific beliefs predict task-specific outcomes better than global worth
Correct: a school-specific belief predicts school results better than overall worth.
High self-esteem causes poor exam performance
A weak positive correlation doesn't show self-esteem harms scores.
questions.x: Self-esteem is your overall sense of worth as a person. Academic self-efficacy is your belief that you can succeed at schoolwork specifically. A general rule: specific beliefs predict specific outcomes better than broad ones. Exam scores are a school outcome, so a school-specific belief tracks them more closely than a general feeling of worth. The different correlations also tell you these are two separate ideas, not one idea with two names.

questions.q: A teen deliberately adopts styles and opinions opposite to those of a clique he dislikes. For him, that clique serves as a:
o: Primary group
A primary group involves close, lasting personal ties, like family.
In-group
He doesn't see himself as a member of this clique.
Secondary group
Secondary groups are large, impersonal and goal-focused.
Negative reference group
Correct: it's a group he defines himself against.
questions.x: A reference group is any group you use as a standard to judge yourself or guide your choices. Usually it's a group you want to be like, a positive reference group. But it can work in reverse. A negative reference group is one you deliberately define yourself against: you do the opposite of what they do, to show who you're not. This teen doesn't belong to the clique or want to copy it. He uses it as an 'anti-model,' so it's a negative reference group.

questions.q: Adolescents' self-ratings of competence correlated more strongly with what they believed their parents thought of them than with parents' actual ratings. This best supports:
o: Cooley's looking-glass self
Correct: imagined, not actual, judgments shaped the teens' self-views.
Bandura's reciprocal determinism
Reciprocal determinism is about person, behavior and environment shaping each other.
Marcia's identity statuses
No exploration or commitment was measured.
Rotter's locus of control
No beliefs about control were measured.
questions.x: Charles Cooley's looking-glass self says we build our self-image from what we imagine others think of us, as if other people were a mirror. The key word is imagine. It's not what others actually think that shapes us, but what we believe they think. In this study, teens' views of their own competence matched what they believed their parents thought more closely than what their parents actually said. That's exactly what the looking-glass self predicts.

questions.q: Piaget held that development must precede learning. Vygotsky instead held that:
o: Development must be complete before any learning
That's close to Piaget's view, which Vygotsky disagreed with.
Development is fixed by genetics alone
Vygotsky stressed social and cultural influences, not genes alone.
Learning through social interaction leads development
Correct: guided social learning in the ZPD pulls development forward.
Only adolescents can learn from peers
Vygotsky applied his ideas across all of childhood.
questions.x: Jean Piaget believed children have to reach a certain developmental stage before they can learn ideas that belong to it. Development comes first, then learning. Lev Vygotsky flipped this. He argued that learning with help from more skilled people actually pulls development forward. This happens in the zone of proximal development (ZPD), the range of tasks a child can't do alone but can do with guidance. So good teaching aims just a bit beyond what the child can already do.

questions.q: In attribution theory, explaining a behavior by pointing to a person's traits, abilities or character is called what?
o: A situational attribution
Situational attributions point to outside circumstances, not to the person's traits.
A stable-external attribution
External means situational, and traits are internal. This isn't a standard label anyway.
A self-serving attribution
Self-serving bias is a pattern across wins and losses, not the name for any trait explanation.
A dispositional attribution
Correct: a dispositional (internal) attribution puts the cause inside the person.
questions.note: Dispositional = internal; situational = external.
questions.x: Attribution theory is about how we explain why people do things. The big split is where you put the cause. A dispositional attribution (also called internal) puts the cause inside the person: their traits, abilities, effort or character. "She aced it because she's smart" is dispositional. A situational attribution (external) puts the cause in the circumstances: "She aced it because the test was easy." Self-serving bias sounds related, but it isn't a type of attribution. It's a habit of taking credit for wins and blaming the situation for losses.

questions.q: Kelley's covariation model predicts a situational attribution when a behavior shows which combination of consensus, distinctiveness and consistency?
o: Low consensus, low distinctiveness, high consistency
This is the pattern that points to the person: a dispositional attribution.
High consensus, high distinctiveness, high consistency
Correct: everyone does it, only here, every time, so the situation is the cause.
High consensus, low distinctiveness, low consistency
Low consistency suggests a fluke, and low distinctiveness points away from the situation.
Low consensus, high distinctiveness, low consistency
Low consensus points to the person, and low consistency rules out any stable cause.
questions.note: Trap: low consensus + low distinctiveness + high consistency = dispositional.
questions.x: Kelley's covariation model says we look at three clues before deciding why someone did something. Consensus: do other people act the same way? Distinctiveness: does this person act this way only with this one thing? Consistency: does it happen every time? When all three are high, everyone reacts this way, only to this thing, and reliably, so the cause must be the situation or the thing itself. Low consensus, low distinctiveness and high consistency points to the person instead. Low consistency means it might just be a one-time fluke.

questions.q: Researchers have participants read an essay they are told was assigned to the writer by a coin flip. Participants still rate the writer's true attitude as matching the essay. What does this most directly demonstrate?
o: Actor-observer bias
Actor-observer bias needs a comparison of explaining yourself versus explaining others.
Cognitive dissonance
Dissonance is about your own clashing beliefs and actions, not judging someone else's essay.
Self-fulfilling prophecy
No expectation changes anyone's actual behavior here.
Correspondence bias
Correct: people assume the attitude matches the essay even though a coin flip forced it.
questions.note: Correspondence bias is another name for the fundamental attribution error.
questions.x: The participants know the essay's side was picked by a coin flip, so it tells them nothing about what the writer really thinks. They still decide the writer believes it. Assuming someone's inner attitude matches their behavior, even when the situation clearly forced that behavior, is called correspondence bias. It's another name for the fundamental attribution error (the habit of blaming someone's character and overlooking the situation). Actor-observer bias doesn't fit, because nobody here is comparing how they explain their own behavior with how they explain someone else's.

questions.q: The self-serving bias is generally thought to serve which psychological function?
o: Reducing cognitive load during social judgments
Saving mental effort explains shortcuts like stereotypes, not feel-good explanations about yourself.
Protecting and enhancing self-esteem
Correct: taking credit for wins and dodging blame for losses protects self-worth.
Increasing accuracy of self-assessment
The bias bends self-assessment, so it makes it less accurate.
Strengthening in-group cohesion
That's the group-serving bias, which favors your group, not yourself.
questions.x: The self-serving bias is the habit of taking credit when things go well ("I studied hard") and blaming the situation when they go badly ("the test was unfair"). Psychologists usually explain it as a way to protect and boost self-esteem, which is how good you feel about yourself. Because it bends the truth, it makes self-assessment less accurate, not more. Saving mental effort is a different reason for bias. That explains shortcuts like heuristics and stereotypes, which work without any feelings about the self.

questions.q: Researchers find that participants who score high on belief in a just world rate an innocent victim of random violence as less likable after learning the perpetrator was never caught. Which explanation best fits?
o: Unresolved crimes trigger stereotype threat in the observers themselves
Stereotype threat affects members of a stereotyped group while they perform a task.
Participants are showing the self-serving bias
Self-serving bias is about explaining your own wins and losses. These aren't the participants' outcomes.
The halo effect reverses when a crime is unsolved
The halo effect is one good trait coloring other traits. It has nothing to do with fairness.
Derogating the victim restores the belief that the world is fair
Correct: when justice can't be done, thinking less of the victim makes the world seem fair again.
questions.note: Just-world beliefs are strongest when victims' suffering cannot be fixed.
questions.x: The just-world belief is the idea that people get what they deserve: good things happen to good people and bad things to bad people. A random attack on an innocent person, with the attacker never caught, threatens that belief. There's no way to make it fair again. So people who hold the belief strongly fix it in their heads by thinking less of the victim. If the victim seems less likable, the outcome feels less unfair. Self-serving bias doesn't fit, because the participants' own successes or failures aren't involved.

questions.q: Compared with people from individualist cultures, people from collectivist cultures are on average more likely to do what when explaining others' behavior?
o: Rely exclusively on dispositional traits
No group uses traits only. A stronger trait focus is typical of individualist cultures.
Show a stronger self-serving bias
Self-serving bias tends to be weaker, not stronger, in collectivist groups.
Ignore social roles and relationships
Collectivist thinking focuses on roles and relationships rather than ignoring them.
Weigh situational and contextual factors
Correct: collectivist cultures pay more attention to context, so their attribution error is weaker.
questions.x: Collectivist cultures, like many in East Asia, put weight on the group, social roles and relationships. So when people there explain someone's behavior, they're more likely to think about the situation and context around that person. That means they show a weaker fundamental attribution error (the habit of blaming character and ignoring circumstances). Individualist cultures, like the US, focus on the independent self and lean toward trait explanations. No culture uses traits only, and the self-serving bias actually tends to be weaker in collectivist groups.

questions.q: A content analysis compared English-language American newspapers and Chinese-language newspapers covering the same murders. The American papers emphasized the killer's personality, while the Chinese-language papers emphasized circumstances and relationships. This finding best supports which claim?
o: The fundamental attribution error is biologically fixed
A difference between cultures argues against a fixed, built-in bias.
East Asian writers show a stronger actor-observer bias
Both sets of papers explained someone else's behavior, so there's no self-versus-other comparison.
The fundamental attribution error is shaped by culture
Correct: the focus on traits changed with culture, so the bias isn't the same everywhere.
American writers show stronger stereotype threat
Stereotype threat is about performance under a stereotype, not news explanations.
questions.x: Here's the logic. If the fundamental attribution error (blaming character and overlooking circumstances) were built into everyone in the same way, news about the same murders should explain them the same way everywhere. Instead, the American papers focused on the killer's personality, and the Chinese-language papers focused on circumstances and relationships. That difference shows culture shapes how strongly people lean toward trait explanations. Actor-observer bias doesn't fit, because every report explained someone else's behavior, and nobody explained their own.

questions.q: A company that holds no negative views of any group requires applicants to have graduated from a few private schools that historically excluded certain minorities. The resulting hiring disparity best exemplifies what?
o: Individual prejudice
The question says the company holds no negative views of any group.
Stereotype threat
Nobody is doing worse on a task because of a stereotype reminder.
Self-fulfilling prophecy
No expectation is shaping the applicants' behavior.
Institutional discrimination
Correct: a neutral-looking rule creates unequal outcomes without anyone being prejudiced.
questions.note: Discrimination can exist without prejudice when it is built into rules.
questions.x: Institutional discrimination is when rules, policies or systems produce unequal outcomes for groups, even if nobody involved holds prejudiced attitudes. That's this company. Its rule only takes graduates of a few private schools, and those schools historically shut out certain minorities. So the past exclusion gets carried forward into today's hiring, without anyone meaning harm. Individual prejudice is ruled out, because the question says the company holds no negative views of any group.

questions.q: Which result would most strongly support the claim that stereotype threat works partly by consuming working memory?
o: Threatened participants report liking the test less
Liking the test is an attitude, not a measure of working memory.
Non-stereotyped participants score equally in both conditions
This shows the effect hits only stereotyped groups. It says nothing about how it works.
Threatened participants spend more time on the first question
Time spent on a question isn't a direct measure of working memory.
Threatened participants show lower working memory span, which statistically accounts for their lower scores
Correct: lower working memory span explains the score drop, so it's the middle step.
questions.note: Mechanism questions need a mediator, not just the main effect.
questions.x: Stereotype threat is the worry about confirming a negative stereotype about your group, which can drag down performance. Showing that it happens is one thing. Showing how it happens needs a mediator: a middle step that the threat changes and that explains the drop in scores. If threatened people have a lower working memory span (less room to hold and juggle information in mind), and that lower span statistically accounts for their lower scores, you've shown the mechanism. Disliking the test, or only stereotyped groups being affected, shows the effect exists but not how it works.

questions.q: Researchers randomly label some students as 'expected bloomers' and tell their teachers. At year's end, labeled students show larger gains. Why is random assignment of the label essential to the conclusion?
o: It guarantees that teachers will not discover the deception
Randomizing the label has nothing to do with whether teachers spot the trick.
It ensures differences in gains are due to teacher expectations rather than preexisting student ability
Correct: chance makes the groups equal in ability, so the gains come from the expectations.
It makes the sample representative of all schools
Representing all schools comes from random sampling, not random assignment.
It eliminates the need for a control group
The unlabeled students are the control group, and it's still needed.
questions.note: Random assignment = internal validity; random sampling = external validity.
questions.x: Random assignment means chance, not the researcher, decides who gets the "bloomer" label. That makes the labeled and unlabeled students about equal on average in ability and motivation before the study starts. So if the labeled students gain more by year's end, the best explanation is the teachers' expectations, not that the label happened to land on stronger students. This protects internal validity, which is how sure you can be about cause and effect. Random sampling is a different idea: it's about whether the people studied represent everyone else.

questions.q: In a summer camp study, two groups of boys became hostile while competing for prizes. Hostility dropped most when they had to cooperate to fix the camp's broken water supply. Which concept explains the reduction?
o: Superordinate goals
Correct: a shared goal that needs both groups to cooperate reduces conflict.
Mere contact
Plain contact during the competition hadn't reduced hostility.
Deindividuation
Deindividuation makes antisocial group behavior more likely, not less.
Social loafing
Social loafing is people putting in less effort in a group.
questions.note: Contact helps most with equal status and shared goals.
questions.x: In this summer camp study, called Robbers Cave, competing for prizes made two groups of boys hostile. Just spending time together, like sharing meals, didn't help. What worked was a superordinate goal: a goal both groups wanted that neither could reach alone, like fixing the broken water supply. Having to cooperate brought hostility down. Mere contact is the tempting answer, but contact only helps under the right conditions, such as shared goals and equal status.

questions.q: Students told a guest lecturer was 'rather cold' rated him less favorably and asked fewer questions than students told he was 'very warm,' though all saw the same lecture. What does the difference in questions suggest?
o: Impressions also shape how people act toward him
Correct: the label changed how students acted toward him, not just how they rated him.
The lecturer gave different lectures to each group
The question says all students saw the same lecture.
Students showed the self-serving bias
The students weren't explaining their own outcomes.
Warm and cold are peripheral traits
The big effect shows warm and cold act as central traits, not peripheral ones.
questions.x: Everyone saw the same lecture, so the only thing that differed was the label: "rather cold" or "very warm." The students who expected a cold lecturer rated him lower and also asked fewer questions. That second part matters. It shows an impression doesn't just change what you privately think of someone. It changes how you act toward them. That's the first step of a self-fulfilling prophecy (an expectation that makes itself come true), because the lecturer may respond to the quieter room by seeming colder.

questions.q: Participants judge a speaker's anxiety while silently memorizing a long number or not. Those memorizing rely more on the speaker's visible fidgeting and ignore a stressful topic. Which model best explains this?
o: A purely situational model of attribution
The results show more focus on the person, not less.
A two-step model: automatic trait inference followed by effortful situational correction
Correct: a busy mind skips the effortful second step of correcting for the situation.
The just-world hypothesis
Nobody is judging whether an outcome was fair or deserved.
Social facilitation theory
Social facilitation is about how an audience changes your performance.
questions.note: Load makes the FAE worse: correction for situation takes effort.
questions.x: Two-step models say explaining behavior happens in two stages. First, you automatically assume the behavior reflects a trait: "she's fidgeting, so she's an anxious person." Second, if you have the mental energy, you correct for the situation: "oh, but the topic is stressful." Memorizing a long number is cognitive load, meaning it keeps your mind busy. Busy participants stop after step one, so they lean on the fidgeting and ignore the stressful topic. A purely situational model can't explain this, since people leaned more on the person, not less.

questions.q: Primacy usually dominates impression formation. Under which condition is a recency effect most likely instead?
o: All information is presented rapidly in one session
Fast presentation in one sitting usually favors the first information.
The perceiver is distracted during the later information
Distraction during the later information weakens it, which helps primacy.
A long delay separates the two sets of information and judgment follows the second set
Correct: the delay lets the first information fade, so the newest information wins.
The first information is especially vivid
Vivid early information makes primacy stronger.
questions.x: Usually the first things you learn about someone matter most. That's the primacy effect, and it happens because early information shapes how you read everything after it. The recency effect is the opposite: the latest information matters most. Recency wins when a long delay separates the two sets of information and you make your judgment right after the second set. By then the first set has faded from memory and the newest one is fresh. Being distracted during the later information would make it weaker, which helps primacy, not recency.

questions.q: When an out-group member performs a positive act, prejudiced observers often say it was luck or an exception. Which bias does this describe?
o: Self-serving bias
Self-serving bias is about your own outcomes, not an out-group member's.
Ultimate attribution error
Correct: out-group good deeds get written off as luck, while bad ones get blamed on character.
False consensus effect
False consensus is overestimating how many people agree with you.
Recency effect
Nothing here is about the order information came in.
questions.x: The ultimate attribution error is a bias in how people explain the behavior of whole groups. When a member of a disliked out-group (a group you don't belong to) does something bad, it's blamed on their character. When they do something good, it's explained away as luck, special circumstances or "an exception." That lets prejudiced beliefs survive evidence that should challenge them. Self-serving bias has a similar shape, but it's about explaining your own successes and failures, not an out-group's.

questions.q: Participants randomly assigned to watch either a frightening or a neutral film clip then rate the same set of ambiguous faces. Those who saw the frightening clip rate the faces as more hostile. Which conclusion is best supported?
o: The faces in the frightening condition were objectively more hostile
Both groups rated the exact same faces.
Frightening films cause permanent hostility
One short session can't show a permanent effect.
The perceiver's emotional state can bias social perception
Correct: random assignment links the scary clip's mood to the hostile ratings.
Perceivers in the neutral condition showed stereotype threat
Stereotype threat is about performance, not rating faces.
questions.x: Chance decided who saw the frightening clip and who saw the neutral one, and everyone rated the exact same faces. So the only real difference between the groups was the clip and the mood it created. Since scared viewers saw the faces as more hostile, the best conclusion is that your emotional state can bias how you read other people. The faces can't be objectively different, because they were the same faces. And one short session can't tell you anything about permanent effects.

questions.q: Perceiving a relationship between two variables, such as a minority group and a rare behavior, when none exists is called what?
o: Confirmation bias
Confirmation bias is looking for evidence that supports what you already believe.
Base-rate fallacy
The base-rate fallacy is ignoring how common something is overall.
Illusory correlation
Correct: unusual pairings feel linked even when they aren't.
Belief perseverance
Belief perseverance is holding on to a belief after it's been disproven.
questions.x: A correlation is a link between two things, so when one changes, the other tends to change too. An illusory correlation is a link you think you see that isn't really there. It's most likely when two rare or unusual things happen together, like a small minority group and an uncommon behavior. Those pairings stick in memory, so they seem connected. Confirmation bias can help keep that false belief going, but it's about hunting for evidence that supports what you already think, not about seeing the link in the first place.

questions.q: Participants read statements about two groups. Group A is described in twice as many statements as Group B, and in both groups undesirable behaviors are a minority of statements in the same proportion. Participants rate Group B more negatively. What best explains this?
o: Group B actually showed more undesirable behaviors per member than A
The proportions were the same in both groups.
Pairing a minority with rare behaviors creates illusory correlation
Correct: two rare things showing up together stand out and seem linked.
Participants showed out-group homogeneity for Group A
No in-group or out-group was set up.
Participants showed a recency effect
The order of the information wasn't changed.
questions.note: Distinctiveness-based illusory correlation helps explain how stereotypes form.
questions.x: Both groups had bad behaviors in exactly the same proportion, so Group B didn't really act worse. But Group B is the smaller group, so statements about it are rarer, and bad behaviors are also rarer. When two rare things show up together, the pairing stands out and gets remembered better. That makes people overestimate how often Group B behaved badly. This is a distinctiveness-based illusory correlation, a false link built from memorable pairings. The answer saying Group B really did act worse is ruled out by the design, which kept the proportions equal.

questions.q: When a prejudiced person meets a friendly, competent member of a disliked group, he labels her 'an exception' and keeps his stereotype. This process is called what?
o: Stereotype threat
Stereotype threat affects the stereotyped person's own performance.
Superordinate goal formation
Superordinate goals are shared goals that reduce conflict through teamwork.
Self-fulfilling prophecy
No expectation is changing her behavior.
Subtyping
Correct: the person who doesn't fit gets her own category, so the stereotype survives.
questions.x: A stereotype is a fixed belief about a whole group. Subtyping is what happens when someone meets a person who doesn't fit the stereotype and, instead of updating the belief, puts that person in a special little category: "she's an exception." The stereotype survives untouched. It's a big reason why meeting one counterexample rarely changes minds. Stereotypes change more when lots of ordinary group members, not just a few standouts, prove them wrong.

questions.q: A sociologist argues that dominant groups promote stereotypes of subordinate groups because those beliefs justify unequal access to wealth and status. Which processes does this argument emphasize as sources of prejudice?
o: Power, prestige and class
Correct: prejudice is seen as a way to keep the existing hierarchy in place.
Individual cognitive limitations
The argument is about group interests, not mental shortcuts.
Random variation in personality
The argument is about social structure, not individual personality.
Biological threat detection
The argument is about social hierarchy, not evolved fear.
questions.x: The sociologist's argument is about groups and resources. The group on top spreads stereotypes about the groups below because those beliefs make unequal access to wealth and status look fair. That points to power (the ability to control others), prestige (social respect) and class (economic position) as the sources of prejudice. This is a conflict or structural view, meaning it looks at how society is organized. Mental shortcuts are a real cause of stereotyping too, but they're an individual-level explanation, and this argument isn't about that.

questions.q: A man diagnosed with depression begins to believe he is weak and worthless because of his diagnosis, and stops seeking help. This illustrates what?
o: Public stigma
Public stigma is other people's negative attitudes, not his own.
Stereotype lift
Stereotype lift is a performance boost from comparing yourself to a stereotyped group.
Courtesy stigma
Courtesy stigma hits people connected to the stigmatized person.
Self-stigma
Correct: he's taken society's negative views and applied them to himself.
questions.x: Stigma is a mark of shame attached to a group or condition. Self-stigma is when a person takes society's negative views about their condition and turns them on themselves. That's this man: he believes he's weak and worthless because of his depression diagnosis, and it stops him from getting help. Public stigma is tempting, but that means other people's negative attitudes. The key detail here is that he believes it himself. Courtesy stigma is aimed at people connected to someone stigmatized, like family.

questions.q: A researcher finds that patients who strongly endorse negative beliefs about mental illness skip more therapy appointments. Which conclusion is justified by this finding alone?
o: Negative beliefs cause patients to skip appointments
A correlation alone can't show cause and effect.
These beliefs are associated with missed appointments
Correct: measuring two things only supports saying they're linked.
Skipping appointments causes patients' negative beliefs
The reverse direction can't be proven either.
Stigma has no effect on treatment
The data show a link, which contradicts "no effect."
questions.x: The researcher only measured two things: how strongly patients held negative beliefs and how many appointments they missed. Nothing was manipulated, so this is a correlation. A correlation shows two things go together, but not which causes which. Beliefs might cause skipping, skipping might strengthen the beliefs, or a third thing, like how severe someone's symptoms are, might drive both. So the only safe conclusion is an association. Saying the beliefs cause the skipping is the tempting overreach.

questions.q: A person scores low on a self-report prejudice scale but shows strong automatic bias on a reaction-time test. What does this pattern best suggest?
o: Explicit and implicit attitudes can diverge
Correct: what you consciously report and what you automatically associate can differ.
The self-report scale measured implicit bias
Self-report scales measure explicit, conscious attitudes.
The person must be lying on the questionnaire
Implicit bias can exist without awareness, so lying isn't required.
Reaction-time tests cannot detect bias
The test did pick up a bias here.
questions.x: There are two kinds of attitudes here. Explicit attitudes are the ones you know about and can report, so they're measured with questionnaires. Implicit attitudes are automatic associations, often outside awareness, so they're measured indirectly, for example by how fast you react. The two can disagree. Someone can honestly report low prejudice and still show automatic bias on a reaction-time test. Lying is the tempting explanation, but implicit bias can exist without the person knowing, so no lying is needed.

questions.q: A person who sincerely endorses equality avoids an out-group member only in ambiguous situations where a nonracial excuse is available. This pattern is best described as what?
o: Overt discrimination
Overt discrimination is open and doesn't depend on having an excuse.
Institutional discrimination
Institutional discrimination comes from policies, not one person's avoidance.
Cultural relativism
Cultural relativism is understanding a culture's practices in their own context.
Aversive racism
Correct: a sincere belief in equality sits alongside hidden bias that shows up when it can be excused.
questions.x: Aversive racism describes people who sincerely believe in equality but carry negative feelings they don't admit, even to themselves. Their bias doesn't show up openly. It shows up mainly in ambiguous situations where they can point to some other, nonracial reason, like "I was busy." That excuse protects their image of themselves as fair. Overt discrimination is open and doesn't need an excuse. Institutional discrimination comes from organizational policies, not one person's avoidance.

questions.q: White male math majors told that a test compares their scores with Asian students' scores perform worse than controls. What does this suggest about stereotype threat?
o: It only affects groups that are historically disadvantaged
This study shows a group that isn't historically disadvantaged being affected.
It depends on actual differences in math ability
Nothing showed the groups really differed in math ability.
It only occurs on verbal tests
The test here was a math test.
It can affect any group facing a negative comparison
Correct: even a high-status group is vulnerable when an unflattering comparison applies.
questions.x: Stereotype threat is the worry that you'll confirm a negative stereotype about your group, and that worry can drag your performance down. People often assume it only affects historically disadvantaged groups. This study says otherwise. White male math majors are a high-status group, but when they were told they'd be compared with Asian students, a group stereotyped as better at math, they scored worse. So any group can be affected when an unflattering comparison stereotype becomes relevant. The effect comes from the situation, not from a real gap in ability.

questions.q: A critic argues that strict cultural relativism makes it impossible to condemn practices that cause serious harm. Which position responds most directly to this critique?
o: Cultural relativism as a research method need not imply that all practices are morally acceptable
Correct: understanding a practice in context isn't the same as approving of it.
Ethnocentrism is the only defensible alternative
Rejecting extreme relativism doesn't mean judging everything by your own culture.
Harmful practices do not exist in any culture
This denies the critic's starting point instead of answering the critique.
Cultural relativism requires adopting other cultures' practices
Relativism is about understanding other practices, not adopting them.
questions.x: Cultural relativism means trying to understand a practice within its own culture before judging it. There are two versions. Methodological relativism is a research habit: understand first. Moral relativism is the much stronger claim that no practice can ever be called wrong. The critic is attacking the moral version. So the most direct reply is that you can use relativism as a way of studying cultures without saying every practice is morally fine. That answers the critique without swinging to ethnocentrism, which judges every culture by your own culture's standards.

questions.q: One explanation for the actor-observer bias is perceptual salience. Which finding best supports this account?
o: Actors know more about their own past behavior than observers do
This supports the explanation based on knowledge, not on what's visible.
Observers make more dispositional attributions for liked targets
Liking someone is about feelings, not about what stands out visually.
When actors watch a video of themselves from the observer's viewpoint, they make more dispositional self-attributions
Correct: changing what actors could see changed how they explained themselves.
Actors make more self-serving attributions after failure
That's the self-serving bias.
questions.x: The actor-observer bias is when you blame the situation for your own behavior but blame personality for other people's. The perceptual salience explanation says it comes down to what you can see. When you act, the situation fills your view, so it looks like the cause. When you watch someone else, that person fills your view, so they look like the cause. The best support is a study that changes only the viewpoint. When actors watched a video of themselves from an observer's angle, they explained their own behavior more by their traits. Knowing more about your own past is a different explanation.

questions.q: In a study, participants randomly assigned to write trivia questions stumped others assigned to answer them. Observers then rated the question writers as more knowledgeable. Why is this an example of the fundamental attribution error?
o: Question writers truly knew more than answerers
Roles were assigned by chance, so knowledge shouldn't differ between the groups.
Observers ignored the questioners' role advantage
Correct: the writing role, not greater intelligence, made the writers look smarter.
Observers attributed the result to the difficulty of the questions
Blaming question difficulty is a situational explanation, the opposite of this error.
Answerers credited their own failures to bad luck
That's self-serving bias, and the question is about observers.
questions.x: The fundamental attribution error is our habit of explaining other people's behavior by their personality or ability and overlooking the situation. In this study, chance decided who wrote questions and who answered, so the two groups weren't really different in knowledge. But the writers had a built-in edge: they could pick questions from their own odd bits of knowledge. Observers ignored that role advantage and decided the writers were smarter. Treating a situational advantage as a personal trait is the fundamental attribution error.

questions.q: Jurors who see themselves as similar to an accident victim assign the victim less blame than jurors who see themselves as dissimilar. This best illustrates what?
o: Just-world hypothesis
Just-world thinking predicts more victim blame regardless of similarity.
Out-group homogeneity
Nobody's view of group sameness is being measured.
Stereotype threat
The jurors aren't performing a task under a stereotype.
Defensive attribution
Correct: blaming a victim like yourself would mean you could be blamed too.
questions.x: Defensive attribution means assigning blame in a way that protects you from feeling like the same thing could happen to you, or that you could be blamed for it. Jurors who see themselves as similar to the victim blame the victim less. Why? Blaming someone just like you would suggest you could be blamed too. Jurors who feel different from the victim don't face that threat, so blaming is easier. The just-world hypothesis predicts victim blaming in general, but it doesn't explain why similarity matters.

questions.q: American and Chinese participants view an animated fish swimming ahead of a group. Americans more often say the lead fish is leading by its own choice; Chinese participants more often say the group is pushing or chasing it. What does this best illustrate?
o: Cultural differences in visual acuity
Both groups saw the same display. Their explanations differed, not their eyesight.
Cultural differences in attending to context
Correct: people from a more holistic culture looked to the group and situation as the cause.
Stereotype threat in the Chinese participants
No performance stereotype was brought up.
A primacy effect in the American participants
The order of the information wasn't changed.
questions.x: Both groups watched the exact same animation, so the difference is in how they explained it. Americans, from an individualist culture that focuses on the separate self, said the lead fish was out front by its own choice. That's a dispositional explanation, one that points to the fish itself. Chinese participants, from a more collectivist culture that focuses on groups and relationships, said the other fish were pushing or chasing it. That points to context. This matches the finding that the fundamental attribution error is weaker in cultures that focus on context.

questions.q: An orchestra begins auditioning musicians behind a screen so judges hear but cannot see them. The share of women advancing rises, while the applicant pool is unchanged. What does this finding most strongly suggest?
o: Women became better musicians once the screens were introduced
The screen changed what judges knew, not how well anyone played.
Evaluators' knowledge of gender had biased earlier decisions
Correct: hiding gender changed results for the same performances.
Screens produced stereotype threat in men
No performance stereotype was activated in men.
Women's applications fell after screens were introduced
The question says the applicant pool didn't change.
