questions.x: A screen hides who's playing without changing the sound at all. The applicant pool stayed the same, so the same people were auditioning. Yet more women advanced once judges couldn't see them. That means knowing the performer's gender had been swaying judges before. This is blind evaluation: hide one detail, and if results change, that detail was biasing the judgment. The tempting idea that women played better doesn't hold, because the screen changes only what judges know, not how anyone plays.

questions.q: A study finds that patients from a minority group receive less pain medication than majority-group patients with identical documented pain scores. Which additional finding would best indicate the disparity reflects provider bias?
o: Minority patients report pain more often
Pain scores were already the same, so this doesn't explain the gap.
Providers with stronger implicit bias scores show larger treatment gaps
Correct: tying each provider's bias to the size of their gap supports a bias explanation.
Majority patients have more insurance coverage
That points to a different cause (insurance), not to provider bias.
The hospital has a diverse staff
A diverse staff alone doesn't test whether bias drives the gap.
questions.x: To show that provider bias causes a gap, you need to connect a measure of bias to the size of the gap. If doctors with stronger implicit bias (automatic, often unconscious associations) show bigger gaps in pain treatment, then the gap grows along with the suspected cause. That's strong support. Insurance differences are tempting, but they're a confound, meaning a different factor that could explain the gap instead of the providers' bias. Pain scores were already identical, so how often patients report pain doesn't help.

questions.q: According to the stereotype content model, a group seen as highly competent but low in warmth is most likely to elicit what?
o: Pity
Pity goes with groups seen as warm but not competent.
Contempt
Contempt goes with groups seen as low on both traits.
Admiration
Admiration goes with groups seen as high on both traits.
Envy
Correct: capable but cold brings envy.
questions.x: The stereotype content model sorts groups on two traits: warmth (how friendly and trustworthy they seem) and competence (how capable they seem). The mix predicts the emotion people feel. A group seen as highly competent but low in warmth comes across as capable but cold, maybe even a threat. That stirs up envy, a mix of resentment and grudging respect. Warm but not competent brings pity. Low on both brings contempt. High on both brings admiration. Envy can turn into open hostility when times get unstable.

questions.q: People judge a likable in-group member more favorably than a similar out-group member, but judge an unlikable in-group member more harshly than a similar out-group member. This is called what?
o: Out-group homogeneity
Out-group homogeneity is seeing members of other groups as all alike.
Ultimate attribution error
That's about explaining out-group behavior, not punishing your own group's bad members.
Group polarization
Group polarization is opinions getting more extreme after group discussion.
Black sheep effect
Correct: unlikable in-group members get judged harshly to protect the group's image.
questions.x: The black sheep effect is a two-sided pattern in how people judge members of their own group (the in-group). A likable in-group member gets judged more kindly than a similar outsider. But an unlikable in-group member gets judged more harshly than a similar outsider. The reason is that people want their group to look good. A bad apple in your own group makes the whole group look worse, so you push them away. This fits social identity theory, the idea that part of our self-esteem comes from the groups we belong to.

questions.q: In a resource allocation task, participants choose between giving both groups more points or giving their own group fewer points but a larger margin over the other group. Many choose the larger margin. What does this suggest?
o: Participants were motivated purely by self-interest
Pure self-interest would pick the option with the most points.
Participants showed cultural relativism
Cultural relativism has nothing to do with handing out points.
Participants were trying to be fair
Fairness would favor an equal split.
In-group favoritism can center on relative advantage rather than absolute gain
Correct: being ahead of the other group mattered more than their own group's total.
questions.x: In these studies by Tajfel, people were put into groups and asked to hand out points. Many chose the option where their own group got fewer points but beat the other group by more. That tells you the goal wasn't the biggest payoff for their own group. It was being ahead. So in-group favoritism (treating your own group better) can be about relative advantage, not absolute gain. Social identity theory explains it: we feel good about ourselves when our group stands out as better, which is called positive distinctiveness. Pure self-interest would grab the most points.

questions.q: In a simulation, participants must quickly 'shoot' armed targets and not unarmed ones. They mistakenly shoot unarmed Black targets more often than unarmed White targets. Which conclusion is most justified?
o: Participants hold conscious, deliberate hostility toward Black people
Mistakes under time pressure don't prove conscious hostility.
Automatic stereotypic associations can bias rapid decisions
Correct: split-second decisions let automatic associations steer behavior.
Black targets held objects that looked more like weapons
The objects were controlled, so they were the same across target race.
The bias would increase with more time to decide
More time to decide usually reduces these errors.
questions.x: Implicit bias is an automatic association between a group and a trait, often outside awareness. In this simulation, people had to decide in a split second, and they mistakenly shot unarmed Black targets more often than unarmed White targets. The objects in the targets' hands were controlled, so race was the only difference. That points to automatic stereotype associations (linking Black people with danger) steering fast decisions. These errors show up even in people with no conscious hostility. Giving people more time usually lowers these errors, because slower, careful thinking can correct the automatic response.

questions.q: A researcher claims stereotype threat lowers scores because of anxiety. In an experiment, threat lowers scores but self-reported anxiety does not differ between conditions. What is the best interpretation?
o: Stereotype threat does not exist
Scores still dropped under threat, so the effect is real.
Anxiety is proven to be irrelevant in every case
One null result on self-report can't rule out anxiety everywhere.
Self-reported anxiety does not appear to mediate the effect in this study
Correct: the proposed middle step didn't change, so something else may explain the effect.
The independent variable was not manipulated
Scores differed, which shows the manipulation worked.
questions.x: A mediator is the middle step that explains how a cause produces its effect. If stereotype threat lowers scores because of anxiety, then anxiety should be higher in the threat condition, and that rise should explain the drop in scores. Here, threat still lowered scores, but self-reported anxiety was the same in both conditions. So self-reported anxiety doesn't seem to be the middle step in this study. Something else, like reduced working memory, may be. One study using self-report can't prove anxiety never matters anywhere.

questions.q: A coach who prizes physical toughness judges other people mainly on how tough they seem and pays little attention to their kindness. Which idea does this illustrate?
o: The fundamental attribution error
The FAE is about traits versus situations, not which traits get noticed.
Out-group homogeneity
No comparison of group members is involved.
Stereotype threat
Nobody's performance is hurt by a stereotype.
Our self-schemas shape the dimensions we use to judge others
Correct: the traits central to his own self-image guide how he sees others.
questions.x: A self-schema is an organized set of beliefs about yourself, like "I'm tough" or "I'm a hard worker." Traits that sit at the center of your self-concept tend to become the yardstick you use to judge other people. That's this coach: he values toughness in himself, so toughness is what he notices in everyone else, and kindness barely registers. The fundamental attribution error is tempting, but it's about explaining behavior by traits instead of situations, not about which traits a person pays attention to.

questions.q: A woman completes residency and becomes a board-certified surgeon. Her status as surgeon is best described as:
o: Achieved
Correct: she earned it through her own effort and training.
Ascribed
Ascribed statuses are handed to you at birth or without choice, like race or age.
Master
Nothing says this status overshadows everything else about her.
Primary
Primary describes a type of group, not a type of status.
questions.x: A status is a position a person holds in society. An achieved status is one you earn through your own effort, choices or merit. Finishing residency and getting board-certified takes years of work, so being a surgeon is achieved. An ascribed status is handed to you without effort, usually at birth, like your age, race or being born royal. Master status isn't about how a status was gained. It means one status overshadows all the others in how people see you, and nothing here suggests that.

questions.q: A man released from prison finds that employers focus only on his criminal record and overlook his degree and work history. His ex-offender status is functioning as a:
o: Role set
A role set is the bundle of roles tied to one status, not a label that dominates.
Ascribed status
A criminal record comes from his own actions, so it isn't ascribed.
Reference group
A reference group is a group you compare yourself to, not a status.
Master status
Correct: one status overshadows all the others and shapes every interaction.
questions.x: A master status is the one status that overshadows all the others and shapes how people see everything about you. That's what's happening here. Employers see "ex-offender" and stop looking, so his degree and work history get ignored. You might be tempted to call it ascribed because the label feels forced on him. But ascribed means handed to you without any action of your own, like your age. His record came from his own actions, so it's achieved. What makes it a master status is how much it dominates, not how he got it.

questions.q: A professor teaches lectures, advises graduate students and serves on hiring committees. These multiple behaviors attached to her single position are called her:
o: Status set
A status set is all the statuses one person holds, not the roles inside one status.
Role set
Correct: a role set is all the roles tied to one status.
Role strain
Role strain needs tension within a role, and none is described.
Master status
A master status dominates someone's identity. Nothing here says that.
questions.x: A status is a position, like professor. A role is the set of behaviors expected of someone in that position. One status usually comes with several roles, and that bundle is called the role set. Her one status, professor, brings teaching, advising and committee work. A status set is different: it's all the statuses one person holds at once, like professor, mother and citizen. Role strain would need some tension between those roles, and the question doesn't describe any.

questions.q: A child born into a royal family is called a prince from birth. His royal status is:
o: Achieved
Achieved statuses need effort or choice by the person.
Instrumental
Instrumental describes task-focused group ties, not a type of status.
Ascribed
Correct: he did nothing to earn it. It was given to him at birth.
Exited
Role exit means leaving a role, and he hasn't left anything.
questions.x: An ascribed status is one you're given without any effort, usually at birth. Royal titles, sex and ethnicity are classic examples. An achieved status is the opposite: something you earn or choose, like becoming a doctor. The prince did nothing to get his title. He was simply born into the family, so it's ascribed. He'll be expected to carry out royal duties later, but that doesn't change how he got the status in the first place.

questions.q: A woman is a respected physician but a member of a group that faces discrimination, and patients sometimes question her authority. Which concept best captures the mismatch?
o: Status inconsistency
Correct: her statuses carry very different prestige, so people treat her in mixed ways.
Role exit
She hasn't left any role.
Role strain
Role strain is clashing demands within one role, not unequal prestige between statuses.
Achieved master status
Her physician status is achieved, but the issue is the clash between two statuses.
questions.note: Status inconsistency: a person ranks high on one status and low on another.
questions.x: Every status carries a level of prestige, meaning social respect. Status inconsistency is when one person holds statuses ranked very differently, so people react to her in mixed, contradictory ways. Being a physician carries high prestige. Belonging to a group that faces discrimination carries lower prestige in the eyes of some people. So some patients respond to the lower-ranked status and question her authority. Role strain is tempting because she's under pressure, but strain is about clashing demands within one role, not mismatched prestige between two statuses.

questions.q: A first-year resident is told by attendings to see patients faster and by patients to spend more time with them. This is best classified as:
o: Role conflict
Role conflict needs clashing demands from two different statuses.
Role strain
Correct: both demands belong to the one status of resident.
Role exit
Nothing suggests the resident is leaving the role.
Role reversal
Role reversal means trading places with another person.
questions.note: Trap: multiple audiences can still create strain within one role.
questions.x: Role strain is tension between expectations that belong to one status. "Be faster" from attendings and "take more time" from patients are both expectations of being a resident, so this is role strain. Role conflict is tempting because two different groups of people are making demands. But role conflict means the demands come from two different statuses you hold, like resident and parent. The trick is to count statuses, not the number of people asking.

questions.q: According to Ebaugh's model of role exit, which stage immediately follows a person's first doubts about a role?
o: The turning point
The turning point comes after the person has weighed alternatives.
Creating the ex-role
Building the ex-role identity is the last stage.
Anticipatory socialization
This is a general socialization idea, not one of Ebaugh's stages.
Searching for alternatives
Correct: after the doubts, the person weighs other possible roles.
questions.note: Ebaugh: first doubts → alternatives → turning point → creating ex-role.
questions.x: Role exit is the process of leaving a role that was a big part of who you were, like a career or a marriage. Ebaugh described it in four stages. First come doubts about the role. Next, the person searches for alternatives, weighing what else they could do. Then comes a turning point, the moment they decide to leave. Last, they build an ex-role identity, like "former nurse." So searching for alternatives comes right after the first doubts. The turning point feels like the dramatic next step, but it comes later.

questions.q: Which is the best example of a primary group?
o: A company's accounting department
A work department is a task-focused, secondary group.
A semester-long lecture class
A class is temporary, impersonal and goal-focused, so it's secondary.
A close-knit family
Correct: primary groups are small, close, long-lasting and based on feelings.
A national professional association
Large formal associations are secondary groups.
questions.x: A primary group is small and close, lasts a long time, and is valued for the relationships themselves. Sociologists call that expressive, meaning it's based on feelings. Family and close friends are the classic examples. A secondary group is larger or more impersonal, often temporary, and formed to get something done. That's called instrumental, meaning goal-focused. A work department, a lecture class and a national professional association all bring people together for tasks, so they're secondary. The close-knit family is the primary group.

questions.q: Researchers randomly label participants as "overestimators" or "underestimators" of dot counts. Participants then give more money to anonymous members of their own label. This best demonstrates:
o: In-group favoritism even with trivial group criteria
Correct: just being sorted into a group, even on trivial grounds, creates favoritism.
Realistic conflict between groups over scarce resources
The groups never competed, so conflict over resources doesn't explain it.
Reference group comparison
Participants were handing out money, not judging themselves.
Primary group loyalty
These made-up groups have no closeness or shared history.
questions.x: Your in-group is the group you belong to, and in-group favoritism is treating your own group better. Tajfel's minimal group studies showed how little it takes. People were sorted by something meaningless, like whether they over- or underestimated dots, or even at random. They still gave more money to strangers with their own label. No competition, history or contact was needed. Just being put in a group was enough. Realistic conflict theory is tempting, but it explains bias as coming from competing for scarce resources, and these groups never competed.

questions.q: A college junior hoping to attend medical school models her study habits after current medical students she admires. The medical students serve as her:
o: Primary group
She has no close, lasting relationship with them.
Out-group
An out-group is a group you don't identify with, and she admires and copies these students.
Reference group
Correct: she uses this group's standards to judge and guide herself.
Dyad
A dyad is just a two-person group.
questions.x: A reference group is any group whose standards you use to judge yourself and guide what you do. You don't have to be a member. This student isn't in medical school yet, but she admires current medical students and copies their study habits, so they're her reference group. Copying the habits of a group you hope to join is also called anticipatory socialization, which means practicing for a future role. They aren't her primary group, because she doesn't have a close, lasting relationship with them.

questions.q: In a hospital's communication map, one nurse is the only link between the ICU staff and the pharmacy staff. Removing her would most likely:
o: Increase the density of connections within each cluster
Connections inside each cluster aren't affected by losing a link between clusters.
Have no effect because weak ties are unimportant
Bridging ties are often the most important ones for spreading information.
Merge the two clusters into one
Removing the only link separates the clusters. It can't merge them.
Cut the flow of information between the two clusters
Correct: she's the only bridge, so losing her disconnects the two clusters.
questions.x: A social network is a map of people and the ties between them. A cluster is a group whose members are tightly connected to each other. A bridge is a tie that's the only link between two clusters, and the gap it spans is called a structural hole. This nurse is the bridge between ICU staff and pharmacy staff. Remove her and the two clusters are cut off, so information can't pass between them. Density, meaning how connected people are inside a cluster, doesn't change, because she was the link between clusters, not within one.

questions.q: Which is a characteristic of Weber's ideal-type bureaucracy?
o: Hiring based on family connections
Weber's model hires based on qualifications, not family ties.
Flexible, informal decision-making
Bureaucracies rely on formal, standard procedures.
A clear hierarchy of authority with written rules
Correct: Weber stressed a chain of command, written rules, specialized jobs and impersonality.
Emotional ties among all members
Bureaucracy is built on impersonal relationships.
questions.x: A bureaucracy is a large organization run by formal rules. Weber described an ideal type, a clean model of its key features. It has a clear hierarchy of authority (a chain of command), written rules and procedures, a division of labor where each person has a specialized job, impersonal relationships, and hiring and promotion based on qualifications. The goal is efficiency and predictability. Hiring through family connections and making decisions informally or based on feelings are exactly what the model is designed to remove.

questions.q: A grassroots patient-advocacy group founded on equal voting gradually comes to be run by a few long-serving leaders who control decisions. This illustrates:
o: The iron law of oligarchy
Correct: Michels argued organizations drift toward rule by a small group of leaders.
McDonaldization
McDonaldization is about efficiency and standardization, not who rules.
Bureaucratic ritualism
Ritualism is rigidly following rules, not power collecting in a few hands.
The strength of weak ties
That idea is about how information flows through a network.
questions.x: Oligarchy means rule by a few. Michels' iron law of oligarchy says that organizations, even ones founded on equal voting, tend to end up controlled by a small group of leaders. As a group grows, it needs coordination and expertise, and the people who handle those jobs gain control over decisions and communication. A grassroots group drifting into rule by a few long-serving leaders is the textbook case. McDonaldization is about efficiency and standardization, not about who holds power.

questions.q: A clinic judges physicians mainly by the number of patients seen per hour rather than by quality of care. Which dimension of McDonaldization does this reflect?
o: Predictability
Predictability means standard, uniform experiences everywhere.
Control
Control means replacing human judgment with technology or rules.
Efficiency
Efficiency is the fastest way to a goal, not judging by quantity.
Calculability
Correct: calculability values what can be counted over quality.
questions.x: McDonaldization is Ritzer's term for society adopting fast-food principles. It has four parts: efficiency, calculability, predictability and control. Calculability means valuing what can be counted, so quantity wins over quality. Judging doctors mostly by patients seen per hour, instead of by how good their care is, is calculability. Efficiency is tempting, but efficiency means using the fastest way to reach a goal. This question is about measuring and prizing a number.

questions.q: A pharmacy chain installs automated dispensing machines that limit what pharmacists can do and dictate each step. Which McDonaldization dimension is most emphasized?
o: Calculability
Nothing here is about counting or quantity.
Predictability
Uniform results may follow, but the main point is limiting workers.
Control
Correct: technology takes over decisions that workers used to make.
Efficiency
Speed isn't the focus. Dictating what workers do is.
questions.x: In McDonaldization, control means replacing human judgment with machines, scripts or rules that dictate how work gets done. Dispensing machines that limit what pharmacists can do and spell out every step are a clear case. Predictability is tempting, because machines may make results more uniform. But the question stresses limiting workers' choices, and that's the heart of control. Nothing is said about counting (calculability) or speed (efficiency).

questions.q: A hospital volunteer program that people join because they value its mission is, in Etzioni's typology, a:
o: Coercive organization
Coercive organizations, like prisons, force membership.
Normative organization
Correct: normative organizations attract members through shared values.
Utilitarian organization
Utilitarian organizations offer pay or material rewards.
Primary group
A volunteer program is a formal organization, not a small intimate group.
questions.x: Etzioni sorted formal organizations by why people join them. Normative organizations draw members who share their values or goals, and joining is voluntary. Coercive organizations, like prisons, hold members against their will. Utilitarian organizations, like a company, offer pay or other material rewards. These volunteers join because they believe in the mission and aren't paid, so the program is a normative organization.

questions.q: In Goffman's dramaturgical approach, a physician's white coat, stethoscope and office décor that help convey competence are part of the:
o: Front
Correct: the front is the setting, appearance and manner that set up the performance.
Back stage
Back stage is where performers relax away from the audience.
Audience
The audience is the people watching, like patients.
Role set
A role set is the roles tied to a status, not props.
questions.x: Goffman's dramaturgical approach treats everyday life like a stage play. People are actors performing for an audience. The front is everything that sets up the performance and tells the audience who you are: the setting (the office décor), your appearance (white coat, stethoscope) and your manner (how you carry yourself). A doctor's coat and stethoscope are props that say "I'm competent." Back stage is the opposite: the place where performers relax out of the audience's view.

questions.q: After a difficult shift, nurses joke and complain freely in a staff room patients cannot enter. In Goffman's terms, the staff room is:
o: Front stage
Front stage is where the performance is given to an audience.
Back stage
Correct: back stage is where performers drop their public role.
A reference group
A reference group is a group you compare yourself to, not a place.
A total institution
A total institution controls every part of residents' lives.
questions.x: In Goffman's dramaturgy, social life is like theater. Front stage is where people perform for an audience, acting the way their role expects. Back stage is where the audience can't see, so people can drop the act and relax. A staff room patients can't enter is back stage, and that's why the nurses can joke and complain freely there. Total institution is also a Goffman term, which makes it tempting, but it means a place like a prison that controls every part of residents' lives.

questions.q: A job applicant who privately dislikes teamwork describes herself as a passionate collaborator because the company values it. Which self is she presenting?
o: Tactical self
Correct: the tactical self is the version we show to match what others expect.
Authentic self
The authentic self is who she really believes she is.
Ideal self
The ideal self is who she wants to become, not what the employer expects.
Looking-glass self
That's Cooley's idea of a self formed from how we imagine others judge us.
questions.x: Impression management is how we shape what others think of us, and it uses three kinds of self. The authentic self is who you believe you really are. The ideal self is who you'd like to become. The tactical self is the version you show to match what others expect. This applicant privately dislikes teamwork, but the company values it, so she presents herself as a passionate collaborator. That's her tactical self. The ideal self is tempting, but she doesn't want to become a team player. She's just performing it for this audience.

questions.q: Two Deaf colleagues discuss a project in American Sign Language. Their exchange is best classified as:
o: Nonverbal communication
Verbal means using language, not using your voice. ASL is a language.
Verbal communication
Correct: sign languages have words and grammar, so they're verbal.
Paralanguage
Paralanguage is how the voice sounds: tone, pitch, volume.
Animal signaling
ASL is a full human language, not animal signaling.
questions.note: Verbal = language-based, whether spoken, written or signed.
questions.x: Verbal communication means communication through language: words put together with grammar. It doesn't have to be spoken. Writing counts, and so does signing. American Sign Language (ASL) is a complete natural language with its own grammar, so a conversation in ASL is verbal. The trap is thinking "verbal" means "using your voice." Nonverbal communication is cues outside of language, like a shrug, posture or a facial expression.

questions.q: Participants from two cultures watch a disgusting film alone and show similar facial expressions, but when an authority figure is present, one group masks its expressions. This best supports:
o: Facial expressions are entirely learned
The matching faces when alone argue against purely learned expressions.
Disgust is not a basic emotion
Both groups showed disgust, which fits disgust being a basic emotion.
Paralanguage varies by culture
The study measured faces, not voices.
Universal basic expressions modified by cultural display rules
Correct: the expressions are shared, but cultural rules decide when they're shown.
questions.x: Ekman and colleagues found that basic emotional expressions, like the face of disgust, are largely universal: people everywhere make and recognize them. But each culture has display rules, which are norms about when it's okay to show an emotion. Alone, both groups made similar disgusted faces, which points to a shared, universal expression. With an authority figure in the room, one group hid its expression, which points to a cultural display rule. The matching faces when alone rule out the idea that expressions are entirely learned.

questions.q: Gazelles that spot a predator sometimes leap high in place (stotting), wasting energy instead of fleeing. The best evolutionary explanation is that stotting:
o: Is an accident with no function
A costly behavior that persists usually has some survival value.
Lures predators toward kin
Leading predators toward relatives would hurt the gazelle's own genes.
Is a costly, honest signal that the gazelle is fit and hard to catch
Correct: only a healthy gazelle can afford the display, so predators may give up.
Is a pheromone release
Stotting is a visual display, not a chemical signal.
questions.note: Handicap principle: costly signals are hard to fake.
questions.x: Zahavi's handicap principle says that signals that are costly to make tend to be honest, because only animals in good shape can afford them. A weak animal can't fake it. Stotting burns energy and time right when a predator is near. A gazelle that can afford to do that is telling the predator, "I'm fit, and you won't catch me." The predator does better chasing an easier target. Calling stotting an accident ignores a basic rule: a costly behavior that sticks around in a population usually does something useful.

questions.q: Men who met a female interviewer on a high, swaying bridge were more likely to call her later than men who met her on a stable bridge. Which explanation best fits?
o: They misattributed fear-related arousal to attraction
Correct: the arousal from the scary bridge was mislabeled as attraction.
Mere exposure to the interviewer had increased their liking
Both groups spent about the same time with her.
Proximity differed between groups
Both groups met her face to face.
The stable bridge produced more arousal
The high bridge produced more arousal, not the stable one.
questions.x: In Dutton and Aron's bridge study, the high, swaying bridge made the men's hearts race from fear. When an attractive interviewer was standing right there, many men read that racing heart as attraction to her, so they were more likely to call her later. That's misattribution of arousal: feeling your body stirred up and pinning it on the wrong cause. It fits the two-factor theory, which says an emotion is bodily arousal plus a mental label you give it. Mere exposure and proximity don't fit, because both groups met her the same way.

questions.q: Children who watched an adult hit an inflatable doll later hit the doll more than children who watched a calm adult. This finding supports:
o: Catharsis reducing aggression
Watching aggression increased aggression instead of reducing it.
Observational learning of aggression
Correct: the children copied the behavior they saw.
Frustration-aggression theory
Nobody was frustrated on purpose, so that can't explain the difference.
Instinctive aggression independent of learning
The groups differed only in what they watched, which points to learning.
questions.x: In Bandura's Bobo doll studies, children who watched an adult hit an inflatable doll were more likely to hit it themselves. That's observational learning: learning by watching someone else, called a model, and copying them. The catharsis idea predicts the reverse, that watching aggression lets off steam and lowers aggression, and the results went the other way. Since the two groups differed only in what they saw, learning explains the difference, not instinct.

questions.q: Which biological profile is most associated with increased impulsive aggression?
o: Low serotonin activity and reduced prefrontal cortex control
Correct: low serotonin and a weak prefrontal brake are linked to impulsive aggression.
High serotonin and enhanced prefrontal activity
These go with better impulse control, so less impulsive aggression.
Low testosterone and a smaller amygdala response
Lower testosterone and a quieter amygdala go with less aggression.
High oxytocin alone
Oxytocin is mainly linked to bonding and trust.
questions.x: Think of the brain as having a gas pedal and a brake for anger. The amygdala is the gas pedal: it fires off fast emotional reactions. The prefrontal cortex, at the front of the brain, is the brake that holds those reactions back. Serotonin is a brain chemical that helps calm mood and control impulses. Impulsive aggression goes with low serotonin activity and weak prefrontal control, often along with a very reactive amygdala and higher testosterone. Low testosterone and a quieter amygdala push the other way, toward less aggression.

questions.q: Angered participants gave more electric shocks to a confederate when a rifle lay on a nearby table than when a badminton racket did. This best illustrates:
o: Catharsis
There was no venting, and aggression went up, not down.
Instrumental aggression
The shocks weren't a means to some other goal.
The weapons effect, in which aggressive cues prime aggression
Correct: a weapon acts as a cue that brings aggressive thoughts to mind.
Social facilitation
The presence of other people wasn't what changed.
questions.x: Berkowitz and LePage made participants angry, then let them give electric shocks to a confederate (someone secretly working with the researchers). People gave more shocks when a rifle was lying nearby than when a badminton racket was. That's the weapons effect. A weapon works as an aggressive cue: just seeing it primes aggressive thoughts, meaning it makes them come to mind more easily. In someone who's already angry, that makes aggression more likely. Catharsis would predict less aggression, the opposite of what happened.

questions.q: A survey finds that teens who play more violent video games report more aggressive behavior. Which additional study would best test whether the games cause aggression?
o: Surveying more teens about their gaming habits
A bigger survey is still just a correlation.
Randomly assigning teens to play violent or nonviolent games and then measuring aggression
Correct: random assignment controls other differences, so you can test cause.
Asking aggressive teens why they like violent games
Asking about preferences can't show cause.
Measuring parents' attitudes toward video games
This adds a variable but no control over who plays what.
questions.x: A survey can only show that two things go together, which is a correlation. It can't show cause. Maybe the games make teens aggressive. Or maybe aggressive teens choose violent games (reverse causation), or a third factor drives both. To test cause, you need an experiment with random assignment: chance decides which teens play violent games and which play nonviolent ones. That makes the groups alike on average, so if the violent-game group ends up more aggressive, the games are the likely cause. A bigger survey doesn't fix the problem.

questions.q: In the Strange Situation, an infant is upset when the mother leaves, greets her warmly when she returns and is quickly soothed. This infant is classified as:
o: Avoidant
Avoidant infants show little distress and ignore the caregiver on return.
Ambivalent
Ambivalent infants are hard to soothe and resist comfort.
Disorganized
Disorganized infants act in confused, contradictory ways.
Securely attached
Correct: secure infants are upset at separation and easily comforted at reunion.
questions.x: Ainsworth's Strange Situation watches how a baby reacts when the caregiver leaves the room and then comes back. A securely attached infant uses the caregiver as a secure base. The baby gets upset when she leaves, is glad when she returns, and calms down quickly. That's this infant. Ambivalent infants are upset too, but they're hard to soothe and may push away comfort. Avoidant infants show little distress and ignore the caregiver when she returns.

questions.q: Newly hatched goslings follow the first moving object they see during a brief period after hatching. This phenomenon demonstrates:
o: Operant conditioning
No reward or punishment shapes the behavior.
Kin selection
The goslings follow any moving object, not just relatives.
Imprinting during a critical period
Correct: the bond forms only during a short window after hatching.
Secure attachment
Imprinting is a fast, fixed animal process, not a human attachment category.
questions.x: Imprinting is a fast kind of learning in which a young animal bonds to the first moving thing it sees. Lorenz showed that goslings would follow him around as if he were their mother. The catch is that it only works during a critical period, a short window of time right after hatching. No reward is needed, so it isn't operant conditioning. And since goslings will follow a person or even an object, it isn't about family, so it isn't kin selection.

questions.q: Participants who felt high empathy for a struggling student helped her even when they could easily leave without helping. Low-empathy participants helped mainly when leaving was difficult. These results best support:
o: The negative-state relief model
That model says helping relieves your own distress, which leaving would also do.
The empathy-altruism hypothesis
Correct: empathy led to helping even when walking away was easy.
Kin selection
The student wasn't related to the participants.
The frustration-aggression hypothesis
That theory explains aggression, not helping.
questions.x: Altruism is helping someone without a selfish payoff. Batson's empathy-altruism hypothesis says that feeling empathy, really sharing someone's feelings, creates a true wish to help them for their own sake. The test is to make it easy to walk away. If people were helping only to ease their own bad feelings, an easy exit would do that just as well, and they'd leave. High-empathy participants still helped when leaving was easy, which points to real altruism. Low-empathy participants helped mainly when leaving was hard, which looks more self-focused.

questions.q: In a hawk-dove model, a population of all doves can be invaded by a hawk mutant, and a population of all hawks can be invaded by doves. What does game theory predict?
o: All doves at equilibrium
An all-dove population gets invaded by hawks.
All hawks at equilibrium
An all-hawk population gets invaded by doves.
A stable mix of hawk and dove strategies
Correct: when neither pure strategy can resist invasion, a stable mix results.
Extinction of both strategies
Invasion leads to a mix, not extinction.
questions.x: An evolutionarily stable strategy (ESS) is one that, once it's common, can't be beaten by a rare alternative. In the hawk-dove game, hawks fight hard over resources and doves back down. In a population of all doves, a lone hawk grabs everything, so hawks invade. In a population of all hawks, constant fights are costly, so a dove that avoids fights does better, and doves invade. Since neither pure strategy can hold off the other, the population settles into a stable mix of hawks and doves. The exact mix depends on the cost of fighting and the value of the resource.

questions.q: Researchers find that social support predicts better health among people facing major life stressors but has little effect among people with low stress. These data best support:
o: The direct (main) effect hypothesis
A main effect would show benefits at every stress level.
The frustration-aggression hypothesis
This hypothesis is about aggression, not health.
The buffering hypothesis
Correct: support protects mainly by cushioning the effects of stress.
The iron law of oligarchy
This is about power inside organizations.
questions.note: Buffering = an interaction; main effect = benefit regardless of stress.
questions.x: Social support means help and caring from the people around you. The buffering hypothesis says support protects your health mainly by cushioning the harm of stress. So its benefits should show up mostly in people under a lot of stress, and that's exactly what these data show. Researchers call that an interaction: the effect of support depends on how much stress you're under. The direct (main) effect hypothesis predicts support helps everyone, at every stress level. Since low-stress people got little benefit, these data don't fit it.

questions.q: In pipefish, males carry and nourish the eggs, and females compete for males while males are choosy. This best supports which idea?
o: The sex that invests more in offspring tends to be choosier
Correct: the amount of investment, not sex itself, predicts which sex is choosy.
Males are always the competitive sex
Pipefish show females can be the competing sex.
Mating behavior is unrelated to parental care
The role swap tracks the swap in who provides care.
Females always invest more in offspring
In pipefish, males invest more.
questions.note: Trivers: higher investment → more selective.
questions.x: Parental investment is the time, energy and risk a parent puts into each offspring. Trivers' parental investment theory says the sex that invests more is choosier about mates, because a bad match costs it more. The sex that invests less competes for mates. In most species, females invest more, so females choose and males compete. Pipefish flip that: males carry and nourish the eggs, so males are choosy and females compete. That shows it's the amount of investment, not being male or female, that sets the pattern.

questions.q: A female bird chooses a mate with bright plumage that signals parasite resistance, though he provides no food or nest. She gains:
o: Direct material benefits such as food or territory
Direct benefits are food, territory or care, and he provides none.
Benefits from kin selection
Her mate isn't her relative.
Indirect genetic benefits for her offspring
Correct: good genes passed to her offspring are an indirect benefit.
Benefits from reciprocal altruism
No trading of favors over time is described.
questions.x: Choosing a mate can pay off in two ways. Direct benefits go to the chooser herself: food, territory, a nest or help raising young. Indirect benefits are good genes passed on to her offspring. Bright plumage can be an honest sign of health, here resistance to parasites. Since this male gives her no food or nest, the only thing she gains is better genes for her chicks. That's an indirect genetic benefit. The detail "provides no food or nest" is what rules out direct benefits.

questions.q: A participant reports no negative feelings toward older adults, but on an Implicit Association Test responds faster when pairing "old" with negative words. This result best indicates:
o: Explicit prejudice
She openly denies any negative attitudes.
Institutional discrimination
No organizational policy is involved.
Individual discrimination
Only reaction times were measured, not how she treats anyone.
Implicit bias that may differ from explicit attitudes
Correct: automatic associations can exist without conscious prejudice.
questions.x: The Implicit Association Test (IAT) measures automatic mental links by timing how fast people pair ideas. Faster pairing means a stronger link. She paired "old" with negative words faster, which points to an implicit bias, an automatic association she may not be aware of. At the same time, she honestly reports no negative feelings, which is her explicit attitude. The two can disagree. Also, an IAT score is an attitude measure. By itself it doesn't show discrimination, which is actual unfair behavior.

questions.q: A shop owner holds no personal prejudice but refuses to hire members of a minority group because he fears customers will object. In Merton's typology, he is a:
o: All-weather liberal
All-weather liberals neither hold prejudice nor discriminate.
Timid bigot
Timid bigots are prejudiced but don't discriminate.
Active bigot
Active bigots are prejudiced and discriminate.
Fair-weather liberal (unprejudiced discriminator)
Correct: he discriminates without prejudice, because of social pressure.
questions.x: Merton sorted people using two questions. Are they prejudiced (a negative attitude)? Do they discriminate (unfair action)? That gives four types. The all-weather liberal has no prejudice and doesn't discriminate. The fair-weather liberal has no prejudice but discriminates when there's social pressure. The timid bigot is prejudiced but doesn't act on it. The active bigot is prejudiced and acts on it. This shop owner has no personal prejudice but won't hire minority workers because he fears customers' reactions, so he's a fair-weather liberal, also called an unprejudiced discriminator.

questions.q: A company that excluded women for decades now lays off workers by seniority, so women are disproportionately let go. This is best described as:
o: Past-in-present discrimination
Correct: a neutral-looking rule carries forward the effects of earlier discrimination.
Individual discrimination
Nobody is acting on personal bias now.
Implicit bias
The gap comes from a policy, not from automatic associations.
Prejudice
Prejudice is an attitude, not a layoff policy.
questions.x: Past-in-present discrimination is when a rule that looks neutral today carries forward the effects of unfair treatment from the past. It's a kind of institutional discrimination, meaning it's built into how an organization works. Seniority means years on the job. Because this company kept women out for decades, women have fewer years, so laying people off by seniority hits them hardest. Individual discrimination doesn't fit, because nobody is acting on personal bias now. The policy produces the gap.

questions.q: A researcher visited many restaurants with a couple from a minority group and was refused service only once, yet most owners later replied by mail that they would refuse such customers. This finding best shows that:
o: Discrimination always follows prejudice
Owners stated prejudice but mostly didn't discriminate.
Institutional discrimination was absent
The study looked at individual owners, not policies.
Stated prejudice does not always predict discriminatory behavior
Correct: what owners said by mail didn't match how they actually treated the couple.
Implicit bias drove the refusals
Implicit associations weren't measured.
questions.x: This is LaPiere's classic study. He traveled with a couple from a minority group, and they were refused service only once. Later, when he mailed the same places asking if they'd serve such customers, most said no. So what people said (their stated attitude, which was prejudiced) didn't match what they actually did (they served the couple). The lesson is that stated prejudice doesn't always predict discriminatory behavior. That directly contradicts the idea that discrimination always follows prejudice.

questions.q: Durkheim compared society to a living organism whose parts each contribute to overall stability. This analogy is central to which perspective?
o: Conflict theory
Conflict theory sees groups competing and unequal, not parts cooperating to keep balance.
Symbolic interactionism
Interactionism looks at small, everyday meaning-making, not society as one body.
Functionalism
Correct: functionalism sees institutions as connected parts that keep society stable.
Rational choice theory
Rational choice looks at one person weighing costs and benefits, not whole systems.
questions.note: Organism analogy, stability, equilibrium: think functionalism.
questions.x: Durkheim's picture of society as a body is the heart of functionalism. Functionalism is a big-picture (macro) theory that sees society as a set of connected parts, like organs. Each institution, such as family, school or government, does a job that helps keep the whole thing stable. Conflict theory is the tempting wrong answer because it also looks at society as a whole. But it sees groups competing over limited resources, not parts working together to stay balanced.

questions.q: A sociologist argues that drug manufacturers shape clinical guidelines to protect profits, even when patients bear higher costs. This argument most reflects:
o: functionalism
Functionalism would ask how guidelines keep things stable, not who's being exploited.
conflict theory
Correct: a powerful group advances its own interests while others pay the price.
symbolic interactionism
Interactionism looks at face-to-face meaning, not institutional power.
social exchange theory
Exchange theory looks at give-and-take between people, not one group dominating.
questions.x: This is conflict theory. Conflict theory sees society as groups with unequal power, where the stronger groups shape the rules to protect their own interests, often at others' expense. Drug makers steering guidelines toward profit while patients pay more fits that perfectly. Functionalism would look at the same guidelines and ask how they keep the health system running smoothly. It wouldn't ask who gains and who loses, and that's exactly what this sociologist is asking.

questions.q: "If people define situations as real, they are real in their consequences." This statement, the Thomas theorem, is most associated with which perspective?
o: Functionalism
Functionalism looks at how institutions keep society stable, not how people define situations.
Conflict theory
Conflict theory focuses on struggles over power and resources, not personal definitions.
Rational choice theory
Rational choice assumes people weigh real costs and benefits, not their interpretations.
Symbolic interactionism
Correct: people act on the meanings they give a situation.
questions.x: The Thomas theorem says people react to how they read a situation, not just to the facts. So even a false belief can lead to real results. That idea, that the meanings we give things guide what we do, is the core of symbolic interactionism. Symbolic interactionism is a small-scale (micro) theory about how people create meaning in everyday life. Rational choice is the trap: it assumes people react to real costs and benefits, not to how they've defined the situation.

questions.q: Paper currency has value only because people collectively agree that it does. This best exemplifies which concept?
o: Cultural lag
Cultural lag is when norms and values fall behind new technology.
Manifest function
A manifest function is an institution's intended purpose, not a shared agreement about value.
Social constructionism
Correct: money's value exists because people agree that it does.
Social exchange
Exchange theory is about trading rewards in relationships, not where value comes from.
questions.x: This is social constructionism: the idea that some things are real only because people agree to treat them as real. A paper bill is just paper. It buys groceries because everyone agrees it's worth something. If that agreement disappeared, so would its value. Social exchange theory is the tempting wrong answer because money gets traded. But exchange theory is about the rewards people trade in relationships. It doesn't explain where money's value comes from in the first place.

questions.q: A sociologist finds that a country's official racial categories on census forms changed several times over one century. This finding most directly supports the idea that race is:
o: socially constructed
Correct: categories that keep changing show race is defined by agreement, not fixed biology.
a latent function
A latent function is an unintended result of an institution, not how a category is defined.
a cultural universal
A cultural universal is found in every culture; shifting definitions are the opposite.
a biological constant
If race were a fixed biological fact, the categories wouldn't keep being redrawn.
questions.x: If race were a fixed biological fact, the official categories wouldn't keep changing. The fact that a census redrew its racial boxes several times in one century shows that people and governments decide where the lines go. That's what it means to say race is socially constructed: the categories are made by social and political agreement. Real physical differences between people do exist. But which groups a society draws around those differences, and what it calls them, is a human choice.

questions.q: A student chooses a college major after weighing expected salary against tuition costs and hours of study required. Which theory best explains this decision?
o: Feminist theory
Feminist theory looks at gender inequality, not one person's cost-benefit decision.
Symbolic interactionism
Interactionism is about shared meanings, not calculating payoffs.
Functionalism
Functionalism explains how institutions meet society's needs, not individual choices.
Rational choice theory
Correct: the student weighs costs against benefits to get the best payoff.
questions.x: This is rational choice theory. It treats people like calculators: before deciding, they compare costs (money, time, effort) with benefits and pick the option with the best payoff. Weighing a future salary against tuition and study hours is exactly that kind of calculation. Social exchange theory is a close cousin that uses the same cost-benefit logic, but it applies it to relationships between people. Choosing a major is one person's decision, so rational choice fits best.

questions.q: Two friends maintain their relationship because each feels that what they receive roughly matches what they give. Which theory best explains this?
o: Conflict theory
Conflict theory looks at groups struggling over resources, not a balanced friendship.
Social exchange theory
Correct: relationships last when rewards balance or beat the costs.
Functionalism
Functionalism looks at society's stability, not reward balance between two people.
Feminist theory
Feminist theory focuses on gender and power, which isn't described here.
questions.x: This is social exchange theory. It treats relationships as trades: each person gives things like time, help and affection, and gets things back. People stay in a relationship as long as what they get is at least as much as what they give. Two friends who feel the give-and-take is balanced is a textbook example. Rational choice uses the same cost-benefit idea, but for one person's decisions in general. Exchange theory is about what happens between partners.

questions.q: A study finds that female physicians spend more unpaid time on patients' emotional concerns than male peers. Explaining this as a product of gendered expectations embedded in medicine reflects:
o: functionalism
Functionalism would ask what need the pattern serves, not call it gender inequality.
rational choice theory
Rational choice would point to personal payoffs, not gender expectations built into medicine.
social exchange theory
Exchange theory would frame it as trading rewards between people, not a gendered norm.
feminist theory
Correct: the gap is blamed on gendered power and expectations inside an institution.
questions.note: Feminist theory is a conflict-family perspective focused specifically on gender.
questions.x: Blaming the extra unpaid emotional work on gendered expectations built into medicine is a feminist explanation. Feminist theory studies how gender shapes power and opportunity, and it looks for the cause inside institutions rather than inside individual people. Rational choice would explain the pattern by each doctor's personal payoff. Functionalism would ask what need the pattern fills for the health system. Neither of those names gender inequality as the cause, and this explanation does.

questions.q: Researchers find that schools funded mainly by local property taxes show outcomes closely tracking neighborhood wealth. A conflict theorist would most likely interpret this as:
o: schools efficiently matching talent to occupations
Sorting talent into jobs is the functionalist view, and these outcomes follow wealth.
students' cost-benefit decisions about effort
Cost-benefit decisions about effort are rational choice, not conflict theory.
teachers and students negotiating the meaning of classroom life
Negotiating classroom meanings is the interactionist, small-scale view.
the education system reproducing existing class inequality
Correct: conflict theory sees schools passing class advantage down the generations.
questions.x: Conflict theory sees institutions like schools as tools that help better-off groups hold on to their advantages. When schools are paid for mostly by local property taxes, wealthy neighborhoods get well-funded schools, their kids do well, and those kids stay ahead. That passing-down of inequality from one generation to the next is called social reproduction. A functionalist might say schools sort students by talent. But here the results follow wealth, not ability.

questions.q: Historians note that childhood as a protected life stage with distinct needs emerged only in recent centuries. This best illustrates:
o: cultural lag
Cultural lag is norms and values trailing behind new technology.
rational choice theory
Rational choice is about one person's cost-benefit decisions.
latent dysfunction
A latent dysfunction is an unintended harmful result of an institution.
social constructionism
Correct: the meaning of childhood was built by society and changed over time.
questions.x: This is social constructionism: the idea that many things we treat as natural are really created by social agreement, and their meaning can change. Childhood as a special, protected stage appeared only as schooling, child labor laws and family norms changed. Society built the idea. Cultural lag is the tempting wrong answer because something changed over time. But cultural lag needs norms trailing behind a specific technology change, and the question doesn't describe one.

questions.q: In social exchange theory, the partner who is less dependent on a relationship for valued rewards typically:
o: has less power because they invest less
Backwards: needing the relationship less gives more power, not less.
has equal power because exchanges always balance
Exchanges are often uneven, and differences in dependence create differences in power.
holds more power over the relationship
Correct: by the principle of least interest, the less dependent partner has more power to set the terms.
exits the relationship immediately
Needing it less doesn't mean leaving; it shifts power toward that partner.
questions.note: Principle of least interest: whoever needs the relationship less controls it more.
questions.x: In social exchange theory, power comes from dependence. The partner who needs the relationship less has other options, so they can walk away more easily. That lets them set the terms. This is called the principle of least interest: whoever cares least about keeping the relationship going holds the most power. It's tempting to think investing less means losing influence, but it works the other way around.

questions.q: In an economic game, many participants refuse a small but nonzero offer they view as unfair, leaving both players with nothing. This finding most directly challenges which theory?
o: Symbolic interactionism
Interactionism easily allows ideas like fairness to guide what people do.
Feminist theory
Nothing in the game involves gender.
Conflict theory
Conflict theory never predicted people would accept any positive payoff.
Rational choice theory
Correct: a pure payoff-maximizer should accept anything above zero.
questions.note: Fairness norms can override material self-interest.
questions.x: This is the ultimatum game. One player offers a split of some money, and the other accepts or refuses. If they refuse, both get nothing. Rational choice theory assumes people maximize their payoff, so they should accept any offer above zero, since a little beats nothing. Many people refuse unfair offers anyway, which shows fairness and emotion can beat pure self-interest. That challenges rational choice. Interactionism has no trouble with it, because it says meanings like fairness guide action.

questions.q: Durkheim's concept of "social facts" refers to:
o: verified statistics collected by governments
Durkheim's idea is much broader than official statistics.
individual personality traits that shape behavior
Social facts exist outside individuals, so they aren't personality traits.
ways of acting and thinking that are external to individuals and constrain them
Correct: norms, laws and values exist beyond individuals and shape how they act.
meanings people create in face-to-face interaction
Meanings made in face-to-face interaction are symbolic interactionism's focus.
questions.x: Durkheim used 'social facts' to mean ways of acting, thinking and feeling that exist outside any one person and push on how we behave. Laws, norms, customs and religious beliefs are examples. No single person invented them, but we all feel pressure to follow them. Durkheim said sociology should study these as real things in their own right. The word 'facts' can make you think of statistics, but the idea is much broader than numbers.

questions.q: Analyzing how race, class and gender combine to shape a working-class Black woman's experience of health care reflects which concept?
o: Intersectionality
Correct: overlapping identities combine to shape advantage or disadvantage.
Anomie
Anomie is normlessness during times of social upheaval.
Cultural relativism
Cultural relativism means judging practices by their own culture's standards.
Organic solidarity
Organic solidarity is social cohesion from people depending on each other's specialized jobs.
questions.x: This is intersectionality, a term from Kimberlé Crenshaw. It says identities like race, class and gender don't act one at a time. They overlap and combine, creating experiences of advantage or disadvantage you can't understand by looking at any one category alone. A working-class Black woman's health care is shaped by all three together. Cultural relativism sounds related but means judging a culture's practices by that culture's own standards, which isn't about overlapping identities.

questions.q: Durkheim argued that industrial societies are held together mainly by interdependence among people performing specialized jobs. He called this:
o: mechanical solidarity
Mechanical solidarity comes from sameness and shared beliefs in simple societies.
false consciousness
False consciousness is a Marxist idea about ideology.
the iron cage
The iron cage is Weber's image of people trapped by rational bureaucracy.
organic solidarity
Correct: specialized jobs make people depend on each other, which binds society.
questions.note: Mechanical = sameness (traditional); organic = interdependence (modern).
questions.x: Durkheim called this organic solidarity. Solidarity just means whatever holds a society together. In modern industrial societies, people do specialized jobs and have to rely on each other, the way organs in a body each do something different but need one another. Traditional societies hold together through mechanical solidarity, which comes from sameness: people share the same beliefs and do similar work. Students often swap the two labels, so tie organic to organs.

questions.q: Everyone in a neighborhood benefits from a park cleanup, yet few residents volunteer. A rational choice theorist would attribute low participation to:
o: latent dysfunction
This functionalist term doesn't explain why individuals skip paying the cost.
the free-rider problem
Correct: people can enjoy the shared benefit without paying its cost, so many sit out.
culture shock
Culture shock is feeling lost in an unfamiliar culture.
false consciousness
False consciousness is a Marxist idea about class beliefs, not shared goods.
questions.x: This is the free-rider problem. A clean park is a public good: everyone gets to enjoy it whether or not they helped. A free rider is someone who enjoys the benefit without paying the cost. A purely self-interested person, the kind rational choice theory pictures, might reason, 'Someone else will clean it, and I'll still get a nice park.' If lots of people think that way, few show up. That's why shared goods often end up short of help.

questions.q: Which statement best distinguishes social constructionism from symbolic interactionism?
o: Constructionism emphasizes how shared knowledge and institutions come to seem objective; interactionism emphasizes meanings made in face-to-face encounters.
Correct: constructionism is broad and society-wide; interactionism centers on face-to-face moments.
Constructionism is a macro theory of class conflict; interactionism is a theory of stability.
Class conflict and stability belong to conflict theory and functionalism, not these two.
Constructionism denies that meanings exist; interactionism affirms them.
Both perspectives treat meanings as real and powerful.
Constructionism studies rational choices; interactionism studies institutions.
These descriptions fit neither perspective.
questions.x: Both perspectives agree that meaning is made by people. The difference is scale. Social constructionism, from Berger and Luckmann, looks at how shared knowledge and institutions, like money or childhood, come to feel objective and natural across a whole society. Symbolic interactionism zooms in on how meanings get created and changed in specific face-to-face encounters. The other choices pin ideas from different theories onto these two, or claim one of them denies meaning exists, which neither does.

questions.q: Two people both identify as members of the same faith, but one prays daily and attends services weekly while the other rarely does either. They differ most in:
o: religious affiliation
Their affiliation is the same, so it can't be the difference.
religiosity
Correct: religiosity is how strongly someone believes, practices and commits.
secularization
Secularization is religion losing influence across a whole society.
ecclesia membership
An ecclesia is a church type tied to the state, not a personal measure.
questions.x: Religious affiliation is which group you say you belong to. Religiosity is how strongly you believe and practice, shown by things like how often you pray or go to services. These two people share an affiliation, since they belong to the same faith. What's different is their religiosity: one prays daily and attends weekly, the other rarely does either. Secularization is a different idea. It means religion losing influence across a whole society, not a difference between two people.

questions.q: After a charismatic religious founder dies, followers create written rules, offices and procedures for choosing successors. Weber called this process:
o: secularization
Secularization is religion losing influence in society.
the routinization of charisma
Correct: personal, charismatic authority is turned into lasting rules and offices.
anomie
Anomie is normlessness, and here people are making more rules, not fewer.
cultural diffusion
Diffusion is cultural traits spreading from one group to another.
questions.x: Charismatic authority rests on one leader's exceptional personal qualities, so it's shaky: when that leader dies, followers face a crisis over who's in charge. Weber called the fix the routinization of charisma. Followers turn the leader's personal pull into lasting rules, offices and ways to pick successors. That turns charismatic authority into traditional or rational-legal authority. Secularization is the tempting mix-up, but it means religion losing influence, not followers building structure.

questions.q: C. Wright Mills argued that a small group of top corporate, military and political leaders controls most national decisions. This view contrasts most directly with the pluralist claim that:
o: religion legitimizes state power
Neither model centers on religion.
the economy determines all other institutions
This is closer to a Marxist claim than to pluralism.
authority rests on tradition
Authority based on tradition is one of Weber's types, not pluralism.
power is spread among many competing interest groups
Correct: pluralism says no single elite dominates; many groups compete.
questions.x: C. Wright Mills's power elite model says a small, tightly connected group of corporate, military and political leaders makes most of a nation's big decisions. Pluralism says the opposite: power is spread among many competing interest groups, like unions, businesses and community groups, and no single group wins every time. The choice saying the economy shapes all other institutions is closer to Marx than to pluralism, so don't let it pull you in.

questions.q: Over a century, most births moved from homes attended by midwives to hospitals run by obstetricians. Feminist critics would most likely argue this change:
o: eliminated all risks associated with childbirth
The feminist critique is about control and power, not claims of total safety.
was driven solely by patients' rational cost-benefit choices
This is a rational choice framing, not a feminist one.
shifted control over childbirth from women to a male-dominated profession
Correct: authority over women's bodies and births moved to a male-dominated profession.
strengthened mechanical solidarity among mothers
Mechanical solidarity is Durkheim's idea and has nothing to do with this critique.
questions.x: Feminist theory looks at how gender shapes power. Feminist critics see the move from midwife-attended home births to hospital births run by obstetricians as medicalization, meaning a normal life event got redefined as a medical problem for doctors to manage. In the process, control over childbirth shifted away from women, both mothers and midwives, to a profession that was then mostly male. The critique is about who holds the power, not a claim that hospitals made birth risk-free.

questions.q: As two-earner households become the norm, demand rises for daycare and after-school programs. A functionalist would interpret this as:
o: evidence that institutions are independent of one another
The example shows the opposite: institutions depend on each other.
the economy losing all influence over the family
The economic change is what's driving the family change, so it hasn't lost influence.
proof that social change is always harmful
Functionalists see society adapting, not change as always harmful.
other institutions adapting to economic and family change
Correct: a change in one institution leads related ones to adjust.
questions.x: Functionalists see institutions as connected parts that adjust to each other to keep society balanced. When the economy pulls both parents into paid work, families suddenly need childcare. Other institutions respond by growing daycare and after-school programs. That's adaptation: one part changes, and the parts around it shift to fill the gap. It shows how much institutions depend on each other, which is the opposite of them acting independently.

questions.q: Ivan Illich argued that modern medicine harms society by making people dependent on professionals to manage ordinary life events such as birth, grief and aging. This critique is known as:
o: social iatrogenesis
Correct: harm comes from medicalizing everyday life and depending on professionals.
clinical iatrogenesis
Clinical iatrogenesis is direct harm from treatment, like drug side effects.
the sick role
The sick role is Parsons's set of expectations for people who are ill.
culture lag
Culture lag is norms and values trailing behind technology.
questions.x: Iatrogenesis means harm caused by medicine itself. Ivan Illich described levels of it. Clinical iatrogenesis is direct physical harm from treatment, like a drug side effect or an infection caught in the hospital. Social iatrogenesis is the harm of medicalizing everyday life: ordinary events like birth, grief and aging get handed to professionals, and people start to feel they can't cope without them. This question describes dependence, not physical injury, so it's social iatrogenesis.

questions.q: The proposal that the structure of a language shapes how its speakers perceive and think about the world is known as:
o: cultural relativism
Cultural relativism is judging a culture by its own standards.
the Thomas theorem
The Thomas theorem says situations defined as real have real consequences.
the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis
Correct: it proposes that language influences how people think.
cultural diffusion
Diffusion is cultural traits spreading between societies.
questions.x: This is the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis, also called linguistic relativity. It proposes that the structure of the language you speak shapes how you notice and think about the world. There's a strong version, that language determines thought, and most researchers reject it. A weaker version, that language influences thought, has some support. Cultural relativism sounds similar but is about judging a culture's practices by that culture's own standards, not about language shaping thinking.

questions.q: Lactase persistence into adulthood is much more common in populations with long histories of dairy herding. This pattern best illustrates:
o: gene-culture coevolution
Correct: a cultural practice changed the pressure favoring a gene.
cultural lag
Cultural lag is norms and values trailing behind technology.
cultural relativism
Relativism is about how we judge cultures, not genes.
cultural diffusion
Diffusion spreads practices between groups but doesn't explain gene frequencies.
questions.note: Culture can shape genes, and genes can shape culture.
questions.x: This is gene-culture coevolution: culture and genes shaping each other over many generations. Lactase is the enzyme that digests milk sugar, and most mammals stop making it after early childhood. In groups that herded dairy animals, milk was a food adults could use, so people who kept making lactase (lactase persistence) did better and left more children. Over time the gene version for it became common. Diffusion could spread dairy herding to new groups, but spreading a practice doesn't change gene frequencies by itself.

questions.q: Surveys show nearly everyone in a country says honesty is important, yet tax evasion is widespread there. This gap illustrates the difference between:
o: material and symbolic culture
Honesty and tax behavior are both nonmaterial; this isn't an objects-versus-ideas contrast.
folkways and mores
Both parts concern the same norm, not two kinds of norms.
subculture and counterculture
No group rejecting or reshaping mainstream values is described.
ideal culture and real culture
Correct: stated values differ from actual behavior.
questions.x: Ideal culture is the values and norms a society says it holds. Real culture is how people actually behave. When nearly everyone says honesty matters but lots of people cheat on their taxes, you're looking at the gap between the two. It's tempting to think about folkways and mores, since honesty is a norm. But folkways versus mores compares two strengths of norms. This question compares what people say with what they do.

questions.q: Sources of cultural change include invention, discovery and diffusion. Scientists' recognition that microorganisms cause many diseases is best classified as:
o: discovery
Correct: discovery is recognizing something that already existed.
invention
Invention creates something new, like a tool or a process.
diffusion
Diffusion is traits spreading from one culture to another.
cultural lag
Cultural lag is a gap between kinds of change, not a source of change.
questions.note: Germs existed already: discovery. The microscope was an invention.
questions.x: Cultures change in three main ways. Discovery is recognizing something that already existed. Invention is creating something new, like a tool or a process. Diffusion is a trait spreading from one culture to another. Germs were causing disease long before anyone knew it, so recognizing that is a discovery. The microscope that let scientists see them was an invention, which is why invention is tempting. But the question asks about recognizing germs, not building the tool.

questions.q: An observational study finds that adults who attend religious services weekly have lower mortality, and that much of the difference disappears after adjusting for social support. Which conclusion is best supported?
o: Attendance causes longer life through belief alone.
Adjusting for social support weakened the link, so belief alone isn't supported.
Religion has no relationship to health.
A link was found, so this overstates the result the other way.
Social support is the only possible cause of the association.
Some difference remained, and observational data can't rule out other factors.
Social networks may partly explain how religious participation relates to health.
Correct: social support looks like one pathway, without proving cause.
questions.note: An attenuated association after adjustment suggests a mediator, not proof of cause.
questions.x: Weekly attenders lived longer, but much of that gap disappeared once researchers adjusted for social support. When a link shrinks after you account for a variable, that variable is probably part of the explanation. Here, the friends and community people get at services may be one pathway linking religion to health. Two cautions: some difference was left over, and this was an observational study, so it can't prove cause and effect. That rules out the choices with 'alone,' 'no' or 'only.'

questions.q: A cohort of medical students shows declining empathy scores between year 1 and year 3. Which additional finding would most strengthen a hidden curriculum explanation?
o: The decline is concentrated in clinical rotations with more exposure to cynical role models.
Correct: tying the drop to cynical role models supports informal, unspoken learning.
Empathy scores also fall among age-matched students in other fields.
This points to a general age or schooling trend, not medical training.
