Students' formal ethics coursework increased in year 2.
Formal coursework is the official curriculum, not the hidden one.
Empathy scores were measured with a new instrument in year 3.
A new measuring tool suggests a measurement problem, weakening any explanation.
questions.x: The hidden curriculum is the set of unofficial lessons people pick up in an institution: attitudes and habits absorbed from role models, not taught in class. If that's why empathy drops, the drop should be biggest where students spend time around cynical role models. Finding exactly that ties the decline to the proposed cause. If students outside medicine lost empathy at the same rate, that would point to a general trend instead, weakening the hidden curriculum explanation.

questions.q: Across 30 countries, religiosity is lower where national income is higher. A researcher concludes that wealth causes secularization. What is the best critique?
o: Religiosity cannot be measured in surveys.
Religiosity is routinely measured with questions about belief and attendance.
The sample of countries is too large.
A bigger sample usually makes an analysis stronger, not weaker.
Correlational data cannot rule out confounders such as education levels.
Correct: a third variable could be driving both income and religiosity.
Wealthier countries have no religious institutions.
This is false, and it doesn't touch the reasoning flaw.
questions.x: Two things moving together across countries is a correlation, and a correlation can't prove cause. A confounder is a third variable that drives both. Education is a good example: more schooling could raise national income and also lower religiosity, making wealth look like the cause when it isn't. The direction could also run the other way. The sample size isn't the problem (30 countries is fine), and religiosity can be measured with survey questions about belief and attendance.

questions.q: Over a decade, diagnoses of an attention disorder rose 40%, while community surveys using a fixed symptom checklist found stable symptom levels. This pattern best supports:
o: a true rise in the disorder's underlying prevalence
Flat symptom levels contradict a real rise in the condition.
demedicalization of the condition
Demedicalization would lower diagnoses, not raise them.
medicalization through broader diagnosis of the same behaviors
Correct: more of the same behaviors are being labeled medical, without more symptoms.
cultural lag in diagnostic technology
Nothing here shows norms trailing behind technology.
questions.x: The checklist stayed the same and symptom levels stayed flat, yet diagnoses rose 40%. So the condition itself didn't become more common. What changed was labeling. That's medicalization: more of the same behaviors getting defined and treated as a medical problem, often because diagnostic criteria or habits got broader. A true rise in prevalence (how common a condition is) would show up as more symptoms on the fixed checklist, and it didn't.

questions.q: In a study of couples, both partners who feel they give more than they get and partners who feel they get more than they give report lower satisfaction than partners in balanced relationships. This finding best supports:
o: equity theory, an extension of social exchange theory
Correct: feeling things are uneven in either direction lowers satisfaction.
pure reward maximization
This predicts the partner getting more should be happiest.
functionalism
Functionalism looks at society's stability, not fairness within a couple.
the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis
Sapir-Whorf is about language and thought.
questions.x: Equity theory builds on social exchange theory. It says people are happiest when what they get out of a relationship matches what they put in. Partners who give more than they get feel resentful. Partners who get more than they give feel guilty. Both end up less satisfied than partners in balanced relationships, which is exactly the finding. If people simply wanted the most rewards, the partner getting more should be the happiest, and the data say otherwise.

questions.q: In the 1850s a physician proposed "drapetomania," a supposed mental illness causing enslaved people to flee captivity. This example best illustrates that:
o: diagnoses always reflect objective biological findings
This diagnosis reflected social interests, not biology.
disease categories can reflect prevailing social values and power relations
Correct: the label turned resistance into illness in a way that served slaveholders.
the sick role exempts patients from blame
The label was used to justify control, not to excuse anyone.
medicalization reduces the influence of physicians
Medicalization expands medical authority; it doesn't shrink it.
questions.x: Drapetomania called enslaved people's attempts to escape a mental illness. It had no basis in biology. It turned resistance into a 'medical problem,' and that served slaveholders. The example shows that disease categories can reflect the values and power relations of their time rather than objective science. It's a case of medicalization, which means defining behavior as a medical issue, and medicalization expands doctors' authority rather than shrinking it.

questions.q: Workers who earn a diploma are paid notably more than workers who completed nearly the same coursework but left before graduating. This finding most strongly supports:
o: the view that education pays off only by raising workers' job skills
Nearly the same coursework means similar skills, yet pay still differs.
the credentialist view that diplomas signal value beyond skills
Correct: the diploma itself is rewarded, not just the learning.
the hidden curriculum's effect on punctuality
The data compare diplomas, not unspoken lessons like punctuality.
de facto segregation in schools
Nothing here involves separation by race or class.
questions.x: These two groups took almost the same courses, so they should have about the same skills. Yet the diploma holders earn notably more. That means the piece of paper itself is being rewarded. Credentialism is the idea that degrees work as signals to employers, beyond the skills they stand for. The extra pay for finishing is sometimes called the sheepskin effect. If education paid only through skills, similar learning would bring similar pay.

questions.q: Why do sociologists distinguish between sex and gender?
o: Sex is socially constructed; gender is fixed by chromosomes
This swaps the two terms.
The two terms are interchangeable in sociological research
Sociologists separate them on purpose, because the two can vary independently.
Gender refers only to legal status on official documents
Legal markers are one way gender shows up, not what gender means.
Sex refers to biological traits; gender refers to socially constructed roles and identities
Correct: sex is biological, while gender reflects cultural expectations and identity.
questions.note: Sex = biology; gender = social roles, norms and identity.
questions.x: Sex means biological traits: chromosomes, hormones and anatomy. Gender means the roles, norms and identities a society attaches to being a man, a woman or another gender. Gender identity is a person's own inner sense of their gender. Sociologists keep the two apart because they can vary separately. Gender expectations change from culture to culture and across history, even when biology doesn't. Watch for the choice that flips them: biology is the sex side, culture is the gender side.

questions.q: Which observation most strongly supports the view that race is a social construct?
o: People of different races can have different average heights
Average differences in a trait don't show the categories themselves are biological.
Skin pigmentation is influenced by melanin production
A biological basis for skin color doesn't make racial categories biological.
Some diseases are more common in certain geographic ancestries
Ancestry-linked variation is real but doesn't line up neatly with socially defined races.
The racial categories on a national census have been redefined several times over a century
Correct: categories that shift with politics and custom reflect social, not biological, borders.
questions.x: A social construct is a category whose borders are set by people's agreement, not by nature. If a national census keeps redrawing its racial categories over a century, those categories must be following politics and custom, not fixed biology. That's the strongest evidence here. The other choices describe real biological variation, like skin pigment or disease patterns. Those differences exist, but they don't show that the racial boxes themselves are natural divisions.

questions.q: In the 19th-century United States, Irish immigrants were often described as a separate, inferior 'race,' a label later dropped as they were absorbed into the category 'white.' This illustrates:
o: Amalgamation
Amalgamation is groups blending into a new culture, not assigning racial labels.
Racialization
Correct: racial meaning was assigned to a group, then later taken away.
Symbolic ethnicity
Symbolic ethnicity is a chosen, low-cost pride in heritage, not a label forced on a group.
Cultural relativism
Cultural relativism is judging cultures by their own standards, unrelated to racial labels.
questions.note: Racialization: attaching racial meaning to a group, often to justify unequal treatment.
questions.x: Racialization is the process of giving racial meaning to a group that wasn't seen as a race before, usually in a way that justifies treating them worse. In the 1800s, Irish immigrants were labeled a separate, inferior race. Later that label was dropped and they were counted as white. The people didn't change; the label did. Amalgamation is tempting because groups did mix, but it means groups blending into a brand-new culture, not a racial label being stuck on and peeled off.

questions.q: A researcher follows everyone born in a city between 1990 and 1994 to study their employment over time. This group is best described as a:
o: Reference group
A reference group is who people compare themselves to, not a group picked by birth year.
Birth cohort
Correct: a birth cohort is people born in the same period, here 1990 to 1994.
Dependent population
Dependents are people under 15 or over 64, not a group defined by birth years.
Primary group
A primary group is a small, close group like a family.
questions.x: A cohort is a group of people who share a defining experience in the same time period. A birth cohort is people born in the same span of years, here 1990 to 1994. Following one cohort over time is a longitudinal study, and it lets researchers watch how a generation's life, like its employment, unfolds. A reference group is tempting only because it's also a 'group,' but it means the people you compare yourself to, not a group picked by birth year.

questions.q: A 2005 survey finds adults over 60 use social media far less than adults under 30. Following the same people to 2025, researchers find the older group's use barely changed, while the 2005 under-30 group, now middle-aged, still uses it heavily. The 2005 gap mainly reflected a(n):
o: Cohort effect
Correct: the gap followed the generation people were born into, not their age.
Age effect
If aging caused it, the younger group would have cut back as they got older.
Period effect
A period effect would shift all age groups together at one point in time.
Hawthorne effect
The Hawthorne effect is behavior changing because people know they're watched.
questions.note: Cohort = generation; age = life stage; period = historical moment affecting everyone.
questions.x: A cohort effect is a difference that comes from when people were born, so it stays with a generation as it ages. Here, after 20 years, the older group still barely uses social media, and the younger group, now middle-aged, still uses it heavily. Each group kept its habits. So the 2005 gap came from generation, not age. If it were an age effect, the younger group would have cut back as they got older, and they didn't.

questions.q: After a severe economic recession, reported financial anxiety rose sharply among teenagers, middle-aged adults and retirees alike, then fell as the economy recovered. This pattern is best explained as a(n):
o: Cohort effect
A cohort effect would mark one generation and stay with it as it aged.
Period effect
Correct: one historical event shifted every age group at the same time.
Age effect
An age effect would show up at a certain life stage, whatever the year.
Selection effect
Selection effects are about who gets into a sample, not a shared historical shift.
questions.x: A period effect is a change caused by a historical event that hits every age group at about the same time. Here a recession pushed up financial anxiety in teenagers, middle-aged adults and retirees alike, and then anxiety fell for everyone as the economy recovered. Everyone moving up and down together is the signature of a period effect. A cohort effect would mark one generation and follow it through life. An age effect would show up at a certain life stage, whatever the year.

questions.q: In every generation studied, voter turnout rises as individuals move from their early 20s into their 50s. This consistent pattern is best described as a(n):
o: Age (life-course) effect
Correct: the change goes with a life stage and repeats in every generation.
Cohort effect
A cohort effect would set generations apart, but here they all follow the same path.
Period effect
A period effect would be tied to a specific year, not to age.
Ecological fallacy
That's a reasoning error about individuals from group data, not a pattern over time.
questions.x: An age effect, also called a life-course effect, is a change tied to a stage of life that repeats in every generation. Turnout climbs from the early 20s into the 50s in every cohort studied, so the pattern follows aging itself. As people get older they tend to settle down, own property and build community ties, and those make voting more likely. A cohort effect would show generations differing from each other, which is the opposite of what's described here.

questions.q: Recently arrived immigrants often have better health than native-born residents of similar income, but this advantage fades the longer they stay. This is called the:
o: Brain drain
Brain drain is skilled workers leaving a country, not a health pattern.
Demographic dividend
That's economic growth from having a large working-age population.
Healthy immigrant effect
Correct: migrants are often healthier on arrival, and the edge wears off over time.
Epidemiologic transition
That's a whole society shifting from infectious to chronic disease.
questions.x: This is the healthy immigrant effect. Newly arrived immigrants are often healthier than native-born people with similar incomes. Part of the reason is self-selection: healthier people are more likely to move and to pass medical screening. Over the years the advantage fades, as new diets, stress and discrimination take their toll. Brain drain is also a migration term, but it means skilled workers leaving a country, not anyone's health.

questions.q: A study finds that U.S.-born children of immigrants have higher obesity rates than their foreign-born parents despite higher incomes. Which explanation best fits this finding?
o: Adoption of the host country's diet and activity patterns through acculturation
Correct: picking up less healthy local habits can wear away the parents' health advantage.
Higher income directly causes obesity
Higher income usually predicts better health, so something else explains the reversal.
Selective emigration of the least healthy parents
Migrants tend to be the healthier ones, which wouldn't explain the children's decline.
Genetic drift between generations
One generation is far too short for genetic drift to explain this.
questions.note: The 'immigrant paradox' often reverses with acculturation.
questions.x: Acculturation means picking up the customs and habits of the culture you live in, including what you eat and how active you are. Children raised in the host country take on local eating and sitting-a-lot habits more fully than their immigrant parents did. So the family's health advantage fades even as income rises. Income is the tempting answer because the question mentions it. But higher income usually goes with better health, so it can't explain things getting worse.

questions.q: Lesbian, gay and bisexual adults show higher average rates of depression than heterosexual adults. The minority stress model attributes this mainly to:
o: Chronic stress from stigma, prejudice and discrimination
Correct: the model blames hostile social conditions, not orientation itself.
An inherent link between sexual orientation and mental illness
The model clearly rejects orientation itself as the cause.
Lower average income in all sexual-minority groups
Income may contribute, but the model centers on stress from stigma.
Overreporting of symptoms by survey respondents
The model treats the gap as real, not as a survey error.
questions.x: The minority stress model says stigmatized groups carry extra, ongoing stress on top of the everyday stress everyone has. That includes discrimination, rejection, having to hide who you are, and internalized stigma, which means turning society's negative messages against yourself. That added stress raises the risk of depression and anxiety. The model puts the cause in hostile social conditions, not in sexual orientation itself. Income can play a part in health gaps, but it isn't the model's main idea.

questions.q: A researcher argues that the workplace discrimination faced by Black women cannot be understood by simply adding the effects of racism and sexism. This argument reflects:
o: Cultural capital
Cultural capital is non-money assets like education and taste.
Social reproduction
Social reproduction is inequality passed down across generations.
Ethnocentrism
Ethnocentrism is judging other cultures by your own culture's standards.
Intersectionality
Correct: overlapping identities create distinct disadvantages, not just added-up ones.
questions.x: This is intersectionality: identities like race, gender and class overlap and combine into experiences you can't get by adding up each one separately. A Black woman at work may face stereotypes that neither white women nor Black men face. That's why 'racism plus sexism' doesn't capture it. Social reproduction is the tempting wrong answer because it's also about inequality, but it describes inequality being passed from parents to children, not identities overlapping.

questions.q: Many recent immigrants from one country settle in a single neighborhood with shops, newspapers and places of worship in their native language. This neighborhood is an example of a(n):
o: Gentrified district
Gentrification is wealthier residents moving in, not immigrants clustering.
Megalopolis
A megalopolis is a chain of big metro areas that have grown together.
Ethnic enclave
Correct: an ethnic group concentrated in one place, with its own institutions.
Suburb
A suburb is a residential area outside a city center, not defined by ethnicity.
questions.x: An ethnic enclave is a neighborhood where one ethnic group lives in large numbers and has built its own businesses, newspapers and places of worship. Think of a Chinatown or a Little Italy. Two things define it: the group clusters in one place, and it has its own institutions. Enclaves often help newcomers settle in by offering a familiar language and support. Gentrification also changes neighborhoods, but it means wealthier people moving in and pushing costs up.

questions.q: Over three generations, an immigrant family stops speaking its native language and adopts the customs of the dominant culture until its origins are no longer visible. This process is:
o: Cultural pluralism
Pluralism means groups keep their own identities while living side by side.
Amalgamation
Amalgamation blends groups into a new culture rather than absorbing one into another.
Assimilation
Correct: a minority group is absorbed into the dominant culture and loses its distinct traits.
Segregation
Segregation is keeping groups physically and socially apart.
questions.x: Assimilation is when a minority group gradually takes on the dominant culture and loses its own language and customs, often over several generations. It's one-way: group A becomes like group B. Here the family stops speaking its native language and adopts mainstream customs until you can't see where they came from. Amalgamation is the tempting alternative, but in amalgamation both groups blend into a brand-new culture, rather than one being absorbed into the other.

questions.q: Two immigrant groups intermarry over generations, and their cuisines and holidays merge into a new tradition that neither group practiced before. This best illustrates:
o: Amalgamation
Correct: the groups blend into a new culture, the 'melting pot.'
Assimilation
In assimilation one group takes on the other's culture; nothing new forms.
Cultural pluralism
Pluralism keeps the groups distinct.
Cultural lag
Cultural lag is norms and values trailing behind material change.
questions.note: Assimilation: A + B → B. Amalgamation: A + B → C. Pluralism: A + B → A + B.
questions.x: Amalgamation is when groups mix, often through intermarriage, and form a new culture that's different from each of the originals. It's the classic 'melting pot.' The giveaway here is the new holiday tradition that neither group practiced before. In assimilation, one group just takes on the other's existing culture, so nothing new gets made. A handy shorthand: assimilation is A + B → B, amalgamation is A + B → C, and pluralism is A + B → A + B.

questions.q: Historical U.S. laws classified anyone with any known African ancestry as Black, regardless of appearance. This 'one-drop rule' best demonstrates that:
o: Race is reliably determined by ancestry testing
No fraction of ancestry biologically defines a race; the cutoff was arbitrary.
Racial categories are fixed across societies
Other societies drew these lines quite differently.
Racial boundaries were set by social and legal convention
Correct: the rule assigned race by law, not by any biological threshold.
Physical appearance determines racial identity
The rule ignored appearance entirely.
questions.x: The one-drop rule said anyone with any known African ancestry was Black, no matter how they looked or how small that ancestry was. That line was drawn by law and custom, not by any biological threshold, and other societies drew their racial lines very differently. That's what it means for racial boundaries to be socially constructed. The rule completely ignored appearance, so the choice saying appearance determines race is ruled out.

questions.q: Genetic studies show that most human genetic variation occurs among individuals within the same socially defined racial group rather than between groups. This finding:
o: Supports the view that racial categories are not discrete biological groupings
Correct: if most variation sits within groups, the categories capture little genetic structure.
Shows that racial groups are genetically identical
Variation within groups is large, so people aren't identical.
Proves that race has no effect on health
Race can still affect health through racism and social conditions.
Shows that ethnicity is purely biological
Ethnicity is cultural, and this finding is about race.
questions.x: Genetic variation means differences in DNA from person to person. Most of it is found between individuals inside the same racial group, and only a small share separates one group from another. So the groups overlap heavily and have no sharp genetic borders. That supports the idea that racial categories aren't separate biological groupings. It doesn't mean people within a group are identical. It also doesn't mean race has no effect on health, because racism and social conditions still shape health.

questions.q: A country's fertility falls to replacement level, yet its population keeps growing for several more decades. The most likely reason is:
o: Replacement fertility always produces growth
Replacement fertility leads to a steady population once the age structure evens out.
A large young cohort is still entering its reproductive years
Correct: population momentum; many young parents still mean many births, even at 2.1 each.
Mortality must be rising
Rising deaths would slow growth, not keep it going.
Crude birth rates are unaffected by age structure
Crude birth rates depend heavily on age structure; that's why growth continues.
questions.note: Population momentum: a young age structure keeps growth going after fertility drops.
questions.x: This is population momentum. Replacement level is the fertility rate where each generation just replaces itself, about 2.1 children per woman. But the population keeps growing anyway, because a big group of young people is still moving into their childbearing years. Even at 2.1 children each, lots of parents means lots of births, while deaths stay fairly low. Growth only stops after that large young group ages and the age structure (how many people are in each age group) evens out.

questions.q: In populations with low mortality, replacement-level total fertility is approximately:
o: 1.0 child per woman
That would cut the population about in half each generation.
2.1 children per woman
Correct: two to replace the parents, plus a little for early deaths and the extra boys born.
3.5 children per woman
That would make each generation much bigger than the last.
2.0 children per woman exactly
Slightly more than 2 is needed, since some children die and more boys are born.
questions.x: Replacement-level fertility is the average number of children per woman needed for each generation to replace itself. Two children replace the two parents. But you need a little more than 2, because some children die before they're old enough to have kids, and slightly more boys than girls are born (about 105 boys for every 100 girls). In low-mortality countries that works out to about 2.1. Where many children die young, the number is higher. That's why exactly 2.0 is tempting but wrong.

questions.q: Country A has excellent health care but a higher crude death rate than Country B, which has poorer health care. The best explanation is that Country A:
o: Has an older age structure
Correct: crude rates ignore age, and lots of elderly people means more deaths per 1,000.
Has a higher infant mortality rate
Excellent health care makes high infant mortality unlikely.
Has a higher birth rate
More births add young people, which tends to lower the crude death rate.
Has more immigration of young workers
Young immigrants would lower the crude death rate.
questions.note: Compare mortality across populations with age-standardized rates.
questions.x: The crude death rate is deaths per 1,000 people in the whole population, and it doesn't adjust for age. Older people die more often, so a country with lots of elderly people will have many deaths per 1,000 even with excellent health care. A young country can have few deaths per 1,000 even with poorer care. That's why fair comparisons use age-standardized rates, which remove the effect of age differences. A higher birth rate or young immigrants would make a population younger and push the crude rate down.

questions.q: Which development most directly undermined Malthus's prediction of mass famine in the 20th century?
o: A sharp rise in global birth rates
More births would support his fear, not undermine it.
The spread of infectious diseases
Disease is one of his positive checks, so it fits his theory.
Agricultural innovations that greatly increased crop yields
Correct: technology raised food output far faster than Malthus expected.
Rising world population after 1950
Fast growth without mass famine challenged him; growth alone doesn't.
questions.x: Thomas Malthus said population grows much faster than food can, so he predicted famine would eventually knock population back down. What he didn't see coming was how much farming technology would improve. Machines, fertilizers and high-yield crop varieties (the Green Revolution) raised food output faster than population in most of the world. That broke the link he predicted between growth and mass famine. Population growth on its own doesn't disprove him. Growth without the famine he expected does.

questions.q: An environmental scientist argues that rising world population will exhaust fresh water and arable land unless birth rates are reduced. This view is best described as:
o: Demographic transition theory
Transition theory describes stages of birth and death rates, not resources collapsing.
World systems theory
World systems theory is about the global economic ranking of nations.
Neo-Malthusian
Correct: it updates Malthus by stressing limited resources and calling for fewer births.
Dependency theory
Dependency theory is about rich nations exploiting poorer ones.
questions.x: This is a neo-Malthusian view. Malthus worried that population would outgrow food. Neo-Malthusians update that worry for today: population growth threatens limited resources like fresh water, farmland and ecosystems, so birth rates need to come down. The clue is the combination of growing population, running out of resources, and a call for fewer births. Demographic transition theory is tempting because it's about population too, but it describes stages of birth and death rates, not resources running out.

questions.q: The population pyramid of an oil-rich Gulf state shows far more men than women aged 20 to 45, while children and elderly are evenly split by sex. The best explanation is:
o: Sex-selective abortion
That would skew the youngest ages, which are balanced here.
Higher female mortality in adulthood
Mortality wouldn't create such a sharp gap limited to certain ages.
Large-scale labor immigration of working-age men
Correct: migration picks certain ages and sexes, swelling only the working-age male bars.
A baby boom 30 years ago
A baby boom would enlarge both sexes equally.
questions.note: Migration distorts pyramids in the working ages.
questions.x: A population pyramid is a chart showing how many males and females are in each age group. Here only one spot is off: far more men than women aged 20 to 45, while children and older people are balanced. Migration is selective, meaning certain kinds of people are much more likely to move. Labor migrants to Gulf states are mostly working-age men, so their arrival swells just those bars. Sex-selective abortion would skew the youngest ages, and those are balanced.

questions.q: A farmer wants to emigrate for higher wages but cannot afford the journey and is barred by the destination country's visa rules. In Lee's model of migration, these barriers are:
o: Push factors
Push factors drive people out of the origin; these barriers block leaving instead.
Intervening obstacles
Correct: barriers between origin and destination that make moving harder.
Pull factors
Pull factors attract migrants to the destination.
Preventive checks
This is a Malthusian term for behaviors that lower births.
questions.note: Lee: push, pull, intervening obstacles, personal factors.
questions.x: Everett Lee's model of migration has four parts: push factors at the origin that make people want to leave, pull factors at the destination that attract them, intervening obstacles between the two places, and personal factors. The farmer wants higher wages, which is the pull. But the cost of the trip and the visa rules stand in the way. Those barriers sit between origin and destination, so they're intervening obstacles. They aren't push factors, because push factors encourage leaving instead of blocking it.

questions.q: A cross-national study finds that countries with higher GDP per capita have lower fertility. A researcher concludes that rising income causes fertility to fall. The strongest criticism is that:
o: The sample includes too many countries
More countries make a cross-national analysis stronger, not weaker.
Fertility cannot be measured across countries
Total fertility rate is routinely compared across countries.
Confounders such as urbanization and women's education may drive both
Correct: correlational data can't rule out third variables that drive both.
GDP and fertility are positively correlated
The study found a negative correlation, not a positive one.
questions.x: This study compares countries at one point in time (cross-sectional data), so it can show a correlation but not a cause. A confounder is a third variable that drives both things. Urbanization, women's education and access to contraception can all raise income and lower fertility at the same time. Any of these could create the link even if income itself had no direct effect. Including more countries would make the analysis stronger, so sample size isn't the problem.

questions.q: Interviews show that residents who stayed in a gentrifying neighborhood enjoyed new parks and lower crime yet felt they no longer belonged as familiar shops and churches closed. Researchers would call this:
o: Cultural displacement
Correct: residents lose their sense of place even without moving.
Physical displacement
These residents stayed in the neighborhood.
Assimilation
They aren't choosing to adopt a dominant culture.
Relative deprivation
That's feeling worse off than others, which can spark protest; it isn't about losing place.
questions.x: Gentrification is when wealthier people move into a poorer neighborhood, raising prices and changing it. It can displace residents in two ways. Physical displacement is being pushed to move out. Cultural displacement is staying put but losing your sense of belonging, as the shops, churches and social ties of your community disappear. These residents stayed and even got some benefits, like parks and less crime, but they no longer felt at home. That's cultural displacement.

questions.q: National surveys report very different percentages of 'gay, lesbian or bisexual' people depending on whether they ask about identity, sexual behavior or attraction. The best explanation is that:
o: Sexual orientation cannot be studied scientifically
Different results call for careful definitions, not giving up on research.
Respondents always answer randomly
Differences that line up with question type aren't random.
Sexual orientation changes daily for most people
Orientation is generally stable; the gaps come from what's being measured.
Identity, behavior and attraction overlap but are not identical
Correct: some people report same-sex attraction or behavior without an LGB identity.
questions.x: Sexual orientation has several parts. Identity is how you label yourself. Behavior is who you actually have sex with. Attraction is who you're drawn to. These usually line up, but not always. Someone might feel same-sex attraction or have same-sex partners without calling themselves gay, lesbian or bisexual. So a survey asking about identity will get a different percentage than one asking about attraction. That's a measurement difference. It doesn't mean orientation is unstable or can't be studied.

questions.q: A country has growing manufacturing and exports some industrial goods, but still relies on foreign investment and buys raw materials cheaply from poorer nations. In world systems theory, it is best classified as:
o: Core
Core nations control investment and don't depend on foreign capital like this.
Semi-periphery
Correct: it's exploited by the core while it exploits the periphery.
Periphery
Periphery nations mainly export raw materials and have little industry.
External area
External areas sit outside the world economy entirely.
questions.x: World systems theory, from Immanuel Wallerstein, sorts countries by their place in the global economy. Core countries are rich, industrial and hold the capital. Periphery countries are poor and mostly supply raw materials and cheap labor. The semi-periphery sits in between: it has growing industry, but it still depends on money from the core, and it buys cheap raw materials from the periphery. This country is exploited by the core while it takes advantage of the periphery, so it's semi-periphery.

questions.q: A newly emerging respiratory virus is detected on five continents within weeks of its first identified case. Which feature of globalization most directly explains this speed?
o: High volume of international air travel
Correct: global air travel moves infected people across continents within hours.
Rising fertility in low-income countries
Birth rates don't decide how fast a germ crosses continents.
Urban gentrification
Change within a neighborhood doesn't explain spread between continents.
Cultural homogenization
Shared culture doesn't physically carry germs.
questions.x: Globalization is the growing connection between countries through trade, travel, media and communication. The piece that matters for a virus is fast transportation, especially international air travel. An infected traveler can cross an ocean in less than a day, so a new respiratory virus can show up on five continents within weeks. Cultural homogenization, meaning cultures becoming more alike, is part of globalization too, but shared tastes and media don't physically carry germs anywhere.

questions.q: A campaign encourages individuals to reduce their meat consumption by one meal per week, without seeking legal or institutional change. Using Aberle's typology, this is a(n):
o: Redemptive movement
Redemptive movements want a total, radical change in individuals.
Alternative movement
Correct: it asks individuals for a small change in behavior.
Reform movement
Reform movements target limited change in society or laws.
Revolutionary movement
Revolutionary movements want radical change in society.
questions.note: Aberle: alternative (limited, individual), redemptive (radical, individual), reform (limited, society), revolutionary (radical, society).
questions.x: David Aberle sorted social movements with two questions. Who does it want to change: individuals or society? And how much: a little (limited) or a lot (radical)? That gives four types. Alternative is individuals and limited. Redemptive is individuals and radical. Reform is society and limited. Revolutionary is society and radical. Asking people to skip meat at one meal a week, with no push for new laws, targets individuals and asks for a small change, so it's an alternative movement.

questions.q: Factory workers whose wages are rising join a protest movement after learning that workers in a neighboring region earn far more. Which theory best explains their participation?
o: Resource mobilization theory
That theory focuses on resources and organization, not on feeling deprived.
Relative deprivation theory
Correct: discontent comes from comparing yourself with others or with expectations.
Malthusian theory
Malthusian theory is about population and food.
Rational choice theory of fertility
Fertility decisions have nothing to do with joining a protest.
questions.x: Relative deprivation theory says people get discontented from comparing themselves with others, or with what they expected, not from how bad things are in absolute terms. These workers' wages are going up. But once they learn that workers next door earn far more, they feel shortchanged, and that feeling pulls them into protest. Resource mobilization theory is the tempting wrong answer. It explains how movements succeed, using money, leaders and organization, not where the grievance comes from.

questions.q: Two movements with equally intense public grievances are compared. One gains funding, trained leaders, and media contacts and wins policy changes; the other does not. Which theory is best supported?
o: Resource mobilization theory
Correct: success depends on resources and organization, not grievance alone.
Relative deprivation theory
Grievances were equal, so feeling deprived can't explain the different outcomes.
Mass society theory
That theory says socially isolated people get drawn into movements.
Value-added theory of crowds
This theory centers on strain and triggering events, not resources.
questions.x: Resource mobilization theory says grievances are common, so what decides whether a movement succeeds is its resources: money, trained leaders, organization and media access. This question is a neat test. Both movements were equally upset, so the grievance can't explain why only one won. The difference is that the winner had funding, leaders and media contacts. Relative deprivation theory explains why discontent arises, so it can't explain different results when the discontent is equal.

questions.q: A grassroots movement opens a national headquarters, hires paid staff and develops formal procedures. In the life cycle of social movements, this stage is:
o: Emergence
Emergence is the early stage of widespread but unorganized discontent.
Coalescence
Coalescence is when discontent gets focused and leaders appear, before things get formal.
Bureaucratization
Correct: the movement becomes a formal organization with staff and rules.
Decline
Decline is when the movement weakens or ends.
questions.note: Stages: emergence → coalescence → bureaucratization → decline.
questions.x: A common model gives social movements four stages. Emergence is widespread unhappiness with no organization yet. Coalescence is when that unhappiness gets focused, leaders step up and a strategy forms. Bureaucratization is when the movement becomes a formal organization, with offices, paid staff and set procedures. Decline is when it fades, wins, fails or gets absorbed. A national headquarters, hired staff and formal procedures mean bureaucratization. Coalescence is tempting, but it comes before the offices and rules.

questions.q: Many residents want cleaner air but stay home from protests, expecting to benefit from any regulations others win. This is called the:
o: Free rider problem
Correct: people enjoy the shared gains without putting in any effort.
Bystander effect
The bystander effect is failing to help in an emergency when others are around.
Social loafing
Social loafing is slacking inside a working group, not staying out entirely.
Groupthink
Groupthink is poor decision-making from pressure to agree.
questions.x: This is the free-rider problem. Clean air is a collective good: everyone breathes it, whether or not they helped win it. A free rider enjoys that benefit without putting in time or effort. If many residents think, 'Others will protest and I'll still get cleaner air,' the movement struggles to get enough people out. Social loafing is the tempting wrong answer, since both involve low effort. But social loafing is slacking while you're part of a group task, and these residents never join at all.

questions.q: A study finds that civil rights protests grew fastest in periods when sympathetic politicians gained office and the state's ability to repress protest weakened. This finding best supports:
o: Political process theory
Correct: political openings shape when movements rise and win.
Relative deprivation theory
The pattern follows political openings, not changes in feeling deprived.
Malthusian theory
Population and food supply aren't involved.
Modernization theory
Modernization theory is about how nations develop.
questions.x: Political process theory says movements grow and succeed when the political system opens a door for them. Openings include sympathetic officials taking office, powerful people splitting, and the state becoming less able to crack down. In this study, protest grew fastest exactly when those openings appeared. Relative deprivation theory would expect protest to rise when people feel more deprived compared with others, but the study measured political openings, not changes in that feeling.

questions.q: Country X and Country Y both have crude birth rates of 20 per 1,000, but X has a total fertility rate of 1.8 and Y has 3.0. The best explanation is that Country X:
o: Has more children per woman
Its TFR is lower, so women there have fewer children.
Has higher infant mortality
Infant mortality doesn't explain a lower TFR alongside an equal crude birth rate.
Has a much older age structure
An older population would lower its crude birth rate.
Has a larger share of women in their reproductive years
Correct: lots of women of childbearing age push the crude rate up even with few children each.
questions.note: TFR removes age structure; crude rates do not.
questions.x: Two different measures are at work. The crude birth rate (CBR) is births per 1,000 people in the whole population, so it depends on how many women of childbearing age there are. The total fertility rate (TFR) is the average number of children each woman has, and it isn't affected by age structure. Both countries have a CBR of 20, but women in X have fewer children (1.8 vs. 3.0). The only way X keeps up is by having a bigger share of women in their childbearing years.

questions.q: A study finds a large Black–white gap in hypertension that shrinks substantially after adjusting for neighborhood poverty, chronic stress and access to care. Which conclusion is best supported?
o: The disparity is caused mainly by genetic differences between races
The adjustment points to social causes, not genetic ones.
Social and structural conditions account for much of the disparity
Correct: the gap narrows when social factors are accounted for.
Race has no relationship with hypertension
A gap was clearly found before the adjustment.
Access to care is the only cause of the disparity
Several factors were adjusted together, so no single one can be singled out.
questions.x: A health disparity is a difference in health between groups. Adjusting, or controlling, for a factor means statistically removing its effect to see what's left. Here the Black–white gap in high blood pressure shrank a lot once poverty, chronic stress and access to care were accounted for. So those social and structural conditions explain much of the gap. That points away from genetic explanations. And because the three factors were adjusted together, you can't say access to care alone is the cause.

questions.q: Rural villages in a developing country now consist mostly of children, women and older adults, while cities have a surplus of young men. This pattern best demonstrates that:
o: Fertility is higher in cities than in villages
Rural fertility is usually higher, and births wouldn't create a male surplus in cities.
Mortality is higher among rural men
Rural deaths wouldn't explain extra young men in the cities.
Migration affects only the destination population
The villages changed too, so the origin was affected as well.
Migration is selective by age and sex
Correct: young men moved in larger numbers, reshaping both villages and cities.
questions.x: Migration is selective, meaning some kinds of people are much more likely to move than others. Migrants tend to be young adults, and in many places men are more likely to leave home for work. When young men head to the cities, the villages are left with mostly children, women and older adults, and the cities end up with extra young men. So migration reshapes the age and sex makeup of both places: the one people leave and the one they go to.
